en: The Sutra on the Causes and Effects of Past and Present, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove together with the bhikṣus.
In the early morning, these bhikṣus donned their robes and took up their alms bowls to enter the city for alms.

Having returned to their quarters and finished eating, they rinsed their mouths and washed; each then gathered up his robe and bowl and assembled in the lecture hall, all desiring to discuss together their past causes and conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine ear which transcends the world, heard the voices of the bhikṣus as they were conversing.
He immediately rose from his seat, went to the lecture hall, and sat among the assembly.
He asked the bhikṣus:
"Gathered together as you are, what Dharma do you wish to discuss?
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having finished our meal and completed our washing and rinsing, we have gathered here together, each desiring to hear you speak of past causes and conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Those of you who wish to hear the past causes and conditions, listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well; I shall now speak for your sake.”
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!

In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was at that time a rishi named Śrīmati who purely cultivated the brahma-faring and sought the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Desiring to accomplish this great wisdom, he delighted in dwelling within birth and death, traversing throughout the five destinies."
When one body dies and decays, one receives another body; thus, births and deaths are immeasurable.
It is like taking all the grasses and trees in the world, cutting them into tally-sticks to count one's past bodies—one could never reach the end of them.
The period from the beginning to the end of heaven and earth is called one kalpa; yet the cycles of their formation and destruction across such kalpas are beyond calculation or description.

It is for this reason that, moved by compassion for all living beings who are mired in delusion and craving, sinking into the ocean of suffering, he gives rise to a heart of mercy, desiring to deliver and rescue them.
Furthermore, he formed this thought:
"Now these sentient beings are submerged in birth and death and cannot emerge on their own;

it is entirely due to greed, hatred, and delusion, and because they delight in and are attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. I shall resolutely sever this sickness of theirs."
"Though he may be born in various realms of existence, he does not forget this mindfulness.

Toward all sentient beings, he maintains equanimity toward both enemies and kin; he gathers the poor through giving, those who violate precepts through upholding the precepts, the angry through patience, the indolent through diligence, the distracted through meditative concentration, and the ignorant through wisdom.
Thus, throughout the long night, he benefits sentient beings and serves as a refuge for all."
He reverently made offerings to all Tathāgatas, delighted in hearing the Dharma, and also expounded it for others.
He constantly provided the four requisites to the Saṃgha, and he respected and protected the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. Such practices as these were beyond counting.
"At that time there was a king named Dīpaṃkara;
the city was named Tāmbapannī.
The people of that country had a lifespan of eighty thousand years; they were peaceful, secure, prosperous, and exceedingly flourishing, possessing all their desires at will, just like the devas."

At that time, the king of that country ruled the world with the True Dharma; he did not oppress the people, nor were there the sufferings of execution or flogging, for he regarded all his subjects as if they were his only son.
At that time, King Dīpaprabha had just given birth to a crown prince who was peerlessly handsome and majestic, fully endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
On the day of his birth, all four directions were filled with light, such that the sun, moon, pearls, and fire were no longer needed.
Seeing that the Prince possessed such auspicious omens, the King immediately summoned his ministers to assemble for consultation, saying:
"The Prince has manifested such extraordinary wonders upon his birth; what name should we give to this Prince?"
The ministers replied,
"The Prince should be named Pūrvaprabha.
They then summoned a physiognomist to examine his marks.
The physiognomist replied:
"Observing the Prince now, if he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning King who governs the four continents;
if he leaves the home life, he will become a Honored One among gods and humans, attaining *sarvajñā*."
When the king, the queen, and the ladies of the inner palace heard the words of the physiognomist, they conceived a deep affection for this prince;
he was likewise venerated, honored, respected, and praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
At that time, the Prince was in the inner palace, expounding various teachings for his consorts and court ladies.
When the Prince reached the age of twenty-nine thousand years, he renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning King and petitioned his parents, seeking to leave the household life;
yet, even after three such requests, they still did not grant him permission.
The Crown Prince, out of compassion and with the resolve to rescue and deliver others, endured minor transgressions in order to achieve great harmony.

He immediately went to the mountains and forests, beneath the trees, where he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and diligently practiced austerities for six thousand years until he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of the devas, humans, and the eight classes of beings, he turns the wheel of Dharma;
this wheel is subtle and wondrous, such that no one in all the worlds—whether devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās—is able to turn it.
He taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; the benefits he brought about were beyond measure.

At that time, the father king, his queen, and the ladies of the inner palace, hearing that Prince Samantaprabha had attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, were filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
At that time, the ministers, the people of the realm, the brahmins, and others, hearing that the Crown Prince had attained the Way, each thought to themselves:

"The Crown Prince Samantaprabha has renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, left the household life to cultivate the Way, and attained Perfect Enlightenment;
we too should now leave the household life."
Having formed this thought, they all went to the place where the Buddha Samantaprabha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha immediately observed their minds and, according to their causes and conditions, preached the Dharma for them;
four thousand great ministers and brahmins attained the state of Arhat.

The people within the kingdom and the other assemblies from the four directions who had gathered there numbered eighty thousand, and they too attained the patience of non-attachment (*anupādāya-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, together with eighty-four thousand arhats, went to that realm to travel about and teach.

Upon hearing this, the father king was filled with great joy; he immediately issued a decree throughout the kingdom to level and repair the roads, sprinkle the ground with fragrant water, hang silken banners, precious victory banners, and canopies, and scatter various famous flowers. Thus adorned, the area extended for twelve *yojanas*.
Furthermore, he beat the drums and proclaimed throughout the kingdom that anyone possessing flowers must not sell them privately, but must deliver them all to the King;
he also commanded the people that none were to make offerings to the Buddha before him.
He then dispatched his ministers, accompanied by musicians, burning incense and scattering flowers, to go and invite the Tathāgata Samantaraśmi.
"At that time, while the Seer Suprabuddha was in the mountains, he experienced five extraordinary dreams:
first, he dreamed of lying upon the great ocean;
second, he dreamed of using Mount Sumeru as a pillow."
Third, he dreams that all sentient beings in the great ocean enter within his body;
fourth, he dreams that he holds the sun in his hand;
fifth, he dreams that he holds the moon in his hand.
Having had this dream, he immediately awoke in great alarm and thought to himself:
"This dream of mine is not of minor significance; whom should I ask about it?"
"It would be appropriate to enter the city and consult the wise.
Having formed this thought, he donned a deerskin garment, took a water flask, a staff, and a parasol in his hands, and proceeded into the city.
On the way, he passed by a dwelling place of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas), where there were five hundred men, with one serving as their leader.
The Wise One thought to himself:
"I shall now question him about my dream, and thereby observe the practices he cultivates.
He then joined the others in discussing the principles of the Way, refuting their heterodox views.
Then the five hundred men immediately yielded, seeking to become his disciples; they conceived deep reverence for Sāṃkṛtyāyana and each offered him a single silver coin as a gift.
Furthermore, there were five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners who, upon seeing that Sudhi’s eloquence was brilliant and his intellect keen, also gave rise to sympathetic joy.
At that time, those non-Buddhists deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Now the Tathāgata Samantaprabha has appeared in the world."

Upon hearing these words, the seer Suprabuddha’s hair stood on end throughout his body; his heart was filled with great joy, and he leaped for immeasurable delight. He then took his leave of the non-Buddhist practitioners and departed.
The non-Buddhists asked,
"Where does the Master intend to go? He replied:
"I shall now go to the presence of the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa, wishing to offer him worship.
The non-Buddhist replied,
"If you, Master, will go, I wish to follow you with joy."
Sudhana replied, "I now have karmic conditions to attend to; it is fitting that I should go on ahead.
At that time, Sudhana took five hundred silver coins and departed along the road.
The assembly of various non-Buddhists, filled with grief, longing, and distress, took their leave and returned home.

When Sudhana arrived before him, he saw the king’s household members leveling the roads, sprinkling the ground with scented water, and arranging banners, streamers, and canopies in manifold adornments.
Even if one were to ask,
"For what cause and condition do you perform this deed?
the royal official would reply:
"A Buddha has appeared in the world, named Samantaprabha; now King Dīpaprabha has invited him to enter the city, which is why we are busily adorning the roads."
Sudhana then asked that traveler again,
"Do you know where there are various famous flowers? He replied:
"O Daoist! King Dīpaṃkara has beaten the drums and issued a proclamation throughout the realm: 'No one shall sell fragrant flowers; they must all be surrendered to the king.
Having heard this, Sudhana was deeply distressed, yet his resolve did not waver as he continued to search diligently for the source of the flowers.
Suddenly, he encountered a maidservant of the royal household who was secretly carrying seven stalks of blue lotuses past him. Fearing the king's decree, she hid them inside a jar.
Moved by the sincerity of Sudhana, the lotuses miraculously leaped out of the jar. Seeing this from afar, Sudhana immediately called out after her, saying, "Sister, please stop!"
"Would you sell this flower?
Upon hearing this, the maidservant was greatly startled and thought to herself:
"I have hidden these flowers very carefully; who is this man that has seen my flowers and seeks to purchase them?"
Looking at the jar, he indeed saw flowers emerging; struck with a sense of wonder, he replied:
"O man! These blue lotuses are to be sent to the palace to be offered to the Buddha; they cannot be given to you."
Sudhana said again,
"Please hire these five stalks for five hundred silver coins.
The maidservant felt suspicious and thought to herself:
"These flowers are worth no more than a few coins, yet this man now seeks to buy five stalks for five hundred silver pieces.
He then asked him, "What do you intend to do with these flowers?"

Sudhana replied, "There is currently a Tathāgata who has appeared in the world; Great King Dīpāṃkara has invited him to enter the city, and that is why I require these flowers, wishing to offer them as an act of worship."
"Sister, you should know that the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are difficult to encounter; they appear only once in a great while, like the udumbara flower.
The maidservant asked again, "In making offerings to the Tathāgata, what do you seek?"
Sudhi replied, "It is because I wish to accomplish all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and deliver immeasurable suffering sentient beings.
At that time, having heard these words, the maidservant thought to herself:
"This man here has a handsome and upright countenance; though he wears only a deerskin garment that barely covers his body, he is so sincere as to disregard wealth and jewels."
She then said to him:
"I shall now give these flowers to you; I pray that in every successive birth I may always be your wife. Sudhana replied:
"I practice the holy life (brahmacarya) seeking the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); I cannot consent to the conditions of birth and death.
The maidservant then said, "If you do not comply with this wish of mine, you shall not obtain the flowers."
Sudhana said again:
"If you are determined not to give me the flowers, I shall grant your wish.

I am fond of practicing generosity and do not oppose the desires of others; if someone were to come to me begging for my head, eyes, marrow, or brain, or even for my wife and children, do not create obstacles that would destroy my resolve to give."
The maidservant replied, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"I respectfully accept your command.

Now, as I am a woman of meager strength, I am unable to come forward; I beg to entrust these two flowers to be offered to the Buddha. May I never lose this vow in every lifetime, and may we never be parted, whether in fortune or in misfortune. Please keep this in your heart and let the Buddha know of it."

At that time, King Lamp-Illumination, together with his sons, his various officials and attendants, and the brahmins, took fine incense, flowers, and various ritual implements and went out to welcome the Tathāgata Universal Radiance; all the people of the kingdom likewise followed along.
At that time, the five hundred disciples of Suṃati said to one another:

"Today the king, along with all his ministers and subjects, have all gone to the place where the Buddha Prabhāsa resides; our teacher must also have departed by now, so we ought to go there to pay our respects."
Having spoken these words, they immediately set out together.
Before they had traveled far on the road, they encountered Śrīmat; as teacher and disciple met, their joy was immeasurable, and they proceeded together to the abode of the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa.

Seeing King Diptarāja, who had already arrived before the Buddha, receive the honor of being the very first to offer worship and prostration, the others followed in this same order until they reached the great ministers; each of them also paid their respects and scattered famous flowers, all of which fell upon the ground.

At that time, when the multitude had finished their offerings, Śrīmat (Good Wisdom), together with his five hundred disciples, gazed intently upon the countenance of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs of excellence. Furthermore, desiring to rescue and deliver all suffering sentient beings and wishing to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he immediately scattered five stalks [of flowers]; these all remained suspended in mid-air, transforming into flower pedestals.
He later scattered two more stalks, which likewise stayed in the air, flanking the Buddha on both sides.

At that time, the king and his retinue, all the subjects and citizens, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, seeing this marvel, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, with unimpeded wisdom, praised Sudhiya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"

By practicing this conduct, after the passage of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At the time when Suvijñāpta received his prediction of enlightenment, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans scattered various exquisite flowers, filling the void of space, and made this vow:
"When Suvijñāpta attains the Way of the Buddha in the future, we all wish to become his retinue."
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaraśmi immediately bestowed upon them this prediction:
"You shall all be born in that land.
When the Tathāgata had finished granting these predictions, he still saw the Well-Aware One (Suṣmṛta) wearing the topknot of a seer and clad in a deer-skin garment.
The Tathāgata, wishing to cause him to cast off this attire and deportment, immediately transformed the ground into muddy mire.
When Śrīmati saw that the Buddha was about to travel by this path and the ground was turbid and wet, he thought to himself:
"How can He, whose feet possess the thousand-spoked wheel mark, tread upon this and pass over it?"
He immediately removed his deerskin garment and spread it upon the ground; as this was insufficient to cover the mud, he further untied his hair and covered it with that as well.
The Tathāgata then stepped across it and passed over. Thereupon, he made a prediction, saying:
"In the future, when you attain Buddhahood, you shall deliver all devas and humans in the five turbidities of an evil age without regarding it as difficult; you shall surely be just like me."
At that time, having heard this prediction, Suprabuddha was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain his happiness.

Immediately, he realized the emptiness of all phenomena and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). His body ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground, and he praised the Buddha in verse:
"Now I behold the Guide of the World, Who has caused me to open the eye of wisdom;”
For my sake, you have preached the Dharma of purity, Causing me to depart from and abandon all attachments.
Now that I have encountered the Honored One of Gods and Men, I have attained the state of non-arising;
May I obtain the fruit in the future, Just as the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings has.

At that time, having spoken these verses of praise, Sudhana descended from the air, approached the Buddha, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will grant permission for my renunciation of the household life."
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha replied,
"Excellent! Welcome, Bhikṣu."
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

At that time, there were two poor old men, each accompanied by a hundred of their kinsmen; beholding the Buddha’s excellent marks and his majestic, radiant virtue, they lamented their own poverty, having nothing with which to make offerings.

At that time, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for their sincere hearts, immediately transformed the ground before them so that various weeds and filth grew there; he caused the two poor men to see the ground as impure, so that they would give rise to a heart of joy and proceed to sprinkle it with water and sweep it clean.
The Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa bestowed upon them this prediction:
"After the passage of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, when Śākyamuni Buddha appears in the world, you shall at that time become his foremost śrāvaka disciples."

At that time, after the Tathāgata Samantaraśmi had bestowed this prediction upon the poor man, he entered the city of Tāpāsī surrounded by eighty-four thousand bhikṣus, King Dīpaprabha, the brahmin, and all the ministers and subjects, who followed him in front and behind.

At that time, King Lamp-Illumination and his retinue provided the four types of offerings to the Tathāgata Universal Radiance and eighty-four thousand bhikṣus for forty thousand years. The king then abdicated the throne and entrusted it to his son;

together with his retinue and the retinues of his consorts—each numbering eighty-four thousand people—they all followed the Buddha-dharma, left the household life to practice the Way, and attained dhāraṇīs and the samādhis of all dharmas.

The bhikṣu Sudhi also followed the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, receiving the king’s offerings for forty thousand years; he attained profound samādhis within all dharmas and transformed and taught sentient beings beyond measure.
At that time, the bhikṣu Suprajñāta addressed the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In days past, while I was in the deep mountains, I had five extraordinary dreams: [text continues]"
First, he dreamed that he was lying upon the great ocean;
second, he dreamed that he had the Mount Sumeru as his pillow;
third, he dreamed that all sentient beings within the ocean entered into the interior of his own body.
"Fourth, I dreamed that I held the sun in my hand;
fifth, I dreamed that I held the moon in my hand.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the significance of these dreams for me."
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha replied: "Excellent!
If you wish to know the meaning of this dream, I shall explain it for you."
To dream of lying upon the great ocean means that your body is immediately within the great ocean of birth and death;
to dream of using Mount Sumeru as a pillow signifies emerging from birth and death to attain the state of parinirvāṇa;
and to dream of all sentient beings entering your body within the great ocean signifies that you shall serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings within the great ocean of birth and death.
Dreaming of holding the sun in one's hand signifies that the light of wisdom universally illumines the dharma-realm;

dreaming of holding the moon in one's hand signifies that, through the wisdom of skillful means, one enters into birth and death to transform and guide sentient beings with the Dharma of coolness, causing them to leave behind the heat of affliction.
"This dream has a causal significance; it is a sign that you will attain Buddhahood in the future.
Having heard this, Sudhana was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
"At that time, after a short while had passed, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha entered parinirvāṇa.

The bhikṣu Suprajña upheld the True Dharma for twenty thousand years, teaching and transforming sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; those whom he benefited were beyond calculation."

At that time, the bhikṣu Suprajña, having passed away there, was immediately reborn above as one of the Four Heavenly Kings; he transformed the hosts of devas through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

When his lifespan in that heaven had ended, he descended to be born among humans as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world with the seven treasures complete:

first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the minister-treasure of the treasury; and seventh, the minister-treasure of the military.
He is endowed with a full thousand sons, all of whom are brave and robust, capable of subduing enemies;
he governs by means of the True Dharma, free from all sorrow and affliction;
and he constantly transforms the people through the ten virtuous deeds.
At the end of this life, he will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the lord of that heaven;
when his life there ends, he will descend to be born as a Cakravartin King;
and at the conclusion of that lifespan, he will eventually be born as high as the seventh Brahmā Heaven.
Above, he became a celestial king, and below, a sagely sovereign, each for thirty-six cycles;
in the intervals between these, he was sometimes a rishi, sometimes one of the six heretical teachers, sometimes a brahmin, or sometimes a minor king;
such manifestations were beyond counting.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprabuddha had fulfilled his meritorious practices and attained the rank of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi). Being in the stage of 'one birth remaining' (ekajātipratibaddha) and close to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), he was born in the Tuṣita Heaven under the name Śubhavyūha.
As the lord of the devas, he taught the conduct of one remaining in his final birth;
he also manifested various bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions, preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs."
When the destined time for enlightenment is approaching and one is to become a Buddha in this very moment, one should immediately contemplate five matters:
first, contemplating whether sentient beings are mature or immature;
second, contemplating whether the time has arrived or not yet arrived.
Third, he contemplates which of all lands is situated in the center;
fourth, he contemplates which of all lineages is noble and flourishing;
fifth, he contemplates past causes and conditions to determine who is most truly fit to be his parents.
Having observed these five matters, he reflected to himself:

"Now, all these sentient beings are those whom I have brought to maturity since my first aspiration; they are capable of receiving the pure and wondrous Dharma. Within this trichiliocosm, this Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, is the most central location. Among all lineages, the Śākyas are foremost—the descendants of the Noble Kings of the Ikṣvāku clan.
Observing the past causes and conditions of King Śuddhodana, his wife and husband are truly worthy to be my parents."

Furthermore, he observed that Lady Māyā’s lifespan was short; having conceived the Prince and carried him for a full ten months, the Prince was born, and seven days after his birth, his mother passed away.
"Having made this contemplation, he further reflected:

'If I were to descend to birth immediately now, I would not be able to bring extensive benefit to the multitudes of devas and humans. Therefore, while still in the celestial palace, I shall manifest five kinds of signs to cause all the sons of gods to become fully aware that the time has come for the Bodhisattva to descend and attain Buddhahood:
first, the Bodhisattva’s eyes will blink;'"
Second, the flowers upon his head wither;
third, his robes become covered in dust and grime;
fourth, sweat breaks out from beneath his arms.
"Fifth, he takes no pleasure in his original seat.

At that time, when the assembly of devas suddenly saw these extraordinary signs in the Bodhisattva, their hearts were filled with great terror; blood flowed from all the pores of their bodies like rain, and they said to one another:
"The Bodhisattva will not long remain with us."
"At that time, the Bodhisattva further manifested five auspicious omens:
first, he emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm;
second, the great earth shook with eighteen signs of movement, and Mount Sumeru, the waters of the ocean, and the palaces of all the devas were all violently shaken."
Third, the palaces and abodes of all Māras were shrouded in darkness and no longer appeared;
fourth, the sun, moon, and stars lost their radiance;
fifth, the bodies of the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all trembled, unable to restrain themselves.

At that time, the devas of Tuṣita, seeing that the Bodhisattva’s body already bore the five signs and further beholding five other rare and wondrous events, all gathered together and went to where the Bodhisattva was. Prostrating with their heads at his feet, they addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"Today we have seen these various signs, and our entire bodies tremble such that we cannot find peace; we only pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for this.
The Bodhisattva then replied to the devas:
"O sons of good family!..."
"You should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent; before long, I shall leave this celestial palace and be born in Jambudvīpa.
When the gods heard these words, they wailed and wept with grief; their hearts were filled with great distress, and blood appeared over their entire bodies like *palaśa* flowers.
Some could no longer find joy in their original seats.
Some cast aside their ornaments;
some rolled about on the ground in confusion and distress;
and some deeply sighed over impermanence and suffering.
At that time, a certain devaputra spoke this verse:
“The Bodhisattva was here, Opening for us the eye of Dharma;
Now he has departed far from us, Like the blind separated from their guide.”
Furthermore, it is like one wishing to cross a river who suddenly loses their bridge or boat;
or like an infant child who has lost its compassionate mother.
We are just the same, having lost our place of refuge.
Now drifting in the stream of birth and death, there is no means of escape at all.
Throughout the long night, we have been pierced by the arrows of ignorance;
having lost the Great King of Physicians, who shall now deliver us?
"Lying prostrate upon the bed of ignorance, long submerged in the sea of craving and desire,
we have forever severed ourselves from the instructions of the Honored One and see no prospect of transcendence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, seeing the sons of the gods weeping in grief and distress, and hearing them recite these verses of longing and attachment, addressed them with a voice of compassion, saying:
"Good son! Among all ordinary people who take birth, there are none who do not die;
where there is the union of affection and love, there must inevitably be separation."
From the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the Avīci Hell below, among all sentient beings therein, there are none who are not scorched by the great fire of impermanence.
Therefore, you should not harbor attachment toward me alone;
for now, both I and you have not yet escaped the blazing fires of birth and death, and even all beings—whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble—are without exception unable to avoid them.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; This is the nature of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, Cessation is bliss."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the devaputras:
"This verse was spoken by all the Buddhas of the past; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are exactly like this.

You should not give rise to grief or distress now. For immeasurable kalpas within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), I have now reached this final birth alone; before long, I shall attain liberation from all conditioned phenomena."

"You should know this: now is the time to deliver and liberate sentient beings; I shall descend to be born in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, within the Śākya clan—the descendants of Ikṣvāku—in the house of King Śuddhodana."

I was born there, distanced myself from my parents, renounced my wife and children as well as the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, left the household life to study the Way, diligently practiced asceticism, subdued the hostilities of Māra, attained all-knowledge, and turned the wheel of Dharma.

It cannot be turned back by any in the world—whether devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās—and it likewise follows the modes of practice of all past Buddhas. It brings vast benefit to all classes of devas and humans, erects the great banner of Dharma, topples the banners of Māra, dries up the ocean of afflictions, purifies the Eightfold Noble Path, and seals the minds of sentient beings with the seals of all dharmas;
it establishes great assemblies of Dharma and invites all devas and humans.
"At that time, you all shall likewise be present together in this assembly to partake of and receive the food of the Dharma;
for this reason, you should not feel sorrow or distress.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"In no long time from now, I shall descend into Jambudvīpa,
at Kapilavastu, to be born in the palace of King Śuddhodana;
there I shall bid farewell to my parents and kinsmen, and renounce the sovereignty of a universal monarch."
Leaving home to practice the Way, one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One raises the banner of the True Dharma, dries up the ocean of afflictions (*kleśa*),
closes the gates to the evil realms, and purely opens the Eightfold Noble Path.
"Benefiting all devas and humans extensively, their number is beyond calculation;
for this reason, you should not give rise to sorrow or distress.
At that time, the Bodhisattva emitted light from every pore of his body.
When the sons of the gods heard the Bodhisattva’s words and again beheld his body emitting great radiance, they leaped for joy and were freed from all sorrow and suffering.
Each thought to himself:
"The Bodhisattva shall soon attain perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, observing that the hour for descending into the womb had arrived, immediately mounted a six-tusked white elephant and departed from Tuṣita Heaven.
Immeasurable devas performed various musical performances, burned diverse sublime incenses, and scattered celestial, wondrous flowers;
they followed the Bodhisattva, filling the void of space, emitting great radiance that universally illuminated the ten directions.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, at the time when the morning star appeared, he descended into his mother’s womb.

At that moment, Lady Māyā, in the transition between sleep and waking, saw the Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant, soaring through the void and entering her right side; his form appeared externally as if within lapis lazuli.
The lady’s body was peaceful and joyful, as if she had consumed ambrosia; looking upon herself, she felt like the sun and moon shining, her heart filled with great joy and immeasurable exultation.
Having seen these signs, he suddenly awakened and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder; he immediately went to King Śuddhodana and addressed him, saying:
"Just now, at the moment I awoke from sleep, as if in a dream, I beheld various auspicious omens that were most extraordinary."
The king then replied:
"I too have just now seen a great radiance, and I also perceive that your countenance is extraordinary. You should explain for me the auspicious signs you have witnessed."
The lady then recounted the aforementioned events in detail, expressing them in verse:
"I saw one riding a white elephant, Pure and bright as the sun and moon;
Śakra, Brahmā, and the hosts of devas All held precious banners."
Incense was burned and celestial flowers scattered, while various musical instruments played;
filling the void of space, they descended surrounding him.
He entered my right side as if dwelling within lapis lazuli.
"Now that these have appeared before Your Majesty, what kind of auspicious omen is this?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having witnessed these various auspicious signs of Lady Māyā, was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;
he immediately dispatched messengers to invite the Brahmins skilled in interpreting signs, honoring them with exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of food and drink.
Having completed the offerings, he showed the lady his right side and described the auspicious signs, saying to the brahmin:
"I pray that you will examine them; what extraordinary portents are there?"
At that time, the Brahmin immediately performed a divination and said:
"Great King! The auspicious marks of the Crown Prince conceived by the Queen are such that they cannot be described in full; I shall now speak of them briefly for Your Majesty."

"Great King, you should know that this child in the womb of your consort will surely bring glory to the Śākya clan. At the time of his descent from the womb, he emitted a great radiance, and the devas, Śakra, and Brahmā attended upon him and surrounded him. These signs are certainly the auspicious omens of Perfect Enlightenment. If he does not leave the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents; the seven treasures will come to him spontaneously, and he will be endowed with a thousand sons."
When the king heard these words of the brahmin, he was deeply moved by a sense of joy and leaped for immeasurable delight;
he immediately provided for this brahmin with gold, silver, various jewels, elephants, horses, chariots, and even entire villages and towns.
At that time, Lady Māyā also offered her handmaidens and precious jewels as gifts.
Since the Bodhisattva had been dwelling within her womb, Lady Māyā had practiced the six pāramitās daily;
celestial food and drink arrived spontaneously, and she no longer took pleasure in human flavors.

The trichiliocosm was perpetually and universally bright; even those dark and obscure regions within its boundaries, which the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not illuminate, were all rendered brilliantly clear.
The sentient beings therein were each able to see one another and said to each other:
"How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here?

When the Bodhisattva descended into the womb, the trichiliocosm shook in eighteen ways, and a cool, fragrant wind arose from the four quarters; all those suffering from illness were completely healed, and greed, hatred, and delusion were all stilled.
At that time, in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, there was a devaputra who thought to himself:

"The Bodhisattva has already been born into the palace of King Śuddhodana; I, too, shall descend to be born among humans. When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, may I be among his foremost retinue, making offerings and listening to the Dharma."
Having formed this thought, he immediately descended to be born in the city of Rājagṛha into the Candana and Bahula families of the Moon-clan (Candragotra).
Furthermore, another son of heaven was born into a royal family in Śrāvastī;
yet another son of heaven was born into a royal family in the kingdom of Thūlakoṭṭhaka.
Furthermore, there were sons of gods born into the royal family of the Vatsa kingdom;
there were sons of gods born into the royal family of the Vaira kingdom;
and there were sons of gods born into the royal family of the Lāḍha kingdom.
Furthermore, there were sons of gods born into royal families in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā;
there were sons of gods born into royal families in the kingdom of Kurava;
and there were sons of gods born into brahmin families.
Furthermore, there were sons of gods born into the families of kṣatriyas, gṛhapatis, vaiśyas, and śūdras;
additionally, five hundred sons of gods were born into the Śākya clan.
Such hosts of sons of gods, numbering ninety-nine billion in total, descended to be born in the human realm.
Furthermore, those who descended from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations down to the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings were beyond calculation.
Moreover, celestial kings of the Form Realm, together with their retinues, also descended to be born as rishis.
"While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he encountered no obstruction, nor did he cause his mother any suffering or affliction.
In the early morning, while still within his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva expounded various teachings for the devas of the form realm."
At the time of midday, he also preached the various dharmas for the devas of the desire realm;
at the hour of late afternoon, he again preached the Dharma for the various spirits and ghosts.
During the three watches of the night, it was likewise so, bringing to maturity and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
While the Bodhisattva was in the womb, there were ladies-in-waiting and court women who came to pay their respects and make offerings;
some even came and made this vow, saying:
"May you become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s heart was not filled with joy.
Or again, there were those who came and made this vow, saying:
"May he attain all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā).
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with great joy.

While the Bodhisattva dwelt in the womb for nearly ten months, all his limbs, joints, and primary and secondary marks were fully perfected; likewise, his mother’s faculties became tranquil and settled, and she took delight in gardens and groves, finding no pleasure in clamor or bustle.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"The Queen is pregnant and her months are nearly full, yet no signs of childbirth are to be seen."
While he was forming this thought, he encountered a messenger sent by the queen to inform the king:
"I now wish to go out to the gardens for sightseeing.
Upon hearing this, the king felt even greater joy.
He immediately issued orders to those outside to thoroughly sweep and sprinkle the Lumbinī Garden, further commanding that various exquisite flowers and fruits be planted;
he had all the flowing springs and bathing pools made pristine,
and the railings and stairways adorned with the seven precious gems.
Emerald-green mandarin ducks, phoenixes, peacocks, and swans—birds of diverse species—gathered there, warbling together;
silken banners and canopies were suspended, flowers were scattered, and incense was burned, while various musical performances were enacted, resembling the Joyful Garden of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Furthermore, he issued an edict that all places along the route to be traversed should be purified and adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
He also commanded that one hundred thousand carriages made of the seven precious gems be prepared, each carriage being exquisitely carved and most magnificent;
furthermore, he ordered outside that the fourfold army—consisting of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—be readied.

Furthermore, he selected eighty-four thousand ladies-in-waiting from the inner palace—women of upright and beautiful countenance, neither too old nor too young, of harmonious temperament, and possessed of intelligence and clarity—to serve as attendants to Queen Māyā.

Furthermore, he selected eighty-four thousand beautiful young maidens, adorned them with exquisite necklaces and ornaments for the body, and having taken fragrant flowers, they went first to dwell in that Lumbinī Garden.
The King further commanded his various ministers and officials that all those who were to accompany the Lady should serve as her attendants.
Thereupon, the Lady ascended a precious palanquin and, together with her officials and court ladies, proceeded toward the Lumbinī Garden, escorted by a procession of attendants before and behind her.
At that time, there were also the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, who likewise followed along, filling the void of space.
"When the lady had entered the garden, her faculties became tranquil;

when ten months had been fulfilled, on the eighth day of the second month at the time of sunrise, the lady saw in that garden a great tree named Aśoka, its flowers fresh and fragrant, its branches and leaves spreading out in extreme abundance."
He immediately raised his right hand, intending to pull and pluck it;
at that moment, the Bodhisattva gradually emerged from the right side [of the tree].
Then, beneath the tree, seven stalks of lotuses made of the seven precious gems also sprang forth, as large as chariot wheels.
The Bodhisattva then descended onto a lotus flower; without anyone to support him, he walked seven paces by himself, raised his right hand, and uttered a lion’s roar:
"Among all devas and humans, I am the most honored and the most supreme; my immeasurable births and deaths have now ended; this life shall benefit all devas and humans."
Having spoken these words, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately received the Prince’s body with celestial silks and placed him upon a jeweled table;
Śakra Devānām-Indra held a precious parasol in his hand, while Mahābrahmā held a white fly-whisk, standing in attendance at his left and right.

The Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda, from within the void, emitted pure water—one warm and one cool—and sprinkled it upon the Prince’s body. His body was the color of gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and he radiated great light that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm. The eight classes of devas and nāgas likewise performed celestial music in the air, singing hymns and offering praises; they burned various famous incenses and scattered myriad exquisite flowers. Furthermore, they rained down celestial robes and necklaces, falling in profusion and beyond counting.

"At that time, after Queen Māyā had given birth to the Crown Prince, her body was peaceful and joyful, free from all suffering and affliction; filled with rapture and exultation, she stayed beneath a tree. Suddenly, four wells spontaneously appeared before and behind her, their waters fragrant, pure, and endowed with the eight meritorious qualities."
At that time, Lady Māyā, together with her retinue, washed and cleansed themselves at will according to their desires.
Furthermore, various yakṣa kings all surrounded them, guarding the Prince and Lady Māyā.
At that time, from the people of Jambudvīpa up to the gods of Akaniṣṭha, though they were free from worldly joy and pleasure, all likewise rejoiced and praised him, saying:
"The Omniscient One has now appeared in the world; immeasurable sentient beings shall all receive benefit.
We pray only that you may swiftly realize the path of Perfect Enlightenment, turn the Wheel of Dharma, and extensively deliver all sentient beings."
Only the Māra King alone harbored sorrow and distress, finding no peace upon his throne.
At that moment, thirty-four auspicious omens were manifested:
first, all the worlds of the ten directions became brilliantly illuminated;
Second, the trichiliocosm shook in eighteen ways, and its mounds and hollows became level;
third, all withered trees flourished once more, and within the realm, extraordinary trees grew spontaneously;
fourth, gardens produced various sweet fruits.
Fifth, precious lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels sprang up from the dry land;
sixth, hidden treasures beneath the earth all spontaneously emerged;
seventh, the various treasuries of precious jewels emitted a great radiance.
Eighth, the exquisite garments of the devas descended spontaneously;
ninth, the myriad rivers and ten thousand streams became tranquil and clear;
tenth, the winds ceased and the clouds dispersed, leaving the sky bright and pure.
Eleventh, fragrant breezes blew from the four directions, and a fine rain moistened the earth, settling the flying dust;
twelfth, all diseases within the kingdom were completely healed;
thirteenth, throughout the palaces and dwellings of the realm there was no place that was not brilliantly illuminated, such that the light of lamps and candles was no longer required.
Fourteenth, the sun, moon, and stars stood still and ceased their movement;
fifteenth, the constellation Viśākhā descended to appear among humans to await the birth of the Prince;
sixteenth, the Brahma Kings held white jeweled parasols, arranged in rows to cover the palace above.
Seventeenth, the masters of the sages from the eight directions came to present precious offerings;
eighteenth, celestial food of a hundred flavors appeared spontaneously before him;
nineteenth, countless jeweled vases were filled with various nectars.
Twentieth: divine, exquisite chariots arrived, laden with treasures;
twenty-first: countless white elephant cubs stood in rows before the palace, each bearing a lotus flower upon its head;
twenty-second: the celestial deep-blue horse-treasure appeared spontaneously.
Twenty-third: Five hundred white lion kings emerged from the Snowy Mountains, their malevolent intentions stilled and their hearts filled with joy, standing in a row at the city gates;
twenty-fourth: celestial maidens performed exquisite music in the midst of the void;
twenty-fifth: celestial jade maidens holding peacock-feather whisks appeared upon the palace walls.
Twenty-sixth: celestial jade maidens each held golden vases filled with fragrant liquid, standing in formation in mid-air;
twenty-seventh: the devas sang hymns in praise of the Prince’s virtues;
twenty-eighth: the hells were stilled, and their agonizing pains ceased to manifest.
Twenty-ninth: venomous insects remain hidden, and malevolent birds develop benevolent hearts;
thirtieth: all those with evil vows simultaneously give rise to compassion; thirty-first:
within the kingdom, all pregnant women shall give birth to sons, and those afflicted by the hundred ailments shall find natural recovery.
Thirty-second: All the tree spirits transformed themselves into human forms and came to pay homage and attend upon him;
thirty-third: the various other kings each brought famous treasures and came together to submit as subjects;
thirty-fourth: among all humans and devas, there were none who spoke at inappropriate times.
At that time, the assembly of court ladies, seeing these auspicious omens, were filled with great joy and said to one another:
"Since such signs of excellence have appeared at the birth of the Prince, we pray only that he may live long, free from all illness and suffering, and that he may not cause us great distress."
Having spoken these words, he wrapped the Prince in fine celestial cotton and carried him to the Lady’s side.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings followed respectfully through the air;
Śakra-devānām-indra held a parasol over him.
There were twenty-eight great ghost-king deities stationed at the four corners of the grove, guarding and protecting it.
At that time, a maidservant of blue-clad dress, who was wise and discerning, returned from the Lumbinī Garden to the palace and, arriving before King Śuddhodana, addressed him, saying:
"The majesty and virtue of the Great King increase ever further."
Lady Māyā had already given birth to the Prince, whose countenance was upright and handsome, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Upon descending onto a lotus flower, he walked seven paces by himself, raised his right hand, and uttered a lion’s roar:
“Among all devas and humans, I am the most honored and supreme; immeasurable births and deaths are ended this day; this life shall benefit all devas and humans.”
"There were such extraordinary and marvelous events as these, which cannot be recounted in full.

When King Śuddhodana heard these words spoken by the maidservant, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately removed the necklaces from his own person and bestowed them upon her.

"At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately arrayed his fourfold army and was surrounded by his retinue, together with one hundred million members of the Śākya clan who escorted him from front and rear as he entered the Lumbinī Garden. He saw that the garden was entirely filled with devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
Upon reaching the Queen’s side, he beheld the Prince’s body, its marks and signs exceptionally sublime; he leaped for joy like the great surging waves of rivers and seas.
Yet, fearing that his life might be short, he was also seized by trepidation, remaining as immovable as Sumeru, the King of Mountains."
When the great earth shakes, these mountains then move.

King Śuddhodana, whose natural disposition has always been tranquil and who was formerly free from both joy and sorrow, now experiences both joy and fear upon seeing the Prince, just as this mountain does.
Lady Māyā was by nature harmonious and gentle.
Having given birth to the Crown Prince, she beheld various auspicious omens, and her gentleness increased all the more.
At that time, King Śuddhodana joined his palms in reverence and paid homage to the various celestial deities.

He took the Prince in his arms and placed him upon a seven-jeweled elephant carriage, followed by the various ministers, the ladies of the inner palace, and the devas in the sky, who played all manner of musical instruments as they entered the city.
At that time, King Śuddhodana and the Śākya clansmen, not yet recognizing the Triple Gem, took the Prince and went to the temple of the gods.
Once the Prince had entered, the images of Brahmā all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Prince’s feet, and said to the King:
"Great King!..."
You should know, O Great King, that this Prince is now the most honored among gods and humans;
the celestial deities of the void all pay him homage and respect.
“Do you not see this? Why have you now come here to pay homage to me?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, the Śākya clansmen, and the officials both internal and external, having heard and seen this, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The Crown Prince was then brought forth from the celestial temple and returned to the inner palace.
At that very time, the Śākya clansmen also gave birth on the same day to five hundred sons;
furthermore, in the king’s stables, an elephant gave birth to a white cub.
Horses gave birth to white foals;
oxen and sheep likewise gave birth to five-colored lambs and calves;
of such kinds as these, there were five hundred of each.
The maidservants of the royal household likewise gave birth to five hundred male slaves.
At that time, five hundred hidden treasuries spontaneously emerged within the palace;
each hidden treasury was surrounded by seven precious jewel-treasuries.
Furthermore, there were merchants from various great kingdoms who had gathered treasures from the sea and returned to the kingdom of Kapilavastu;
those merchants each brought rare and wondrous jewels and came to present them to the king.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the merchants:
"Did you enter the sea to gather various precious treasures, and were all your endeavors auspicious and free from suffering?"
"And as for his companions, have none been left behind? Those merchants replied, "Great King!"
"The roads we have traveled are exceedingly peaceful and secure.
Upon hearing these words, the king was greatly delighted and immediately dispatched messengers to invite the various brahmins.
When the assembly of brahmins had all gathered, he prepared various offerings—giving them elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, as well as fields, houses, and servants.
Having completed the offerings, he took the Prince out in his arms and addressed the brahmins, saying:
"What name should be given to the Prince?"
The Brahmins then deliberated together and replied to the king:
"When the prince was born, all the treasuries were opened and revealed; every auspicious sign was of a most propitious nature. For this reason, the prince should be named Sarvārthasiddha."
When these words were spoken, the devas of the void immediately struck celestial drums, burned incense, scattered flowers, and cried out:
"Excellent! All the devas and humans then proclaimed:
“Sarvārthasiddha. At that time, eight kings also gave birth to crown princes on this same day as King Śuddhodana.
Those various kings each harbored great joy:
"I have now given birth to a son with many extraordinary signs," they said, yet they did not know these were the auspicious omens of Sarvārthasiddha.
They gathered all the brahmins together, each of whom composed a favorable name for the prince; the prince of Rājagṛha was named Bimbisāra.
The crown prince of Śrāvastī was named Bimbisāra;
the crown prince of Thūlakoṭṭhaka was named Kṛkī;
the crown prince of Vatsa was named Udayana.
The crown prince of the country of Vārāṇasī was named Udrāyaṇa;
the crown prince of the country of Roruka was named Jitaprabha;
the crown prince of the country of Takṣaśilā was named Puṣkarasārin.
The crown prince of the kingdom of Kuru was named Kuru.

At that time, King Śuddhodana issued a general command to his ministers, ordering them to seek out one who was intelligent, widely learned, possessed of wisdom, skilled in the interpretation of signs and omens, and well-known to the people of the world.
Upon hearing this, the ministers searched for him in all four directions.
At that time, the king immediately constructed a great palace within his rear garden, adorned with seven precious jewels, complete with windows, lattices, and balustrades.

At that time, the ministers learned that five hundred Brahmins, who were wise and skilled in reading signs and had witnessed various auspicious omens, were about to come to visit the king; it was then that the king dispatched a messenger, who arrived with great speed.
The ministers addressed the king, saying,
"The Brahmin Jñānanimitta has now arrived. Upon hearing this,
the king was filled with joy and immediately commanded him to be invited forward to enter the palace hall to sit, providing him with various offerings.
That brahmin then addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard, Great King, that a crown prince has been born to you, endowed with various marks and extraordinary auspicious signs; I pray that we may all be granted the opportunity to behold him."
At that time, the king immediately ordered the prince to be carried out.
Upon seeing the prince’s auspicious marks and majestic dignity, the brahmins marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The king then asked:
"Now, regarding the examination of the Crown Prince, what are his marks?
The Brahmin replied, "All sentient beings desire their children to be excellent; [but such excellence is rare]."
"Great King!
The prince now born is a most rare and extraordinary being; do not give rise to sorrow or fear.
He then spoke again, saying:
"O Great King! Although it is said that the newborn prince is the son of Your Majesty, he is in fact the eye of the world for both gods and humans.
The king asked again:
"How do you know this?

the Brahmin replied, "I observe that the Prince’s physical radiance is like that of pure gold; he possesses the various marks and signs of excellence, which are exceedingly bright and pure. If he should renounce the world, he will attain all-encompassing wisdom."
If he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King who governs the four continents; just as among rivers and streams the ocean is foremost,
among all mountains Mount Sumeru is most excellent,
and among all luminous bodies the sun is unsurpassed.
"Everything is cool and refreshing, with nothing but the bright moon;
among gods, humans, and the world, the Prince is the most honored.
Upon hearing these words, the King’s heart was filled with great joy, and he was freed from all anxiety and fear.
That brahmin spoke again to the king, saying:
"There is a brahman-seer named Asita who possesses the five supernatural powers; he resides on Mount Gandhamādana and is able to resolve all of Your Majesty's doubts."
After the brahmins had spoken these words, they took their leave and departed.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"The seer Asita dwells on Mount Gandhamādana; the path is perilous and impassable, beyond the reach of ordinary men. By what means should I invite him to come here?"
At the very moment the King gave rise to this thought, the seer Asita perceived his intention from afar;
furthermore, having previously observed various auspicious omens, he deeply understood that the Bodhisattva had manifested birth for the sake of destroying birth-and-death.
By means of his supernormal powers, he soared through the air and arrived at the gate of the royal palace.
At that time, the gatekeeper entered and addressed the king, saying, "The seer Asita has come through the air and is now outside the gate.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and immediately commanded him to be ushered forward; the king went to the gate himself to welcome him.
Having seen the seer, he paid him respectful homage and immediately asked:
"Venerable sir, you have arrived and remained at the gate without proceeding further; was it because the gatekeeper did not permit you to enter?"
The seer replied, "There is no such thing as a guest who comes to visit without first being announced.
The king then followed him into the inner palace, respectfully invited him to be seated, and greeted him, saying:
"Venerable One!
Are the four great elements always in a state of peaceful harmony? The seer replied:
"By the grace of the Great King, we have fortunately attained peace and happiness.
Then King Śuddhodana said to the Rishi:
"Venerable One!"

Since you have been able to descend here today, our clan shall now flourish greatly; from this day forward, we shall daily attain auspiciousness. Have you come here for the purpose of passing through?

The seer replied: "While I was on Mount Gandhamādana, I beheld great radiance and various extraordinary signs; furthermore, I knew what was in Your Majesty’s mind. For these reasons, I have come here.
By means of my supernatural power, I traveled through the air and heard the higher devas say:"
"The Prince will surely attain all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā) and deliver gods and humans;

furthermore, the Prince was born from the right side [of his mother], descended onto a lotus flower made of the seven treasures, and walked seven steps, raising his right hand and roaring like a lion:
'Among gods and humans, I am the most honored and the most supreme.'"
"The immeasurable cycle of birth and death has now come to an end; this life has benefited all devas and humans.
Furthermore, the various devas surrounded him with reverence, having heard of such a great and extraordinary event:
"How wonderful, Great King!"
"You ought to rejoice!
Is it possible for you to see the Prince now?
He then led the seer to the Prince's location; the King and Queen took the Prince out in their arms and wished to pay homage to the seer.
Then that seer stopped the king, saying, "This one is the most honored among gods, humans, and the three realms; how can you command him to pay homage to me?
Thereupon, the seer rose, joined his palms, and prostrated at the feet of the Prince.
The King and the Queen said to the rishi,
"We pray that you, Venerable One, will act as the prince's counselor. The rishi replied:
"Excellent," he said,
and immediately performed a divination of the signs; having fully observed the signs,
he suddenly wept with grief, unable to restrain himself.

When the king and his consort saw that seer weeping with streaming tears, their entire bodies trembled with fear and they were overcome with great distress, like a small boat tossed by mighty waves. They asked the seer:
"Our son was born with all auspicious signs; what inauspiciousness is there that you should weep?"
At that time, the rishi sighed and replied, "Great King!
The Prince is endowed with all the marks of excellence; there is nothing inauspicious about him."
The king asked again:
"I pray that you will further examine the prince for me: does he possess the marks of long life?
Will he attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and rule over the four quarters of the world?"

My years are now advanced, and I wish to entrust the entire kingdom to him; I intend to retire to the mountain forests to leave the household life and study the Way, for this alone is my heart's aspiration.
"Venerable One, do you observe that this is the fruit of certainty?
At that time, the seer again replied to the king, saying: "Great King!"
The Crown Prince was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man: first, the soles of his feet were level and even, like the bottom of a casket;
second, the soles of his feet were marked with wheels with a thousand spokes and all their characteristics complete;
third, the fingers and toes of his hands and feet were long and surpassed those of other men.
Fourth, his hands and feet are supple and superior to other parts of the body;
fifth, his heels are broad, complete, full, and beautiful;
sixth, his toes are joined by a web-like membrane, which is superior to that of other men.
Seventh, the insteps are high, level, and well-proportioned to the heels;
eighth, the calves are slender and beautiful like those of the eneya deer king;
ninth, standing upright, his hands reach down to touch his knees.
Tenth, his male organ is concealed within a sheath, like that of a horse king or an elephant king;
eleventh, his body is equal in height and breadth, like a nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, from each and every pore grows a single hair, which is blue-black, soft, and curls to the right.
Thirteenth, his body hairs point upward, are blue-black and soft, and curl to the right;
fourteenth, he has a golden complexion, so subtle and exquisite that it surpasses Jambūnada gold;
fifteenth, the radiance of his body extends one fathom in every direction.
Sixteenth, his skin is thin, fine, and smooth, such that it does not retain dust or grime, nor do mosquitoes or gadflies alight upon it;

seventeenth, he has seven rounded parts—the two soles of the feet, the two palms of the hands, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—all of which are full, and the marks of the letters are distinct and clear;
eighteenth, the areas beneath both armpits are as full as mani-jewels.
Nineteenth, his body is like that of a lion;
twentieth, his body is broad, upright, and straight;
twenty-first, his shoulders are rounded and well-formed.
Twenty-second: he has forty teeth in his mouth;
twenty-third: his teeth are white, even, closely set, and deeply rooted;
twenty-fourth: his four canine teeth are the whitest and largest.
Twenty-fifth, his jawbones are square like those of a lion;
twenty-sixth, he attains the supreme flavor among all flavors, with two streams of saliva flowing from the two parts of his throat;
twenty-seventh, his tongue is large, soft, and thin, capable of covering his face up to his ears and the hairline.
Twenty-eighth, his Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like the song of the kalaviṅka bird;
twenty-ninth, the color of his eyes is like refined gold;
thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king.
Thirty-first, the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows is soft and white like tūla-cotton;
thirty-second, the crown of his head is formed as a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
Possessing a body endowed with such marks and signs, if he remains a householder, at the age of twenty-nine, he becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin-rāja).
If one leaves the household life, they will achieve all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and extensively deliver gods and humans.

However, Prince, you shall certainly study the Way and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; before long, you shall turn the pure wheel of Dharma, benefiting gods and humans and opening the eye of the world.

"I am now one hundred and twenty years of age; my life will soon come to an end, and I shall be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought. There, I shall not behold the arising of a Buddha nor hear the Dharma; for this reason, I grieve for myself."
He asked the seer again,
"Venerable sir, you previously stated that there were two possibilities:
first, that he would become a king;..."
"Secondly, you have already attained perfect enlightenment;
why do you now say that you will definitely realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
At that time, the seer said:

"Regarding the dharma of the marks of a self: if there is a sentient being who possesses the thirty-two marks, yet they appear in improper locations or are not clearly manifest, this person will surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
if the thirty-two marks all appear in their proper locations and are further clearly manifest, this person will surely attain all-encompassing wisdom."

"I observe that the various marks of the Great King’s son have all attained their proper place and are exceedingly distinct; therefore, I know with certainty that he will achieve perfect enlightenment.
Having spoken these words to the king, the seer took his leave and withdrew.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard the sage’s definitive words, was filled with sorrow and anxiety, fearing that the prince would renounce the world.

He immediately selected five hundred intelligent and wise young women of noble birth to serve as nurses to care for the prince. Among them, some provided breast milk, some held him in their arms, some bathed him, and some washed his clothes;
in this manner, they provided for the prince with every necessity in full abundance.
Furthermore, he separately constructed palaces for the three seasons—warm, cool, and cold—each located in a distinct place;
these palaces were all adorned with the seven treasures, and the clothing and ornaments provided were entirely suited to the season.
Fearing that the prince might abandon his home to study the Way, he ensured that the sound of the city gates opening and closing could be heard for forty li.

Furthermore, he selected five hundred courtesans who were of upright appearance—neither fat nor thin, neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark—and possessed great skill, each proficient in several arts. He adorned them all with famous jewels and necklaces; they were stationed in groups of one hundred, taking turns by rotation to provide guard duty.
Before his palace, rows of trees bearing sweet fruits were planted, their branches and leaves forming a lush canopy, while flowers and fruits grew in profusion.
There was also a bathing pool, pure and crystal clear, its banks carpeted with fragrant herbs and lotuses of various colors, which spread out in such abundance that they could not be counted.
Birds of various species, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were so radiant and beautiful that they delighted the eyes and minds of all; they flocked to please the Prince.

Seven days after the Prince’s birth, his mother passed away; because she had conceived the Prince through such great merit, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where she received its natural, spontaneous rewards.

The Prince knew for himself that his merit, fortune, and majestic dignity were such that no woman was capable of receiving his prostrations; therefore, at the end of his life, he entrusted himself to her and was born again through her.
At that time, the Prince’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, nursed him and raised him without any difference from a mother.
At that time, King Śuddhodana ordered the crafting of celestial crowns made of the seven treasures as well as necklaces and gave them to the Prince.

As the Prince gradually grew older, the King prepared for him carriages drawn by elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; indeed, there was no toy or object of enjoyment for a youth that was not provided to him.

At that time, all the people of the kingdom practiced benevolence and kindness; the five grains ripened in abundance, wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, and there were no thieves or bandits. All lived in happiness and security, which was entirely due to the power of the Prince’s merit and virtue.
At that time, the King also provided five hundred young male servants, such as Chandaka and others born of his own attendants, to serve the Prince.
When he reached the age of seven, the Father King thought to himself:
"The Prince has grown up; it is fitting that he be taught to write."
He sought out a wise Brahmin within the kingdom who was skilled in all arts and sciences, and invited him to come and instruct the prince.
At that time, there was a Brahmin named Bhadranī, who came with a retinue of five hundred Brahmins to accept the king's invitation.
He then addressed the brahmin, saying:
"I wish to request that you, Venerable One, serve as the preceptor for the crown prince;
would this be acceptable? The brahmin replied:
"You should teach the Prince according to what you know.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana built a great academy for the Prince, adorned with the seven treasures; its couches, mats, and study implements were made exceedingly exquisite and beautiful.
Having selected an auspicious day, he immediately entrusted the Prince to the Brahmins to be instructed.
At that time, the brahmin took the fundamental texts of forty-nine scripts and instructed him to read them.
When the Prince saw this, he asked his teacher,
"What kind of script is this?"
"In Jambudvīpa, how many kinds of books are there in total?
The teacher remained silent, not knowing how to answer. He asked again:
"What meaning does this single syllable 'A' have?
The Master remained silent once more and was unable to answer;
harboring shame within, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Prince's feet, and praised him, saying:

"When the Prince first took seven steps after his birth, he declared himself to be the most honored and supreme among gods and humans; these words were not false. We pray that you will explain for us how many kinds of scripts there are in Jambudvīpa."
The Prince replied:
"Within Jambudvīpa, there are the Brahmī script, the Khaḷu script, the Padma script, and so forth—sixty-four such varieties in total.

This letter 'A' is the sound of the Brahmā language; furthermore, its meaning is indestructible and it is the meaning of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path. Such meanings as these are immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, the brahmin was deeply filled with shame and remorse.
He returned to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"The Prince is the foremost teacher among gods and men; how could you wish for me to instruct him?

At that time, when the King, his father, heard the words of the brāhmaṇa, he felt redoubled joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He immediately provided the brāhmaṇa with lavish offerings and allowed him to go wherever he pleased.
In all arts and crafts, canonical texts and discourses, astronomy and geography, mathematics, archery, and charioteering, the Prince naturally mastered them all.

"At that time, when the Prince reached the age of ten, there were five hundred youths among the Śākyas who were all of the same age."
The Crown Prince’s younger cousins included Devadatta, next named Nanda, and next named Sundarananda;
some possessed thirty marks or thirty-one marks, while others, though possessing all thirty-two marks, had them indistinct.
Each was skilled in the arts and possessed great physical strength.
At that time, Devadatta and five hundred other youths, having heard that the Prince was proficient in all arts and his fame had spread throughout the ten directions, said to one another:
"Although the Prince is indeed clever and wise, and well-versed in writing and treatises, as far as physical strength and prowess are concerned, how could he surpass us!"

Desiring to compete with the Crown Prince in martial prowess, the King at that time sought out those within the kingdom who were skilled in archery and summoned them to instruct the prince. They immediately went to the rear garden, intending to shoot at an iron drum;
Devadatta and five hundred other youths also followed along.
Then the teacher immediately handed a small bow to the Prince; the Prince smiled and asked him, "You give this to me;
what do you wish for me to do with it?"
The master archer replied,
"I wish to have the Prince shoot this iron drum.
The Prince spoke again:
"This bow lacks strength; seek out seven more such bows and bring them here.
The master immediately handed them over, and the Prince took up the seven bows and, with a single arrow, shot through all seven iron drums.
Then that master archer went to the king and said: "Great King!
The Crown Prince himself knows the art of archery; with the power of a single arrow, he shot past seven drums, such that there is no one in Jambudvīpa who can equal him."
"How could I possibly act as his teacher?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these words, was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"My son is intelligent; he knows writing, treatises, and mathematics throughout the four distant quarters."
"Yet among the people of the four quarters, there is no one who knows his skill in archery.
He then commanded the Crown Prince, Devadatta, and five hundred other youths, and further beat the drums to proclaim throughout the realm:
"Seven days hence, Prince Sarvārthasiddha shall go to the rear garden to test his martial arts."
"Let all those among the people who possess courage and strength come here.
On the seventh day, Devadatta, together with sixty thousand followers, was the very first to leave the city.
At that time, there was a great elephant stationed at the city gate; all these military forces did not dare to advance.
Devadatta asked the people, "For what reason do you stay here and not move forward?"
The people replied, "There is a great elephant standing at the gate; the entire multitude fears it, and therefore none dare to go forward.
Having heard these words, Devadatta went alone to where the elephant was and struck its head with his hand, whereupon it immediately fell to the ground.
Thereupon, the multitude of troops passed through in succession.
At that time, Nanda, together with his retinue, also wished to leave the city; as the various troops advanced slowly and gradually, Nanda asked:
"For what reason are you walking so slowly?"
The people replied, "Devadatta struck an elephant with his fist and felled it at the city gate; because it is obstructing the path for travelers, we are delayed."
Nanda then immediately went to where the elephant was and, picking it up with his toe, tossed it to the side of the road;
countless crowds of people gathered together to watch.

At that time, the Prince, surrounded before and behind by a retinue of one hundred thousand, was just beginning to exit the city gate when he saw a crowd of people gathered by the roadside watching something.
He immediately asked them: "For what are all these people watching?"
The attendant replied, "Devadatta once struck an elephant with his bare hand and felled it at the city gate, obstructing the path for travelers;
Nanda followed him out and, using his toe, picked it up and threw it here. For this reason, all the passersby have gathered to look at it."
Thereupon, the Prince thought to himself:
