"Now is precisely the time to manifest my power.
The Prince then seized the elephant with his hand and hurled it outside the city; he then caught it again with his hand, ensuring that it was not injured.
The elephant regained consciousness once more, free from all pain and suffering.
At that time, the people marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with profound wonder.
"In this way, the Prince, along with Devadatta and Nanda, as well as the people from all four quarters, all gathered together in that garden."
At that time, that garden was adorned in various ways, with golden drums, silver drums, brass drums, and drums of copper and iron arranged in rows, seven of each kind.
At that time, Devadatta was the first to shoot, piercing through three golden drums;
next came Nanda, who likewise pierced through the three drums;
all the assembled multitude sighed in admiration.
At that time, the ministers said to the Crown Prince:
"Devadatta and Nanda have both already finished shooting; now it is the turn of the Crown Prince. We pray that the Crown Prince will shoot these drums."
When he had thus requested three times, the Prince said,
"Excellent! and spoke to him, saying:
"If I wish to shoot at all these drums, this bow is too weak; let us seek one that is stronger.
The ministers replied, "The Grandfather King possessed an excellent bow, which is now in the royal armory."
The Prince said, "Bring it here at once.

Once the bow had arrived, the Prince drew it and released a single arrow; it pierced through all the drums and then entered the pool, causing the spring water to gush forth, and furthermore, it passed right through the Great Iron Ring Mountains.
"At that time, Devadatta again engaged in a wrestling match with Nanda; as the two men were of equal strength, neither emerged victorious.
The Prince then stepped forward, grasped his two younger brothers with his hands, and threw them to the ground; yet, by the power of his compassion, he caused them no injury or pain."
At that time, the multitudes of people from the four quarters, having witnessed that the Prince possessed such power, cried out in a loud voice:
"The Prince of King Śuddhodana not only excels all men in wisdom, but his heroic strength is likewise peerless."
There was none who did not sigh in admiration and submit, increasing their reverence all the more.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately assembled his ministers and deliberated together, saying:

"The Prince is now grown to maturity; his wisdom, courage, and strength are all fully perfected. It is now appropriate that we should perform the consecration upon the Prince’s crown with the waters of the four great oceans."
Furthermore, he issued a decree to the other minor kings:
"On the eighth day of the second month, when the prince’s head is to be anointed, you must all assemble.
When the eighth day of the second month arrived, the various other kings, along with the rishis and brahmins, all gathered like clouds.
Silk banners and canopies were suspended; incense was burned and flowers scattered; bells were rung and drums beaten, while various musical performances were rendered.
Using vessels made of the seven precious gems to hold the waters of the four oceans, the assembly of rishis each took one upon their heads and presented it to the Brahmin;
in this manner, it proceeded until it reached all the ministers, who likewise took them upon their heads and passed them on to the king.

At that time, the king immediately performed the consecration upon the crown of the prince's head, entrusted him with the seals of the seven treasures, and beat the great drum, proclaiming in a loud voice:
"I now establish Sarvārthasiddha as the Crown Prince."
At that time, the devas of space, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others performed celestial music and, with one voice and in unison, praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
When the Crown Prince was installed in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, eight other kings likewise installed their own crown princes on that same day.
At that time, the Crown Prince requested the King’s permission to go out on a journey, and the King granted his consent immediately.
At that time, the king, together with the crown prince and his various ministers, preceded and followed him as he traveled along, inspecting the borders of the kingdom;
proceeding further on his way, he arrived at the site of the royal fields and rested there, sitting beneath a jambu tree to observe the farmers at their work.
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into an earthworm, which a crow then pecked at.
Having seen this, the Prince gave rise to a heart of compassion, thinking, "How pitiable are sentient beings, who devour one another! He then reflected:
"Having become detached from the craving of the desire realm, he thus attained up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, the sunlight was scorching and intense, yet the trees bent their branches so that their shade followed the Prince.
At that time, King Śuddhodana searched in all four directions, inquiring after and seeking the Prince;
those he questioned replied,
"The Prince is now beneath the Jambu tree."

At that time, the king, together with his ministers, proceeded to the place where the tree stood. Before they had yet arrived, they saw from afar the Prince sitting upright in contemplation; moreover, seeing the tree’s branches bending to shade his body, they were struck with profound wonder.
Then the king stepped forward, took the prince’s hand, and asked:
"For what reason are you now sitting here?
The prince replied:
"Beholding all sentient beings devouring one another, it is truly a matter of great pity.

Upon hearing these words, the king felt deep distress and anxiety; fearing that [the prince] might renounce the household life, he thought it best to arrange a marriage immediately to gladden his heart, and so he summoned him, saying:
"Let us return to the kingdom together."
The Prince replied, "I wish to stay here.
Upon hearing these words, the King thought to himself:
"What Āsita spoke in the past, the Prince now seems to be fulfilling according to his words.
The King then shed tears and called out repeatedly,
"Return to the kingdom!"
When the Prince saw that his father, the King, was thus [distressed], he immediately followed him back to his quarters.
Fearing that the Prince would fall into sorrow and find no joy in remaining at home, the King increased the number of courtesans to provide him with entertainment.
"At that time, when the Prince reached the age of seventeen, the King assembled his ministers and deliberated together, saying:
'The Prince is now grown; we ought to seek out a marriage for him.'"
The ministers replied:

"There is a Śākya brahmin named Mahānāma; he has a daughter named Yaśodharā, whose countenance is upright and beautiful, who is intelligent and wise, whose talents surpass those of others, and who is fully endowed with propriety and ritual decorum. Possessing such virtues, she is worthy to be the Prince's consort."
The king then replied, "If it is as you say,
I shall accept her. The king returned to his palace and immediately issued an order to the elderly women within the harem who were clever and wise:
"You should go to the house of the elder Mahānāma and observe his daughter: what is her appearance, demeanor, and conduct like?
You may stay there for a full seven days."
Having received the king’s command, he immediately went to the house of that elder and observed the girl closely for seven days.
Upon his return, he replied to the king:
"I have observed this girl; her features are upright and beautiful, and in her deportment and movements, there is no one who can equal her."
When the king heard these words, he was filled with great joy and immediately dispatched a messenger to say to Mahānāma:
"The prince has reached maturity, and I wish to take a consort for him."
The ministers all said, "Your daughter is virtuous and refined;
she is well-suited for this undertaking, and we now wish to request her hand.
Then Mahānāma replied to the king's messenger:
"Respectfully acknowledging the imperial decree," the King immediately ordered his ministers to select an auspicious day and dispatched ten thousand chariots to go and welcome him.
Once he had arrived at the palace, the full rites for the marriage of the Prince were performed; furthermore, the number of courtesans was increased, and they provided entertainment day and night.
At that time, the Prince was always with his consort—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—and they were never apart;
from the beginning, he had no worldly thoughts, but in the stillness of the night, he practiced meditative contemplation alone.
At that time, the king asked his court ladies every day,
"Are the Crown Prince and his consort drawing near to one another?
The ladies replied:
"I have not seen the Prince engage in the way of husband and wife.
When the King heard these words, he became sorrowful and unhappy; he increased the number of court ladies to entertain him, yet even as time passed, they still did not draw near.
At that time, the King harbored deep suspicions, fearing the Prince might be incapable of procreation.

At that time, having heard the singing of the court ladies and seeing the lush abundance of flowers and fruits in the gardens, as well as the cool clarity of the flowing springs, the Prince suddenly desired to go out for a stroll and sightseeing.
He immediately sent the ladies to inform the King, saying:
"I have been in the palace for a long time; I wish to go out briefly to play and enjoy myself in the gardens."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he thought to himself:
"The prince must have grown weary of living in the palace and performing the rites of husband and wife; that is why he has sought to depart for the gardens."
The King immediately granted his permission and commanded his ministers:
"Prepare the gardens and pavilions, and ensure that all roads along the route are made clean and pure.
The Prince then proceeded to the King's presence, prostrated himself at the King's feet in salutation, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, the king immediately commanded an old minister who was intelligent, wise, and skilled in eloquent speech to accompany the crown prince.

Then the prince, together with his various officials and attendants leading and following him, exited through the eastern gate of the city. When the people of the kingdom heard that the prince was departing, men and women filled the roads, and those who came to watch were as numerous as clouds.
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into an old man with white hair and a hunched back, leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps.
The Prince immediately asked his attendant, "Who is this person?"
The attendant replied, "This is an old man.
The Prince asked again:
"What is meant by 'old age'? He replied:

"This person was once an infant, a child, and a youth; yet these stages passed away without remaining. Eventually, the faculties matured, the form changed, and the complexion decayed. Food and drink were no longer digested, physical strength became depleted and feeble, and sitting or rising was an extreme hardship. With little life remaining, it is therefore called 'old age.'"
The Prince asked again:
"Is this person alone old, or is it so for all?"
The attendants replied,
"All things must indeed be thus.
When the Prince heard these words, he was overcome with great anguish and thought to himself:
"The sun and moon flow on, seasons change and years pass; old age arrives like a flash of lightning—how can this body be relied upon?
Though I am wealthy and noble, how could I alone escape it?"
"How can the people of the world not feel fear?
Having never since his birth taken pleasure in dwelling in the world, the Prince heard these words and felt an even deeper sense of weary detachment;
he immediately turned the chariot back, filled with sorrowful reflection and no joy.
When the king heard this, his heart was filled with anxious distress, fearing that the prince would renounce the world to study the Way;
he therefore increased the number of court dancers to entertain him.
At that time, after a short while had passed, the prince again requested the king’s permission to go on an excursion.
Upon hearing these words, the king felt anxiety arise in his heart and thought to himself:
"Previously, when the prince went out and encountered an old man, he was filled with sorrow and found no joy; how is it that now he seeks to go out once again?"
The King loved his crown prince and could not bear to go against his wishes, so he reluctantly complied;
he immediately assembled his ministers and deliberated with them, saying:
"Previously, when the crown prince went out through the eastern gate of the city, he encountered an old man and upon returning was immediately unhappy."
"Now he has again requested to go out for an excursion; I cannot refuse him, so I have granted his request.

The ministers replied, "We shall issue strict orders to all the officials outside to repair and clear the roads, to hang silk banners and canopies, to scatter flowers and burn incense, making everything magnificent and beautiful, and ensuring that no foul odors, impurities, or those who are old or sick remain by the roadside."

"At that time, outside each of the four gates of the city of Kapilavastu, there was a garden; with its trees, flowers, fruits, bathing pools, and pavilions, all were adorned in various ways, none differing from one another."
The king asked his ministers,
"Among the various gardens and parks outside, which one is the most excellent?
The ministers replied:
"The various gardens and pavilions outside are all equal and without difference, like the Garden of Joy in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The King further commanded, saying:
"The Prince went out previously by way of the eastern gate; [he shall now depart by the southern gate]."
"Now you may depart through the southern gate.
At that time, the Prince, escorted by a hundred officials, went out through the southern gate of the city.

Then a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested as a sick man, his body emaciated and his belly distended; he gasped and moaned, his bones protruding and his flesh withered away; his complexion was sallow and haggard, and his entire body trembled so violently that he could not support himself, leaning on the arms of two men who supported him under his armpits as he stood by the side of the road.
The Prince then asked,
"Who is this person? His attendants replied:
"This is a sick person.
The Prince asked again,
"What is meant by 'sickness'?"

He replied: "Generally speaking, what is called 'sickness' arises from indulgence in desires and immoderate eating and drinking, which causes the four elements to become unbalanced and transform into illness. One suffers pain in the hundred joints, physical strength becomes depleted and feeble, food and drink are taken sparingly, and sleep is restless. Although one possesses hands and body, they cannot move them by oneself; one must rely on the assistance of others before being able to sit or rise."
At that time, the Prince, with a heart of compassion, looked upon that sick man and felt sorrow arise within himself.
He further asked:
"Is this person alone like this?"
"Is it the same for all others? He replied, "Among all the people,
regardless of whether they are noble or humble, everyone equally suffers from this disease."
Having heard this, the Prince thought to himself:
"Such suffering of illness should universally afflict all; why then do people of the world indulge in pleasure without fear?"
Having formed this thought, he was deeply struck with terror; his body and mind trembled like the reflection of the moon in rippling water.
He said to his attendants:
"Such a body as this is a great mass of suffering, yet worldly people perversely give rise to joy within it; they are ignorant and without discernment, lacking the wisdom of awakening."
"Now why is it that you wish to go to that garden to wander, observe, and sport?
He then turned the chariot around and returned to the royal palace, where he sat and reflected, sorrowful and unhappy.
The king asked his attendants:
"Now that the prince has gone out, was there any joy for him?
The attendants replied:
"Upon first exiting through the southern gate, he encountered a sick man; because of this, he became disenchanted and immediately turned his chariot back.
When the King heard these words, his heart was filled with great sorrow and anxiety, fearing that [the prince] would leave the household life.
Then the king immediately questioned his ministers, saying:

"Previously, when the prince went out through the eastern gate of the city, he encountered an old man and became sorrowful and unhappy. Because of this matter, I commanded you all to thoroughly clean the roads so that no one who was old or sick would be by the side of the lanes. Why is it that now, as he goes out through the southern gate of the city, there is again a person with a disease?"
"Furthermore, we shall ensure that the Prince encounters and sees him.
The ministers replied:

"Recently, we received Your Majesty’s decree and strictly commanded our external officials not to allow any who are foul-smelling, impure, aged, or infirm to remain by the roadside. We have conducted mutual inspections and audits with no negligence; we do not know for what reason a sick person has suddenly appeared here—it is not our fault."
At that time, the king asked his attendants, saying:
"Did you all see where this sick man came from as he traveled along the road?
The attendants replied:
"Having no trace of his departure, we do not know where he has gone.

At that time, the king felt deep uncertainty regarding the prince and feared he might leave to study the Way; thus, he increased the number of court ladies to please him and further sought to cause him to develop a mind of attachment to the five desires.
"At that time, there was a son of a Brahmin named Udāyin, who was intelligent, wise, and possessed of great eloquence.
The king immediately invited him to enter the palace and spoke to him, saying:
'The prince now finds no pleasure in remaining in the world to experience the five desires; I fear that before long he will leave home to study the Way.'"
"You should become his companion and associate, and describe in detail the pleasures of the five worldly desires to move his heart and make him unwilling to leave the home life.
At that time, Udāyin immediately replied:
"The Prince is intelligent and peerless; the books and treatises he knows are all profound and vast, none of which I have ever heard before. How could I be asked to seduce him with such talk?"
It is like attempting to suspend Mount Sumeru with a lotus fiber; I am likewise unable to turn back the Prince’s mind.
Since Your Majesty has commanded me to be his friend, I must exhaust all that I know and see for his sake.
Then, having received the king’s command, Udāyin followed the Prince, never daring to leave him whether he was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
At that time, the king further selected various courtesans who were intelligent and wise, of upright countenance, skilled in song and dance, and capable of enchanting others;
adorned in various ways so that they were radiant and pleasing to the eye, he sent them all to attend upon the Prince.
"At that time, after a short while had passed, the Prince again requested the King’s permission to go on an excursion.
Upon hearing these words, the King thought to himself:

'Since Udāyin has become a close friend of the Prince, if he goes on this excursion, his state may improve even further than before, and he will no longer have the mind to weary of worldly pleasures and leave the household life.'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately granted permission.
The King then assembled his ministers and said to them all:
"The Prince now wishes to go out on an excursion again; I cannot bear to refuse him, so I have granted it once more."
Previously, when the Prince went out through the eastern and southern gates and encountered old age and sickness, he returned in constant sorrow;
now it is fitting that he be sent out through the western gate,
for I fear that upon his return he will again be unhappy.
However, Udāyin is his good friend; we hope that upon his return from his journey today, he will no longer act in such a manner.

You all must ensure that the roads, gardens, groves, and pavilions are well-maintained and kept in perfect order. Let the incense, flowers, banners, and canopies be many times more abundant than before, and do not allow anyone who is aged, infirm, or foul-smelling to remain by the roadside.
Having received the command, the minister immediately informed the outer officials to strictly prepare the roads as well as the gardens, making them twice as magnificent and beautiful as usual.
The king also first sent various exquisite courtesans to be stationed within those gardens;
furthermore, he issued a decree to Udāyin, saying:
"If there should be any inauspicious occurrence by the roadside, you may use skillful means to soothe their minds.
He further commanded his ministers to follow the Prince, instructing them all to keep watch and, should anything ill-omened appear, to drive it far away.

"At that time, the Prince, accompanied by Udāyin and a retinue of hundreds of officials, burned incense, scattered flowers, and performed various musical entertainments as he departed through the western gate of the city."
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven thought to himself:
"I shall first manifest old age and sickness at the two city gates so that the entire multitude may see them, causing King Śuddhodana to reprimand his attendants as well as the external officials."

"The Prince is now departing, and the King’s regulations are strict and severe. If I were to manifest my death now and everyone were to see it, it would increase the King’s wrath, and he would surely impose punishment and execution upon us, unjustly involving the innocent.
The events I have manifested today shall be seen by only two people—the Prince and Udāyin—so that the other officials and attendants do not suffer retribution."

Having formed this thought, he immediately descended and transformed himself into a dead man. Four men carried his bier, scattering various fragrant flowers over the corpse, while the entire household, both old and young, wailed and wept as they escorted him away.
At that time, the Prince and Udāyin were the only two who saw it.
The Prince asked, "What is this object?"
"And it was adorned upon with flowers and perfumes; furthermore, a multitude of people followed in a procession of wailing and lamentation.
At that time, because of the King’s command, Udāyin remained silent and did not answer.
When he had asked this three times, through the majestic spiritual power of the King of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven,
Udāyin unconsciously replied, “This is a dead man.
The Prince asked again:
"What is meant by death?

Udāyin replied, "That which is called death is when the 'sword-wind' dissolves the physical form and the conscious spirit departs; the four limbs and all the sense organs no longer possess any further cognition."

While this person was in the world, they were greedily attached to the five desires and cherished wealth; they labored and toiled in business, knowing only how to accumulate, yet failing to recognize impermanence.

Now, in a single moment, they have abandoned it all and died. Furthermore, though they were loved and cherished by their parents, relatives, and kin, after the end of life they become like grass and wood; their feelings of affection and aversion no longer have any connection.
"One who dies in such a manner is truly to be pitied.
Upon hearing this, the Prince’s heart trembled with great fear.
He then asked Udāyin:
"Is it only this person who dies,
or is it the same for all others? He then replied:
"All people of the world must be like this; there is no one, whether noble or base, who can escape it.
Having heard these words, the Prince—whose natural disposition was serene and difficult to disturb—could no longer remain at ease.
Then, in a low voice, he said to Udāyin:
"In this world there is even such suffering as death; how can one act with heedlessness therein, with a mind like wood or stone, knowing no fear?"
He immediately commanded his charioteer to turn the carriage back.
The charioteer replied, "We have already passed through two gates; to return midway before reaching the garden would cause the Great King to be deeply displeased and reprimand us."
"How could I dare to act like this again?
At that time, Udāyin said to the charioteer,
"According to what you have said, we should not return yet."
He then proceeded further until he reached that garden, where there were fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, and various musical performances were being given.

The many female dancers were so exquisite that they were no different from the celestial maidens of the devas; before the Prince, they vied with one another in song and dance, hoping to delight and move his heart with their graceful charms.

The Prince’s mind was settled and could not be moved; he remained within the garden, resting in the shade of the trees. Having dismissed his attendants, he sat upright in contemplation, recollecting how in the past, beneath the Jambu tree, he had distanced himself from the realm of desire and attained even the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, Udāyin went to where the Prince was and spoke these words:
"The Great King has commanded me to become a friend to the Prince so that, should there be gain or loss, we may mutually enlighten one another. The essentials of the way of friendship are threefold:
first, to immediately offer counsel and admonition whenever a fault is observed;..."
Second, upon seeing good deeds, one should deeply give rise to sympathetic joy;
third, when others are in distress or hardship, one must not abandon them.
I now offer these sincere words, hoping you will not reproach me.
"From the kings of antiquity down to those of the present day, all have first experienced the pleasures of the five desires before renouncing the world.
Why then, Prince, do you forever sever these ties and disregard them?"
Furthermore, as humans live in this world, they ought to follow the ways of men; there has never been one who abandoned their kingdom to study the Way.
We only pray that the Prince will accept the five desires and produce offspring, so that the royal lineage shall not be severed.
At that time, the Prince replied to him, saying: "It is indeed as you have said;
however, it is not because I wish to abandon my kingdom that I am thus, nor do I say that there is no pleasure in the five desires.
It is because I fear the suffering of old age, sickness, and birth-and-death that I dare not feel attachment to the five desires."
Regarding what you have just said— that the kings of antiquity first experienced the five desires and only then left the household life— where are those kings now?
Because of craving and desire, one may be born in the hells, or among the hungry ghosts, or as an animal, or among humans and devas;
because there is such suffering of cyclic existence, I wish only to be free from the dharma of birth, death, old age, and sickness.
"How can you now expect me to accept it?
At that time, although Udāyin exhausted his eloquence and persuasive skill to urge and encourage the Prince, he could not turn him back; he then withdrew from his seat and returned to his quarters.

The Prince then commanded his carriage to be prepared for the return to the palace; the assembly of female entertainers and Udāyin were filled with sorrow and grief, their faces contorted with distress like those of people who have recently lost beloved relatives.
When the Prince arrived at the palace, his heart was moved by a compassion twice as great as usual.
At that time, King Śuddhodana called for Udāyin and asked him,
"When the Prince went out today, was he happy? Udāyin replied:
"Not far from leaving the city, we encountered a dead man; we did not know from where he had come, but the Prince and I saw him at the same time."
The Crown Prince asked,
"Who is this? Startled, I replied that it was a dead man.
Then the king again asked his attendants:
"Do you all see a dead person outside the western gate of the city?
The attendants replied:
“We did not see him. Upon hearing these words, the king’s spirit was suddenly enlightened, and he thought to himself:
“Only the Prince and Udāyin saw him; this must be the power of the heavens and not the fault of my ministers. It will certainly be just as Asita said.”
Having formed this thought, his heart was filled with great anguish and distress. He further increased the number of courtesans to entertain him;
every day he sent messengers to comfort and entice the prince, saying to him:
"The kingdom is yours; why do you grieve and not rejoice?"
The King further strictly commanded the assembly of courtesans to please the Crown Prince’s heart, never ceasing day or night.
At that time, although King Śuddhodana knew that this was the power of Heaven and no longer a matter of human effort, he cherished the Crown Prince so deeply that he could not refrain from speaking.
He thought to himself:
"The Prince has already exited through the three city gates previously; now only the northern gate remains untraversed. He will surely seek another excursion before long.
I must once again adorn those outer gardens and groves, making them even more magnificent and beautiful, ensuring that nothing unpleasant is present."
Having reflected thus, he issued full instructions to his ministers.
At that time, the king further made a silent vow within his heart:
"When the prince goes out through the northern gate, I pray that all the devas will no longer manifest inauspicious sights, lest they cause my son’s heart to be filled with sorrow and distress."
Having thus formed his wish, he then commanded his charioteer:
"When the Prince goes out, you must have him ride a horse so that he may look around in all directions and see the various people adorned with radiant beauty."
At that time, the Prince requested the King to go on an excursion;

the King, unable to bear the thought of refusing him, set out through the northern gate of the city accompanied by Udāyin and other officials, with attendants leading and following them before and behind.

Upon reaching that grove, the Prince dismounted from his horse and rested beneath a tree; he dismissed his attendants and sat upright in contemplation, reflecting upon the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death in the world.

At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven transformed himself into a bhikṣu; wearing the dharma robes and holding an alms bowl, he carried a khakkhara staff in his hand and walked while looking at the ground, appearing before the Prince.
Having seen him, the Prince immediately asked,
"Who are you? The bhikṣu replied:
"I am a bhikṣu. The Prince asked again,
"What is meant by 'bhikṣu'?"
He replied: "Because he has been able to destroy the thieves of the fetters and will not undergo future rebirths, he is called a bhikṣu.

All that exists in the world is impermanent, precarious, and fragile; what I have cultivated and studied is the untainted Noble Path, which does not cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, and through which one eternally attains the unconditioned and reaches the shore of liberation."
Having spoken these words, he manifested his supernormal powers before the Prince and ascended into the void, departing.
At that moment, all the attending officials beheld him.

Having seen this bhikṣu and heard his extensive exposition on the merits of leaving the household life, the Prince—realizing that it accorded with his long-held aversion to desire—exclaimed: "Excellent!"
"Excellent!
Among gods and humans, this alone is supreme; I shall resolutely practice and study this path.
Having spoken these words, he immediately sought his horse and returned to the palace city.
At that time, the Prince felt great joy in his heart and thought to himself:
"Previously, I saw the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, and day and night I was constantly afraid of being oppressed by them;
now, seeing this bhikṣu, he has awakened my mind and shown me the path to liberation."
Having formed this thought, he immediately reflected upon skillful means to seek out the causes and conditions for renunciation.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked Udāyin:
"Now that the Prince has gone out, was there any pleasure for him?"
Then Udāyin replied to the king, saying:
"The Prince went out a short while ago; the roads he traversed were free of any inauspicious omens.

Having arrived at the garden, the Prince was sitting alone beneath a tree when he saw a man from afar—one who had shaved off his beard and hair and wore dyed robes—who came before the Prince and conversed with him."
When his speech was concluded, he ascended into the void and departed; in the end, it remained unknown what had been discussed. Consequently, the Prince prepared his carriage and returned home.
At that moment, his countenance was joyful and serene, yet upon arriving back at the palace, he was immediately overcome with sorrow.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, doubt arose in his heart; not knowing what kind of omen this was, he felt deep distress and thought to himself:

"The Prince will certainly leave home to study the Way. Furthermore, although he has taken a consort, a long time has passed without issue. I must now command Yaśodharā to devise some expedient means so that the royal lineage is not cut off;
at the same time, I must remain vigilant so that the Prince does not depart without my knowledge."
Having formed this thought, he immediately issued a command to Yaśodharā according to what he had contemplated.
Upon hearing the king’s command, Yaśodharā was filled with shame and remained silent; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, she did not leave the Prince’s side.
At that time, the king further increased the number of exquisite female musicians to entertain him.
Then, when the prince reached the age of nineteen, he thought to himself:
"Now is precisely the time for me to leave the household life."
He then proceeded to the presence of his father, the King, with a dignified and composed bearing, like Śakra approaching Brahmā. When the attendants saw him, they addressed the King, saying:
"The Prince has now come to the presence of Your Majesty."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.
When the prince arrived, he prostrated himself before him;
thereupon, the father-king embraced him and commanded him to sit.
Once the Prince had taken his seat, he addressed his father, the King, saying:
"Where there is a gathering born of affection, there must inevitably be separation; I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the home life to study the Way."
"May all sentient beings be liberated from the suffering of separation from those they love.
I pray that you will surely grant this wish and not impose any obstacles.
When King Śuddhodana heard the Prince’s words, his heart was filled with great anguish.

Like a diamond mountain shattered to pieces, his entire body trembled and he could not remain steady on his seat; grasping the Prince’s hand, he was unable to speak further, weeping with flowing tears, sighing and sobbing with a choked voice.
After a long silence, he spoke in a low voice:
"You should now desist from the intention to leave the household life. Why is this so?"
"My years are yet young and strong, and the kingdom has no heir; yet you have already entrusted me [to others] without so much as looking back.
At that time, the Prince, seeing his father the King weeping and refusing his request, returned to his quarters, contemplating renunciation and dwelling in sorrow and unhappiness.

"At that time, the great soothsayers of the kingdom of Kapilavastu divined and knew that if the Prince did not leave the home life, after seven days had passed, he would attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and rule over the four quarters of the world, with the seven treasures appearing spontaneously."
Each reported what they knew to the king, saying:
"The Śākya clan is flourishing here.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately issued an edict to his ministers and the sons of the Śākyas:
"Did you hear the words of the physiognomist?
You must all attend upon the Prince day and night; at each of the four gates of the city, station one thousand men at every gate;
and within a distance of one *yojana* surrounding the city walls, deploy troops to patrol and provide protection."
He further commanded Yaśodharā and all the palace attendants to redouble their vigilance, ensuring that for seven more days the Prince would not depart as a renunciant.

At that time, the King came once again to the Prince’s quarters; seeing him from afar, the Prince immediately went out to welcome him, prostrating his head at the King’s feet and inquiring after his well-being.
The King said to the Prince:
"In the past, having heard the words of Asita as well as those of the various physiognomists, and considering all these auspicious omens, I am certain that you do not wish to remain in the world."

"The succession of the state is of great importance and must be maintained in continuity; I only wish that you would bear me one son for my sake, after which I shall renounce the world, and no longer oppose your wishes."
At that time, having heard the words of his father, the king, the prince reflected within himself:
"The reason the Great King earnestly detains me is precisely because the kingdom has no heir."
Having formed this thought, he replied to the king, saying:
"Excellent! As you have commanded."
He then pointed to his consort’s belly with his left hand; at that moment, Yaśodharā felt a change in her body and knew for herself that she was pregnant.

When the King heard the Prince’s words in accordance with his command, he was filled with great joy, thinking that within seven days the Prince would certainly have no child, and that if this period passed, the rank of a Wheel-Turning King would come to him naturally, and he would no longer renounce the world.
At that time, the Prince thought to himself:
"I have now reached the age of nineteen; it is currently the second month and the seventh day. I ought to employ skillful means and seek to renounce the household life."
"Why is this? Now is precisely the right time, and furthermore, the wishes of my father the King have been fulfilled.

Having formed this thought, his body emitted a radiance that illuminated the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, extending even as far as the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, yet he did not allow those in the human world to see this light.
At that time, when the devas saw this light, they all knew that the time for the Prince’s renunciation had arrived.
They immediately descended and went to where the Prince was; bowing their heads at his feet in salutation, they joined their palms and said:
"The vows and practices you have cultivated throughout immeasurable kalpas have now reached the very moment of their fulfillment."
Thereupon, the Prince replied to the devas, saying:
"As you have said, now is indeed the right time;
however, my royal father has commanded his inner and outer officials to maintain strict guard over me, so that I have no way to depart."
The devas replied,
"We ourselves shall employ various skillful means to cause the Prince to emerge, ensuring that no one knows. Thereupon,
by means of their supernatural powers, the devas caused all the officials and attendants to fall into a deep, unconscious sleep.
"At that time, while Yaśodharā was lying asleep, she had three great dreams:
first, she dreamed that the moon fell to the earth;
second, she dreamed that her teeth fell out."
Third, he dreamed that his right arm was lost.
Having had this dream, he woke up in a state of alarm within his sleep, his heart filled with great terror.
He addressed the Prince, saying:
"I had three evil dreams while asleep.
The Prince asked, "What were your dreams?"
Yaśodharā then related in detail the events of her dream.
The Prince said to her:

"The moon is still in the sky, the teeth have not yet fallen out, and the arm is still intact; you should know that all such dreams are false and unreal. You ought not now to give way to groundless fear."
Yaśodharā spoke again to the Prince:
"According to my own reflections on the matters of my dream, it must surely be an omen of the Prince's renunciation."
The Prince replied again:
"Sleep peacefully; do not harbor such anxieties. I shall ensure that no misfortune befalls you.
Having heard these words, Yaśodharā immediately went back to sleep.
The Prince immediately rose from his seat and surveyed the female musicians and Yaśodharā; they all appeared like wooden figures, resembling plantain trees that have no solid core within.

Some were leaning or propped against musical instruments, their arms and legs hanging down to the ground, lying with one another as pillows, with mucus from their noses, tears from their eyes, and saliva flowing from their mouths.

Furthermore, he observed his wife and the female entertainers in their entirety: seeing their bodies, hair, nails, marrow, and brain; bones, teeth, and skulls; skin, flesh, tendons, veins, fat, and blood; heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach; excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva—externally they were but leather bags, internally filled with foul filth, with nothing at all to marvel at.
Though forcibly perfumed with incense and adorned with flowers and silks, they are like borrowed goods that must be returned;
they cannot last long, for of a hundred-year lifespan, half is consumed in sleep, and much of it is spent in sorrow and affliction, such that true joy is but slight.
"How is it that worldly people constantly witness this matter yet fail to awaken, and furthermore, within it, become greedily attached to lustful desire?
I shall now train myself in the practices cultivated by the Buddhas of antiquity; I must urgently distance myself from this mass of great fire."

At that time, after the Prince had reflected thus, during the final watch of the night, the kings of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the various devas of the desire realm filled the void. They then spoke with one voice to the Prince, saying:
"Your inner and outer retinues are all fast asleep; now is precisely the time for you to renounce the world."
At that time, the Prince immediately went in person to where Chandaka was;
by the power of the devas, Chandaka woke up of his own accord, and the Prince spoke to him, saying:
"For my sake, you must bring Kaṇṭhaka here."
At that time, having heard these words, Chandaka’s entire body trembled with fear and his mind was filled with hesitation;
for on the one hand, he did not wish to disobey the Prince’s command,
and on the other, he feared the severity of the King’s decree.
After reflecting for a long time, he shed tears and said:
"The Great King’s compassionate decree is so stern;

moreover, this is neither a time for pleasure excursions nor a day for subduing enemies. Why, in the midst of these final watches of the night, do you suddenly seek a horse? Where do you intend to go?"
The Prince spoke again to Chandaka, saying:
"I now wish, for the sake of all sentient beings, to subdue the thieves of the afflictions and fetters.
You must not now oppose this intention of mine."
At that time, Chandaka raised his voice and wailed, wishing to let Yaśodharā and all her attendants know that the Prince was about to depart.
By the power of the devas, he remained lying there in a stupor as before;
Chandaka then led the horse forward,
and the Prince walked slowly ahead, speaking to both Chandaka and Kanthaka:
"All those bound by affection must inevitably part;
worldly affairs are easily brought to fruition, but the conditions for leaving the household life are extremely difficult to accomplish."
Having heard this, Chandaka remained silent and spoke no word.
Thereupon Kanthaka ceased its neighing.
At that time, the Prince, seeing the appearance of dawn, emitted a radiance from his body that illuminated the ten directions, and he uttered a lion’s roar, saying:
"The Dharma of renunciation followed by all Buddhas of the past is likewise my own now.
Thereupon, the devas supported the four hooves of the horse and assisted Chanda;
Śakra-devānām-indra held a parasol and followed behind. The devas then caused the north gate of the city to open spontaneously, without making a sound.
Thereupon, the Prince went out through the gate, followed by the devas of the void who offered praise.
At that time, the Prince again uttered a lion’s roar:
"If I do not sever birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, I shall never return to the palace."
"If I do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and furthermore cannot turn the wheel of the Dharma, I shall certainly not return to see my father, the King;
nor, unless I have exhausted all ties of affection, shall I ever again see Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā."
When the Prince uttered this vow, the devas in the void praised him, saying:
"Excellent! These words shall surely bear fruit."
When dawn arrived, the distance traveled along the road was already three *yojanas*.
At that time, the host of devas, having followed the Prince to this place and completed their task, suddenly vanished.
"At that time, the Prince proceeded next to the forest of asceticism belonging to the seer Bhārgava.
Upon seeing this grove, which was tranquil and free from all clamor, his heart was filled with joy and his faculties were delighted."
Even after dismounting, he patted [Chandaka’s] back and said,
"The task that was difficult to accomplish has been completed by you.
He then spoke again to Chandaka:
"Your gallop is swift and noble, like that of the King of the Golden-Winged Birds; you have always followed me, never leaving my side.
Among the people of the world, some may possess a virtuous mind while their bodies do not follow, or they may exert physical strength while their minds do not correspond;
now, both your mind and body are entirely without discord."
Furthermore, when people of the world dwell in wealth and nobility, they vie with one another to serve and attend upon them;
yet now that I have renounced my kingdom to come to this forest, you alone are able to follow me—this is truly rare.
"Now that I have already reached this secluded and tranquil place, you may return to the palace together with Kaṇṭhaka.
When Chandaka heard these words, he wailed and wept piteously; overcome with grief and confusion, he fell to the ground, unable to sustain himself.
Thereupon, having heard that he was being sent away, Kaṇṭhaka knelt down, licked [the Prince’s] feet, and tears fell like rain.
Chanda replied, "How could I now bear to listen to such words from the Prince? Within the palace,
I disobeyed the Great King’s command and forcibly saddled Kaṇṭhaka to give him to the Prince, which has led to his arrival here this very day."
Because the King, our father, and Mahāprajāpatī have lost their crown prince, they will surely be filled with grief and distress;
likewise, both the inner and outer quarters of the palace will be thrown into agitation.
Furthermore, this place is full of many perils; fierce beasts and venomous insects swarm across the roads. How could I now abandon the Prince and return to the palace alone?
The Prince then replied to Chandaka, saying:
"According to the laws of the world, one is born alone and dies alone; how could there ever be a companion?
Furthermore, there are the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death; how could I possibly be a partner to these?"
I have now come here for the purpose of severing all sufferings;
once suffering is severed, I shall thereafter act as a companion to all sentient beings.
"At this very moment, I have not yet escaped from my own sufferings; how could I possibly become your companion?

Chandaka replied again, "Since the Prince was born, he has been raised within the deep palace; his body, hands, and feet are all exceedingly soft and supple, and there is no bedding or mat upon which he has ever slept that was not fine and smooth."
"How can one suddenly tread upon thorns, rubble, mud, and soil, and dwell beneath trees?
The Prince replied, "It is truly as you say;
had I remained in the palace, I might have avoided this affliction of thorns."
"The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death will inevitably assail me.
Having heard these words of the Prince, Chandaka wept bitterly with tears streaming down his face and stood there in silence.
At that time, the Prince approached Chandaka, took up his sword of seven precious gems, and uttered this lion’s roar:
"The Buddhas of the past, for the sake of accomplishing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, abandoned their finery and shaved off their hair and beards;
I now likewise shall follow the Dharma of those Buddhas."
Having spoken these words, he then removed his jeweled crown and the bright pearl from within his topknot, gave them to Chandaka, and said to him:
"Take this jeweled crown and the bright pearl and present them at the King’s feet. You may report to the Great King on my behalf:

'I do not now seek the bliss of rebirth in heaven, nor am I unfilial toward my parents; I harbor no heart of resentment or anger. It is only because I fear birth, old age, sickness, and death that I have come here for the purpose of severing and ending them.'"
"You should assist me in rejoicing and celebrating; do not give rise to further sorrow or grief regarding this auspicious event.
If the Father King should say that my current renunciation is not yet the right time, you must convey my words to the Great King, saying:
"When old age, sickness, and death arrive, how can there be a fixed time? Though a person be young and strong, how can they escape these?"
If my father, the King, were again to reprove me, saying:
"I originally stipulated that you should be permitted to leave home only when you have a son; now that you have no son, why do you depart?"
Furthermore, regarding the time of my departure from the palace, you have not informed me.
You should report this in detail to my father, the King, saying:
"Yaśodharā has long been pregnant; let the King himself inquire of her."
"Formerly, such was the imperial decree; it was not a matter of acting on my own authority.

In antiquity, there were various Wheel-Turning Sage Kings who, weary of their royal positions, entered the mountain forests to leave the household life and seek the Way, never returning midway to accept the five desires again.
My present departure from the household is likewise so: until I have attained Bodhi, I shall never return to the palace."

"My inner and outer kinsmen all harbor feelings of affection and attachment toward me; you should use your eloquence to explain this for them, so that they do not give rise to groundless grief and distress on my account."
The Prince again removed the necklaces from his body and gave them to Chandaka, saying to him:

"You should take these necklaces for me and present them to Mahāprajāpatī, saying: 'I have now left the palace city for the sake of severing the root of all suffering; I seek to fulfill this vow. Do not cause me further grief by grieving for me.'"
He then removed the remaining ornaments from his body and gave them to Yaśodharā, speaking to her again:
"In life, there is the suffering of separation from those one loves;
it is because I now wish to sever all such sufferings that I have left the home life to study the Way."
"Do not, on my account, constantly give way to sorrow and anxiety; let it be the same for all your kinsmen as well.
When Chandaka heard these words, his grief intensified even further.
Unable to disobey the Prince’s command, he immediately knelt down, took from him the precious crown, the bright pearl, the necklaces, and the ornaments, and spoke with tears falling:
"Upon hearing that the Prince’s aspirations are such as these, my entire body trembles.
Even if there were someone whose heart was like wood or stone, they would feel sorrowful upon hearing these words;
how much more so for me, who have served the Prince since birth—how could I not be moved to despair upon hearing this vow?"
I only pray that the Prince will renounce this resolve, so as not to cause Great Sorrow and Suffering to his Father the King, Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and his other kinsmen.
If you are determined not to turn back this resolve, do not abandon me here once again;
I now take refuge at the feet of the Prince, for there is no reason to believe you will ever depart from me.
Even if you were to return to the palace, the King would surely reproach me: "How could you leave the Prince alone and return? What words would you have to offer in reply to the Great King?"
The Prince replied: "You should not speak such words now;
all in this world are subject to separation, for how could they ever remain gathered forever?
Seven days after I was born, my mother passed away; if even a mother and son must part through death and birth, how much more so the case of others?"
"Do not harbor excessive attachment to me; you may return to the palace together with Kaṇṭhaka.
Although he issued this command twice, [the groom] still refused to depart.
At that time, the Prince took a sharp sword and shaved his own beard and hair.
He immediately made this vow:
"Now that I have shaved off my beard and hair, I vow that together with all beings, I shall sever all afflictions as well as the hindrances of habitual tendencies.
Śakra-devānām-indra received the hair and departed.
The devas in the void burned incense and scattered flowers, praising him with one voice:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
At that time, having shaved off his beard and hair, the Prince looked at the garments he was wearing and saw that they were still made of the seven treasures. He then thought to himself:
"The dharma of renunciation practiced by the Buddhas of the past regarding the clothing worn is not like this."
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a hunter before the Prince, wearing a *kāṣāya* robe.
Upon seeing him, the Prince was filled with great joy and said to him:
"The garment you wear is the attire of tranquility; it is the emblem of all Buddhas of the past."
"How is it that by wearing this, one commits a sinful act?
The hunter replied, "I wear the *kāṣāya* robe to lure the deer; when the deer see the robe, they all come near me, and I am able to kill them."
The Prince spoke again:
"If it is as you say, that one wears this kashaya merely for the purpose of killing deer and not for the sake of seeking liberation while wearing it."
I now offer these robes made of the seven precious jewels to trade with you; I wear these robes because I desire to gather in and rescue all sentient beings, severing their afflictions.
The hunter replied, "Excellent! I shall do as you have instructed."
He immediately removed his precious robes and gave them to the hunter;
he donned the *kāṣāya* himself, following the manner of the robes worn by the Buddhas of the past.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsakāyika deva returned to his Brahma-body, ascended into the void, and departed for his own abode.
"At that time, there was an extraordinary radiance in the sky;
seeing this, Chandaka felt a sense of wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence:
'This auspicious omen cannot be due to a minor cause.'"
When Chandaka saw that the Prince had shaved off his hair and beard and was clad in dharma robes, he knew for certain that the Prince could never be turned back;
he fell to the ground in a swoon, his grief and distress redoubled.
At that time, the Prince spoke to him, saying:
"You should now abandon this grief and sorrow, return immediately to the palace city, and fully convey my intentions."
Thereupon, the Prince proceeded forward slowly;
Chandaka, sobbing and weeping, prostrated himself with his head at the ground. Only when he could no longer see the Prince from afar did he finally rise.
His entire body trembled so violently that he could not control himself; looking back at Kanthaka and the ornaments, he wailed with choked sobs, his tears and mucus flowing together.
He immediately led Kaṇṭhaka and took up his precious crown and ornaments for adorning the body; while Chandaka wailed and Kaṇṭhaka neighed mournfully, they returned along the road.
At that time, the Prince proceeded forward to the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava.
At that time, there were various birds and beasts in that forest; upon seeing the Prince, they all fixed their gaze upon him, standing still and blinking not.
From afar, the seer Bhārgava saw the Prince and thought to himself:
"What deity is this? Is it the Sun or the Moon?"
"Are you Śakra? Then, together with his retinue, he came to welcome the Prince, conceiving deep reverence and saying these words: "Welcome!"
"O Benevolent One!

Having seen the assembly of sages, whose minds were gentle and whose deportment was dignified and composed, the Prince immediately approached their dwelling place. The sages, no longer possessing their usual majestic radiance, all came together to invite the Prince to sit.

Once the Prince was seated, he observed the practices of those sages: some wore grass as clothing, while others used tree bark or leaves for garments; some consumed only grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits, while others ate once a day, once every two days, or once every three days, thus practicing the method of self-starvation.
Some serve fire and water; some revere the sun and moon; some stand on one leg; some lie in dust and soil; some lie upon thorns and brambles; and some lie beside fire and water.
Having witnessed such ascetic practices, the Prince immediately questioned the seer Bhārgava:
"The ascetic practices you are currently cultivating are truly extraordinary; what kind of karmic fruit do you all seek to attain?"
The seer replied, "I practice these austerities because I desire to be reborn in heaven.
The prince asked again:
"Though the heavens are pleasant, when merit is exhausted, one falls into destitution; wandering through the six realms of rebirth, one ultimately encounters a mass of suffering.
Why do you cultivate the causes of suffering in order to seek its retribution?"
The Prince then sighed to himself and said:
"Merchants enter the great ocean for the sake of jewels;
kings raise armies to wage war for the sake of territory."
"Now these various sages practice these ascetic penances for the sake of being born in heaven.
Having uttered this exclamation, he remained silent.
Then the sage Bhārgava asked the Prince:
“Virtuous ones, for what reason do you remain silent and say nothing? Is that which we practice not the true and correct path?
The Prince replied, “The practices you perform are not without reaching suffering; however, though you seek their rewards, in the end you shall not escape suffering.”
The Prince engaged in this exchange of discourse with the various seers until sunset.
The Prince then stayed there for one night; when the following morning arrived, he reflected again:
"Although these seers practice asceticism, none of it is the true path to liberation."
"I should not remain here any longer," he thought, and immediately took his leave of the rishis, wishing to depart.
At that time, the rishis said to the prince:
"We all rejoice at your coming here, O Benevolent One."
It was because of us that the majesty and power of our assembly increased and flourished.
For what reason do you now suddenly wish to depart?
Is it because we have lost our dignified deportment?
"Is it because you have offended or provoked someone among this assembly?
For what reason do you not remain here?
The Prince replied:
"It is not that you have committed such a fault, nor is there any deficiency in the etiquette between host and guest;
however, what you practice increases the causes of suffering, whereas I now study the Path for the sake of severing the root of suffering. For these reasons, I am departing."
The assembly of seers deliberated among themselves, saying:
"The path he cultivates is exceedingly vast; how can we possibly detain him?"
At that time, there was a seer who was well-versed in the science of marks. He spoke to the crowd, saying:
"This noble person here is endowed with all the auspicious marks; he will surely attain the knowledge of all modes and become a teacher of gods and humans."
They immediately went together to where the Prince was and spoke these words:
"The path you cultivate is different [from ours], so we dare not detain you;
if you wish to depart, you should travel northward. There is a great seer there named Ārāḍa Kālāma; you, O Benevolent One, should go to him to engage in discourse."
"I observe that you, O noble one, likewise need not remain in that place.
Thereupon, the Prince immediately traveled north.

When the assembly of seers saw the Prince depart, they were filled with distress; they joined their palms and escorted him for some distance, watching until he was out of sight, and only then did they return.
"At that time, after the Prince had departed from the palace and dawn had broken, Yaśodharā and the various court ladies awoke from their sleep;
not seeing the Prince, they wailed and wept in grief, and immediately went to inform Mahāprajāpatī:
'This morning, we have suddenly lost sight of the Prince's whereabouts.'"
Upon hearing these words, Mahāprajāpatī fainted and fell to the ground. This distress spread from one to another until it reached the King.
When the King heard this, he stood motionless and silent; his spirit was lost as if his four limbs had perished. Throughout the entire palace, both inside and out, all were likewise affected.

At that time, the ministers immediately entered to inspect the Prince’s quarters and toured the palace city; they saw that the northern gate of the city had opened of its own accord, and furthermore, neither Chandaka nor Kanthaka was to be seen.
He immediately asked the gatekeeper,
"Who opened this? As they examined one another, they all said they did not know.
He also questioned the guards, who likewise replied that they did not understand the intention behind opening this gate.
At that time, the minister thought to himself:
"Since the north gate has been opened, the Prince must surely depart by way of it; I ought to search for the Prince's whereabouts with all speed."
He immediately ordered a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry to set out in all directions in a continuous stream to pursue the Prince;
yet, due to the power of the heavens, they lost their way and could not discover his whereabouts.
Even as they returned, they addressed the Great King, saying:
"We have searched for the Prince, but do not know his whereabouts.
At that time, Chandaka, walking and leading Kaṇṭhaka along with the ornaments, followed the road back home, weeping and sobbing with deep grief.

The people of the entire town, seeing this, were struck with amazement; none failed to feel deep distress, and they all vied with one another to come forward and ask Chandaka, "Where did you leave the Prince when you sent him away?"
"Now, will you return alone with Kaṇṭhaka?
Having received this question from the people, Chandaka was doubly overcome with grief and could not answer them.

Although these people saw Kanthaka adorned with a saddle and bridle and embellished with the seven treasures, they did not see the Prince; it was as if a dead man were decorated with flowers and silks.
Thereupon, Chandaka entered the palace city; Kanthaka neighed piteously, and all the horses in the stables simultaneously let out mournful cries.
The various officials outside informed Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā, saying:
"Chandaka has returned alone with only Kanthaka."
Having heard these words, he rolled upon the ground and thought to himself:
"Now I hear only that Chandaka and Kanthaka have returned together, yet I do not hear the sound of the Prince’s return."
Mahāprajāpatī then spoke these words:
"I raised the Prince until he reached adulthood, yet one day he abandoned me, and I know not where he is?"
It is like a fruit tree that has blossomed and borne fruit, which falls to the ground just as it is about to ripen;
or like a hungry person who encounters a banquet of a hundred flavors, yet suddenly overturns the vessel just as he is about to eat.
Yaśodharā spoke again, saying:
"The Prince and I were never apart in our walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;
now that he has abandoned me, I know not where he has gone."
In ancient times, when kings entered the mountains to study the Way, they all took their wives and children with them, never abandoning one another for even a moment;
yet people of the world, having met but once as acquaintances, do not forget each other upon parting.
Given that the affection between husband and wife and the depth of their mutual love are so profound, how is it that [the king's conduct] has instead become so thin and callous?
He rebuked Chandaka, saying:
"It is better to be an enemy to the wise than to be intimate with the foolish;
you, a dull-witted and obstinate man, have stolen away the Prince and placed him where he is, causing this Śākya clan to no longer flourish."
He further rebuked Kanthaka:
"When you carried the Prince out from this royal palace and departed recently, you were silent and made no sound;
now that you return empty-handed, for what reason do you neigh so mournfully?"
At that time, Chandaka immediately replied:
"Do not blame me or Kaṇṭhaka. Why is this so?..."
"This was the power of the devas, not the work of humans.
On that very night, while the queen and the court ladies were all fast asleep,
the Prince commanded me to rise and saddle his horse."

At that time, I raised my voice in a great cry to admonish the Prince, wishing that the Queen and all the court ladies might hear it and be startled into awakening; yet neither the horse Kanthaka nor anyone else perceived anything.
The city gates usually open to a sound heard forty *li* away, yet at that moment they opened spontaneously without a single sound.
How could such a thing not be the power of Heaven?

When I departed from the city, the gods were commanded by Heaven to support the hooves of my horse with their hands and receive me; the devas in the void followed in countless numbers—how could I have possibly stopped?

When the night had turned to dawn, we traveled three *yojanas* and arrived at the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava. Furthermore, there were many extraordinary and marvelous events; please listen as I recount them:

"Once the Prince reached the forest of austerities where the seer Bhārgava dwelt, he immediately dismounted from his horse, stroked its back with his hand, and commanded me to return to the palace city.
At that time, I followed the Prince with no intention of ever returning home; yet when the Prince sent me away, I would by no means consent to stay."
Furthermore, he approached me, took a sword made of the seven precious gems, and proclaimed:
"In order to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddhas of the past discarded their finery and shaved off their hair and beards; I, too, shall now follow the Dharma of those Buddhas."
Having spoken these words, he immediately removed his jeweled crown and the bright pearl, handing them both over to me to place at the feet of the King;
he further gave the necklaces to Mahāprajāpatī, and the remaining ornaments to Yaśodharā.
At that time, although I heard these instructions, I still remained by his side, having no desire to return home.

Then the Prince took a sharp sword and shaved off his own beard and hair; the heavens received them in mid-air as they fell and carried them away. He then proceeded forward and encountered a hunter, with whom he exchanged the exquisite robes of seven precious jewels he was wearing for the hunter’s *kāṣāya* robe. At that moment, a great radiance appeared in the void.

Seeing that the Prince’s appearance and attire had already changed, I knew deeply that his resolve was impossible to turn back; I immediately fainted from distress, my heart filled with great anguish.
When the Prince arrived at the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava, I took my leave there and returned home.
"These extraordinary marvels were all due to the power of the devas and were not the work of human effort; I pray you do not reproach me or Kaṇṭhaka.
When Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā had heard these words spoken by Chandaka, their hearts were slightly awakened, and they remained silent without a word.
"At that time, King Śuddhodana, having recovered from his fainting spell, commanded Chandaka to be summoned and spoke to him, saying:
'How could you cause such great suffering and distress to arise among the Śākya clan?'"
"I have issued strict orders, commanding all officials both inside and outside the palace to guard the Crown Prince, fearing his departure from home.
What was your intention that you would suddenly saddle Kanthaka and enable the Crown Prince to depart in secret?"
Having heard this, Chandaka was seized with great terror and addressed the King, saying:
"The Prince's departure from the city was truly not my fault; I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me leave to explain the matter in full."
He then placed the jeweled crown and the bright pearl from his topknot at the King’s feet, saying:
"The Prince has commanded me to place this crown and pearl at Your Majesty’s feet; the seven-jeweled necklace is for Mahāprajāpatī, and the remaining ornaments are for Yaśodharā."
When the king saw these various objects, his grief and desolation redoubled; even wood and stone still evoke such a response, how much more so the profound affection between father and son!
Chanda recounted the previous events in detail and addressed the King,
saying: "The Crown Prince commanded me, 'If my father the King says,
"I originally required a son before you were permitted to leave the home life," and now that I have no son, why do you depart?'"
"Even as he was departing, he did not speak further.
You should answer the King, my father, on my behalf:
"Yaśodharā has been pregnant for a long time; Your Majesty should question her."
"Formerly, the imperial decree was such; it was not a matter of acting on my own authority.
When the King heard these words, he immediately sent someone to question Yaśodharā:
"The Prince said that you have been pregnant for some time already; is this truly so?"
Yaśodharā replied: "It is true. When the Great King came to this palace, the Prince pointed at me, and I immediately perceived that I was pregnant."
Upon hearing these words, the king felt a sense of wonder; his grief and distress were momentarily stilled, and he thought to himself:

"The reason I previously granted that my son might renounce the world was because it would be impossible for a son to be born within seven days, and the throne of a Wheel-Turning King would naturally fall to him."

She did not expect to become pregnant before the seven days were complete, and she deeply reproached herself for her shallow wisdom, lamenting that the skillful means she employed could not sustain the pregnancy.
Having made this promise lightly, I now suffer heavy regret.
The Prince’s divine strategy transcends human comprehension.
Furthermore, today’s events were also brought about by the power of the great devas; I ought not to reproach Chandaka.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"The Prince’s renunciation of the household life is inevitable; even if I were to employ further expedient means, I could not retain him."
"Although I have renounced my kingdom to leave home and study the Way, I already have a son so that the lineage is not severed.
I should now command Yaśodharā to carefully protect the child she carries."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, his affectionate love profound, spoke to Chandaka, saying:
"I shall now go to search for the Prince; I do not know where he surely is at this very moment."
"Now that he has already abandoned me to study the Way, how could I bear to live and exist alone? I must immediately pursue him wherever he may be.
At that time, the royal preceptor and the great minister, hearing that the King wished to go forth in search of the Crown Prince, both came together to admonish the King, saying:
"Great King!..."
"You should not give rise to grief or distress within yourself. Why is this?
As I observe the Prince and examine his physical characteristics, I see that in past lives he has long since cultivated the practice of renunciation."
Even if one were made Śakra Devānām Indra, one would still find no joy; how much less, O Great King, could one remain in the position of a Wheel-Turning Monarch now?
I do not recall that when the Prince was first born, he walked seven steps and raised his hand, standing and saying:
"My births are ended; this is my final body.
All the Brahma Kings and Śakra Devānām-Indra descended from above to follow him.
"How extraordinary this is! How can you find pleasure in the world?
He further addressed the King:

"In the past, the seer Asita examined the Prince's marks and prophesied that at the age of nineteen, he would leave the household life to study the Way and would surely achieve all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā)."
Now that the time has arrived, Great King, for what reason do you give rise to such sorrow and suffering?
Furthermore, Great King, you strictly commanded those both within and without to guard the Prince, fearing he might renounce the world;
yet the devas have come to lead him out of the city—such a matter is no longer within human power.
"I only pray that Your Majesty will give rise to joy and not harbor sorrow or distress; there is no need for you to go out yourself.
If your longing for the Crown Prince still does not cease, I shall now accompany the great ministers to seek his whereabouts."
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"I know that although the prince cannot be turned back, I cannot yet bear to abandon him and cease my pursuit; I shall now test whether the teachers and great ministers can search for him once more."
He then replied to his teacher and the great minister, saying:
"Excellent! You may go;
the entire palace, both inside and out, is filled with grief and distress, waiting for you to return at once."
Thereupon, the royal preceptor and the great ministers took their leave and departed to search for the Prince.
*The Sutra on Past and Present Causes and Effects*, Scroll Two;
*The Sutra on Past and Present Causes and Effects*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty:
"At that time, King Śuddhodana, having dispatched the royal preceptor and the great ministers,
immediately gave the prince’s jeweled necklace to Mahāprajāpatī and spoke to her, saying:"
"This is the necklace worn by the Prince; it was entrusted to Chandaka for his return, with instructions that it be given to you.
Upon seeing the necklace, Mahāprajāpatī’s grief intensified all the more, and she thought to herself:
"The people of the four continents are exceedingly unfortunate to have lost this wise and enlightened Wheel-Turning Sage-King."
Furthermore, he sent other articles of adornment to Yaśodharā, saying to her:
"The Prince has sent these ornaments for you to wear."
When Yaśodharā saw these objects, she fainted and fell to the ground.
The King again sent a messenger with instructions for Yaśodharā, telling her to take care of herself and ensure that the child in her womb remained safe and well.

"At that time, the royal preceptor and the great ministers went to the forest of the ascetic Bhārgava; having dismissed their attendants and removed all their regalia, they proceeded to the place where the seer resided."
The rishi invited him to sit, and after they had exchanged greetings, the royal preceptor said to the rishi:

"I am the preceptor of King Śuddhodana. The reason I have come here today is that King Śuddhodana’s son, who possesses the marks of a great man, has grown weary of the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and has left the household life to study the Way. He passed through this forest; did the Great Rishi see him?"
The seer Baka replied to the king’s counselor, saying:

“Recently, I saw a youth here whose countenance was upright and handsome, endowed with all the marks of excellence. He entered this grove and engaged me in discussion, staying with me for one night; I did not know him to be the prince of the king.
He disparaged the path we practice and departed from here toward the north, going to those seers Ārāḍa and Kālāma.”

At that time, having heard these words, the royal preceptor and the great minister immediately hastened to where the seer was. On the way, they saw from afar the Prince sitting upright beneath a tree in deep contemplation; his marks of excellence and radiant light surpassed those of the sun and moon.
Even though he dismounted, dismissed his attendants, and removed his ceremonial robes, he approached the Prince and sat to one side, where they exchanged greetings with one another.
Thereupon, the royal preceptor addressed the Crown Prince, saying:
"The Great King has sent me to seek you out, wishing to say something.
The Crown Prince replied:
"What does the King, your father, wish for you to say?

The royal preceptor replied, "The Great King has long known that the Prince deeply delights in leaving the household life and that this intention is difficult to turn back. Nevertheless, the King’s affection for the Prince is profound; the fierce fire of his grief constantly blazes within him, and he requires the Prince’s return to extinguish it."
I pray that you will turn your carriage back and return to the palace city; though there are worldly affairs, do not allow the Prince to completely abandon his spiritual practice.
A place for quieting the mind need not necessarily be among the mountains and forests.
Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and all our internal and external kinsmen have all sunk into a great ocean of grief and affliction; they long for the Prince’s return to rescue them.
At that time, having heard the words of the royal preceptor, the Prince replied to him in a deep and solemn voice:
"How could I not know that my father, the King, possesses such profound affection for me?"
I have come here solely out of fear of the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and for the purpose of severing them.
If one could ensure that loved ones were united with me day and night, and moreover, were free from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, why would I have come here at all?
The reason I have now distanced myself from my father, the King, is solely for the sake of future reconciliation.

Although the great fire of my father’s grief is blazing fiercely at present, for both my father and me, this is the only suffering remaining in this life; in the future, this affliction shall surely be extinguished forever.
