If it were as you say, that I should dwell in the palace to practice the path, would there be anyone capable of remaining in a house made of the seven treasures that was filled with blazing flames?
It is like food mixed with poison; even if there were a hungry person, they would never eat it.
Since I have already renounced my kingdom to leave home and cultivate the Way, how could I be made to return to the palace city to practice the Way?
People of the world, even while immersed in great suffering, remain addicted to minor pleasures and cannot abandon them for even a moment;
how much more so should I, being in this place of supreme tranquility and free from all afflictions and pain, renounce it to return to what is evil?
"In ancient times, when kings entered the mountains to study the Way, none returned midway to indulge in sensual desires;
if my father the king were to insist on making me return, it would be a violation of the laws of former kings."
At that time, the royal preceptor said to the prince:
"It is indeed as the prince has now stated.

However, among the various sages and saints, some say that there will certainly be retribution in the future, while others say there will certainly be none. Since these two types of sages and saints cannot even know for certain whether there will definitely be [retribution] or not in future lives, how can the prince wish to abandon present happiness to seek a future retribution that is uncertain?"
Since the karmic retribution of birth and death cannot even be definitively known as existing or non-existing, how can you seek to attain the fruit of liberation?
We only pray that the Prince will return to the palace at once.
The Prince replied: "Those two seers speak of future fruits; one says they exist and the other says they do not. Both are matters of doubt and are not definitive teachings."
I shall never practice in accordance with their teachings; you should not challenge me on this account. Why is this?

I have not come here out of a desire for karmic rewards; rather, seeing with my own eyes that birth, old age, sickness, and death must inevitably be undergone, I seek liberation only to escape this suffering.
"I shall cause you to see me achieve the Way before long; this vow of mine can never be turned back.
Having thus addressed his father the King, he returned to inform him of these matters.

At that time, having spoken these words, the Prince rose from his seat and, bidding farewell to the royal preceptor and the great ministers, departed northward to visit the sages Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra.
At that time, the royal preceptor and the great minister, seeing the Prince depart, wept and were filled with anguish:
first, because their affection for the Prince was deep;
and second, because they had accepted the King’s command to come to the Prince's side, yet were unable to change his resolve.
Pacing back and forth by the roadside, unable to turn back, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Having been sent as the King's envoys, yet being unable to perform our duties, we now return empty-handed; how shall we offer a report?"

"We shall leave behind five of our followers who are intelligent and wise, gentle in mind, loyal and upright by nature, and of noble lineage, and secretly command them to observe and watch his every movement."
Having spoken these words, he looked around at his side, saw the five men including Kauṇḍinya, and said to them:
"Are you all able to remain here?"
The five men replied:
"Excellent! We shall do as you command."
"His every movement, whether departing or arriving, must be closely observed.
Having thus taken their leave, the royal preceptor and the great ministers departed for the palace city, while [the prince] proceeded to where the Crown Prince was.
"At that time, the Prince went to the dwelling place of the seers Ārāḍa and Kālāma; crossing the Gaṅgā River, he traveled by way of Rājagṛha."
Once they had entered the city, the masses of people, seeing that the Prince’s countenance and marks were exceptionally sublime, were filled with joy, love, and reverence;
the entire kingdom rushed to gaze upon him, and such a clamor reached King Bimbisāra.
The king was startled and asked, "What sound is this?
The ministers replied:

"The Prince of King Śuddhodana is named Sarvārthasiddha. Formerly, various physiognomists prophesied that he should attain the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and rule over the four quarters of the world; furthermore, they prophesied that if he were to leave the household life, he would certainly achieve all-knowledge (sarvajñā)."
"That person has now entered this city; the people outside are rushing and competing to come and see him, which is why there is such a clamor.
When King Bimbisāra heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and his entire body leaped with excitement.
He immediately commanded a man to go and observe where the prince was located.
The messenger received the decree and sought out the Prince, finding him on Mount Paṇḍava, sitting upright upon a rock in deep contemplation.
The messenger immediately returned and reported everything in detail to the Great King.
The King then prepared his carriage and, accompanied by his ministers and subjects, proceeded to the Prince’s location.
Upon reaching Mount Paṇḍava, he saw the Prince from afar; his marks of excellence and radiant light surpassed those of the sun and moon.
He immediately dismounted, removed his royal regalia and attendants, and sat before him to offer greetings:
"Is the Prince’s four great elements in perfect harmony?
When I see the Prince, my heart is filled with great joy;
yet there is one sorrow: the Prince is by lineage of the Solar Clan, and for generations his line has been passed down as that of a Wheel-Turning King."
The Prince now possesses all the marks of a Wheel-Turning King; why have you abandoned them to enter these deep mountains, treading upon the sand and dust, and come so far as this?
It is because I see this that I am moved to grief.
If the Prince, because his father the King is still living, wishes not to accept the position of Holy King, I shall divide my kingdom and govern half of it with him;
if he deems that too little, I shall relinquish the entire kingdom to serve as his minister and attend upon the Prince.
"If you do not wish to take this kingdom of mine, I shall provide you with the fourfold army so that you may attack and seize another kingdom yourself.
Whatever the Prince desires, I shall not go against it."
At that time, having heard these words spoken by King Bimbisāra, the Prince was deeply moved by his intention and replied to the king:
"The lineage of Your Majesty is originally like the bright moon; its nature is naturally lofty and cool, never engaging in base matters. Whatever it does is without exception pure and sublime;
thus, for you now to utter such words is not at all surprising."

However, as I observe Your Majesty, your inner sincerity is now even more profound than it was before; you should now cultivate the three enduring dharmas regarding your body, life, and wealth, and you ought not to encourage others by means of things that are non-enduring.
Since I have now renounced the position of a universal monarch (cakravartin), for what reason should I take possession of a kingdom?
Even though the king, out of a virtuous mind, offered his kingdom to me, I still did not accept it; how then could I use military force to seize another kingdom?

The reason I now take my leave of my parents, shave off my hair and beard, and renounce my kingdom is for the sake of severing the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is not for the sake of seeking the pleasures of the five desires.
“The five desires of the world are like a great mass of fire that burns all sentient beings, from which they cannot escape on their own; how can you urge me to be greedily attached to them?”

The reason I have come here now is that there are two sages, Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra, who are the supreme guides for seeking liberation; I wish to go to them to seek the path to liberation, so it is not fitting for me to remain here for long.
Since I have already violated the King’s initial word, which was granted with a joyful heart, please do not harbor resentment;
Your Majesty should now govern the kingdom with the True Dharma and must not oppress the people.
Having spoken these words, the Prince immediately rose and took his leave of the King.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, seeing the Prince depart, was deeply and profoundly grieved; with palms joined and tears flowing, he spoke these words:
"When I first saw the Prince, my heart leaped with great joy; now that the Prince has departed, my sorrow and suffering have redoubled."
Since you now wish to depart for the sake of great liberation, we dare not detain you;
we only pray that the Prince may swiftly attain his goal, and if he achieves the Way, we hope to be the first to receive his deliverance.
The Prince then took his leave and departed;
the King escorted him for some distance along the roadside, gazing at him with all his might until he could no longer see him, whereupon he returned.
"At that time, the Prince immediately proceeded to the dwelling of the seer Ārāḍa.
Then the devas spoke to the seer, saying:
'Sarvārthasiddha has abandoned his kingdom and bid farewell to his parents in order to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path, desiring to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.'"
"Now that you have come, you have finally arrived here.
At that time, having heard the words of the deity, the rishi was filled with great joy; in an instant, he saw the prince from afar and immediately went out to welcome him, exclaiming:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
They returned together to their dwelling and invited the Prince to sit.

At that time, when the seer beheld the Prince—his countenance upright and handsome, his marks and signs complete, and his faculties serene—he conceived deep love and reverence, and immediately asked the Prince:
"On the road you have traveled, did you not grow weary?"
I know all of this: from the Prince’s initial birth, his renunciation of the world, and his arrival here;
how he was able to awaken himself and emerge from amidst the mass of fire;
and how, like a great elephant, he freed himself from the snares.

In ancient times, when kings were in the prime of their youth, they indulged at will in the five desires; only when their faculties had matured did they subsequently renounce their kingdoms, cities, and pleasures to leave the household life and study the Way—this is not yet to be considered extraordinary.
That you, Prince, at this stage of your vigorous youth, have been able to renounce the five desires and come far to this place is truly extraordinary;
you ought to apply yourself with diligent vigor and swiftly cross to the other shore.
Having heard this, the Prince immediately replied to him, saying:
"I am exceedingly joyful to hear your words. You should explain to me the method for severing birth, old age, sickness, and death; I now desire to hear it."
The seer replied: "Excellent! Excellent!"
He then spoke thus:
"The beginning of sentient beings begins with primordial darkness;
from primordial darkness, the conceit of 'I' arises."
From the conceit of "I," delusion arises;
from delusion, defiled craving arises;
from defiled craving, the five subtle dust-elements arise.
From the five subtle particles of air, the five great elements arise;
from the five great elements, the various afflictions such as greed and hatred arise;
and therein one wanders through the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress—this is what I have briefly described for the sake of the Prince.
At that time, the Prince immediately asked:
"I have now understood what you have said regarding the root of birth and death; by what further skillful means can it be severed?"
The seer replied:
"If you wish to sever this root of birth and death, you must first leave the household life to cultivate the practice of the precepts, practicing humility and patience;
dwell in a secluded place and cultivate meditative concentration."
Detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, one attains the first dhyāna;
with the subsiding of directed thought and sustained evaluation, one enters a state of concentration born of rapture and attains the second dhyāna;
relinquishing rapture, one attains right mindfulness and, endowed with the faculty of pleasure, attains the third dhyāna.
Having abandoned pleasure and pain, one attains pure mindfulness and enters the faculty of equanimity, attaining the fourth dhyāna and obtaining the retribution of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).
Another teacher says that this state is called liberation;
however, once one has awakened from that meditative absorption, one then realizes it is not a place of liberation.
Free from the perception of form, one enters the sphere of infinite space;
with the cessation of the perception of resistance, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;
with the cessation of the perception of infinite consciousness, contemplating only a single consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness.
Free from various perceptions, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this state is called ultimate liberation, the further shore for all those in training.
"If the Prince wishes to sever the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, he ought to practice and study such conduct as this.
At that time, having heard the words of the seer, the Prince’s heart was not gladdened.
He then reflected to himself:
"What he knows and sees is not the ultimate state; it does not constitute the permanent severance of all fetters and afflictions.
He then spoke these words:
"I now have something within the Dharma you have taught that I do not yet understand, and I wish to question you about it.
The rishi replied, "I respectfully welcome your inquiry."
He then asked him: "In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is there a self,
or is there no self?"
If one says there is no self, one should not say it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception";
if one says there is a self, is that self conscious or is it unconscious?
If I were without cognition, I would be the same as wood or stone;
if I possess cognition, then there is objective grasping (*ālambana*). Since there is grasping, there is defiled attachment; because of this attachment, there is no liberation.
Because you have exhausted the gross fetters yet do not realize that subtle fetters still remain, you consider yourself to have reached the ultimate goal;
however, as these subtle fetters continue to grow, you will again undergo rebirth in the lower realms. For this reason, it is known that you have not crossed to the other shore.
"If one can eliminate the self and the notion of a self, relinquishing everything entirely, this is what is called true liberation.
The rishi remained silent, reflecting within his mind:
"What the Prince has said is most subtle and profound."
At that time, the Prince again asked the seer:
"At what age did you leave the household life?
And how many years have passed since you began practicing the holy life?"
The seer replied,
"I left home at the age of sixteen, and it has been one hundred and four years since I began practicing the holy life.
Having heard this, the prince thought to himself:
"Since I left the household life until now, such a long time has passed, yet the Dharma I have attained is truly like this?
At that moment, the Prince, seeking the supreme Dharma, rose from his seat and took his leave of the rishi.
At that time, the seer said to the prince:
"I have practiced this asceticism for a long time, yet the fruit I have obtained is merely this;
you are of royal lineage—how could you possibly practice such asceticism?"
The Prince replied, "What you practice is not the ultimate suffering; there is another path that is most painful and difficult to perform.

Having observed the Prince's wisdom and seeing that his resolve was firm and unyielding, and knowing that he would certainly attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), the seer addressed the Prince, saying:
"If you achieve the Way, I pray that you will deliver me first.
Thereupon, the Prince replied, "Excellent!"
Next, he went to the place where Kālāma resided; the debates and questions and answers were likewise the same, and the Prince then proceeded forward on his way.
At that time, seeing the Prince depart, the two sages each thought to themselves:
"The Prince’s wisdom is profound, subtle, and extraordinary, such that it is difficult to fathom."
With palms joined, they escorted him away, and only when his figure vanished from their sight did they return.

At that time, having subdued the two seers Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra, the Prince proceeded forward to the forest of asceticism on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, the dwelling place of the five men, including Kauṇḍinya;
there, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he sat in quiet meditation and reflection.
"Observing the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings, it would be appropriate to deliver them through six years of ascetic practice.
Having reflected thus, he undertook asceticism;
thereupon, the devas offered him hemp and rice.
For the sake of seeking the true and correct Way, the Prince maintained a pure mind and observed the precepts, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice daily;
even when there were beggars, he gave these to them as well.

"At that time, the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, having seen the Prince sitting upright in contemplation and practicing austerities—sometimes eating a single sesame seed per day, or a single grain of rice per day, or again eating a single sesame seed or grain of rice every two days, up to every seven days—[were moved]."
At that time, Kauṇḍinya and the others were also practicing austerities, attending upon the Prince and never leaving his side;
having witnessed this, they immediately dispatched one man back to inform the King’s preceptor and the great ministers, detailing everything the Prince had done.

At that time, the royal preceptor and the great ministers returned together to the palace gate; their countenances were haggard with grief and their bodies were withered and emaciated, like men who, having lost a close relative and finished the funeral rites, return home while suppressing their sorrow.
At that time, the gatekeeper addressed the king, saying, "The teacher and the great minister are now outside the gate.
Upon hearing this, the king’s breath rushed out and his voice failed him; only his head and body moved slightly. The gatekeeper, understanding the king's intention, immediately called them forward.
When the king met with them, he was so overcome with grief that he could not speak;
after a long while, he asked in a low voice:
"The Prince is my very life. Now that you have returned alone, how can my life survive?"
The royal preceptor replied:
"Having received the King’s command to seek the Prince, I went to the dwelling place of the seer Bhārgava to inquire after him;
the seer told me where the Prince was and recounted the words the Prince had spoken."

I then proceeded forward, and midway along the road, I encountered the Prince sitting upright in contemplation beneath a tree; his marks and signs were radiant, surpassing the light of the sun and moon.
I immediately approached the Prince and fully recounted the state of grief and suffering felt by the Great King, Mahāprajāpatī, and Yaśodharā.
The Crown Prince then replied with a deep and solemn voice:
"How could I not know that my father the King’s affection for his kin is profound?
It is only because I fear the suffering of birth, death, and the pain of parting from those I love that I have come here, desiring to sever and eliminate it."
"Though addressed with such various words as these, his resolve remains as firm as Mount Sumeru, unshakable; he abandons me and departs, as if discarding a blade of grass."
At that time, he immediately selected five men to follow and attend him, observing his whereabouts.
Among those dispatched, one man returned and reported:
"The Prince shall go to the hermitage of the seers Ārāḍa and Kālāma; traveling by way of the Ganges, he will cross the river through the power of a deva and arrive at Rājagṛha."

At that time, King Bimbisāra came to visit the Prince and, through skillful means and parables, urged him not to leave the household life, offering to share the kingdom with him or even to give it to him entirely, as well as wishing to provide him with an army to conquer other kingdoms;
yet the Prince accepted none of these things. He then proceeded further until he reached the abode of a rishi, where he preached the Dharma and subdued his mind.

Subsequently, he went to the forest of asceticism on Mount Gayā, by the side of the Nairañjanā River, where he sat in silent meditation and reflected, subsisting on only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these words from the royal preceptor and the great minister regarding the messenger, was filled with great sorrow and distress;
his entire body trembled and the hairs on his skin stood on end.
He then spoke to the royal preceptor and the ministers, saying:
"The prince has utterly renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and the joys of affection for his parents and kinsmen to dwell far away in the deep mountains, practicing these ascetic penances;
I am now of meager merit, having lost such a precious son at birth."
The King then repeated what the messenger had said to Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā, explaining it to them.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately prepared five hundred chariots, while Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā likewise each provided five hundred; all necessities of life were fully provided.
He immediately summoned Chandaka and said to him:
"You have escorted the Prince far away into the deep mountains; now I further command you to lead these thousand chariots, laden with provisions, to deliver them to the Prince.
Provide for his needs at all times so that he lacks for nothing, and when this is finished, come back again to invite me."
"Chanda, having received the command, immediately led a thousand chariots and departed with great speed.
Upon reaching the Prince’s location, he saw that his form was emaciated, skin and bone joined together, and his veins all visible like *pāṭala* flowers.
He prostrated himself at the Prince’s feet, fell unconscious upon the ground, and after a long while, rose and spoke through his tears:"

"Your Majesty has not ceased thinking of the Prince day or night; for this reason, I have now been sent to lead these thousand chariots, carrying provisions for daily life, to provide sustenance for the Prince."
At that time, the Prince replied to Chandaka, saying:
"I have disobeyed my parents and abandoned my kingdom to come here from afar for the sake of seeking the ultimate Way."
"How could I possibly accept these provisions again?
At that time, having heard these words, Chandaka thought to himself:
"Since the Prince now refuses to accept such offerings, I shall seek out another person to lead these thousand chariots back to the King's presence, while I remain here to serve the Prince."
He immediately dispatched one man to lead the chariot away.
Thereupon, Chandaka attended the Prince in secret, never leaving him for even a moment from dawn until dusk.
At that time, the Prince thought to himself:
"Today I eat but one sesame seed and one grain of rice; even for seven days I have eaten but one sesame seed and one grain of rice. My body has become emaciated, like withered wood.
I practiced asceticism for nearly six years, yet I did not attain liberation; therefore, I know this is not the Way.
It is not as when I was formerly beneath the Jambu tree, contemplating the Dharma, free from desire and in tranquility—that is the most true and correct."
If I were now to attain the Way with this emaciated body, those non-Buddhists would claim that self-starvation is the cause of parinirvāṇa.
Although I now possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa in every limb, I shall not attain the fruit of the Way by means of this; rather, I must receive food before I can achieve enlightenment.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, went to the Nairañjanā River, and entered the water to bathe.
When his bathing was finished, his body was so emaciated that he could not emerge on his own;
a deva descended and pressed down a tree branch for him, by which he was able to grasp it and exit the pool.
At that time, outside the forest, there was a cowherd woman named Nandabalā. Then, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven descended and exhorted her, saying:
"The Prince is currently in this forest; you should make offerings to him."
Upon hearing this, the woman was filled with great joy; at that moment, a thousand-petaled lotus flower spontaneously emerged from the earth, and upon the flower was milk-gruel.
When the woman saw this, she was struck with wonder; she immediately took the milk gruel, went to the Prince’s location, prostrated herself at his feet, and offered it to him.
The Prince then accepted the girl’s offering and recited this prayer for her:
"May this food now offered cause those who eat it to gain strength and vigor;
may it cause the donor's family to attain courage and joy, to dwell in peace and freedom from illness, to preserve their lifespan until the end, and to be fully endowed with wisdom."
The Prince then spoke again in this way:
"I accept this food for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
Having finished the prayer of blessing, he immediately accepted and ate it.
His body was radiant and pleasing, his physical strength was fully restored, and he was capable of attaining bodhi.
At that time, when the five men saw this, they were startled and marveled at it; thinking that he had regressed from his resolve, they each returned to their respective dwellings.
The Bodhisattva proceeded alone toward the Pippala tree and made this vow:
"Seated beneath that tree, if my Way is not accomplished, I shall certainly not rise."
The Bodhisattva’s virtue was so profound that the earth could not support his weight; at every step he took, the ground shook and a great sound resounded.
At that time, the blind dragon, hearing the sound of the earth trembling, felt great joy in his heart, and his two eyes opened wide with clarity:
"I have seen such auspicious omens before in the presence of previous Buddhas."
Having formed this thought, he leaped forth from the earth and prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet.
At that time, five hundred blue jays flew up into the void and circled the Bodhisattva to the right;
variegated auspicious clouds and fragrant winds followed, illuminating and brushing against him.
At that time, the blind nāga praised him with a verse:
“Wherever the Bodhisattva’s feet tread, The earth quakes in six ways;
A great, deep, and far-reaching sound arises, And upon hearing it, my eyes open and become clear.”
Furthermore, I saw in the void blue magpies circling the Bodhisattva;
auspicious clouds were exceedingly bright and radiant, and the fragrant breeze was most cool.
These auspicious signs of the Bodhisattva are entirely identical to those of the Buddhas of the past.
"By this I know that the Bodhisattva will certainly attain perfect enlightenment.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:
"Upon what seat did the Buddhas of the past sit when they attained the Unsurpassed Way?"
He then realized for himself that he would use grass as his seat.
Śakra-devānām-indra transformed himself into an ordinary man and held some clean, soft grass.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What is your name? He replied, "My name is Śrī."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was filled with great joy, thinking, "I have dispelled inauspiciousness and shall thereby achieve auspiciousness.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"May I have those blades of grass from your hand?"
Thereupon, Śiva immediately offered the grass to the Bodhisattva.
He then made this vow:
"When the Bodhisattva attains the Way, I pray that you will deliver me first."
Having accepted them, the Bodhisattva spread them out to serve as his seat and sat upon the grass in the full lotus posture,
making this vow: "In accordance with the manner in which past Buddhas sat,
I shall not rise from this seat until I have attained perfect enlightenment."
"I am likewise so. When he made this vow, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all rejoiced; cool and pleasant breezes blew from the four directions;

birds and beasts ceased their cries; trees did not rustle their branches; wandering clouds and flying dust were all cleared and purified. Knowing this to be a Bodhisattva, they recognized it as the sign that he would surely attain the Way.

"At that time, when the Bodhisattva made his vow beneath the tree, the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, were all filled with joy; they leaped for joy in the midst of the void and offered their praise."
At that time, the palace of Māra, the King of the Sixth Heaven, shook spontaneously;
thereupon, Māra’s heart was filled with great distress and his spirit was agitated. Unable to control his senses of sound and taste, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is now beneath a tree, having renounced the five desires and sitting upright in contemplation; before long, he shall attain the Way of Perfect Enlightenment."
‘Once his path is perfected, he will extensively deliver all beings and transcend my realm.
Before his path is perfected, I shall go to ruin and disorder it.
At that time, the son of Māra, Satata, seeing his father’s emaciated state, went to him and said:
“Father King, I do not understand why you are so sorrowful.
The Māra replied, “The śramaṇa Gautama is now sitting beneath a tree; his Way is about to be perfected, surpassing even mine, and I now wish to destroy it.”
The son of Māra immediately stepped forward and admonished his father, saying:

"The Bodhisattva is pure and has transcended the triple world; his supernormal powers and wisdom are such that there is nothing he does not clearly understand. The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, all join in praising him."
"This is not something that even our father, the King, could have overcome; there is no need to commit evil and bring calamity upon yourself.

Māra had three daughters whose physical forms and features were exceedingly beautiful, seductive and artfully alluring, capable of bewitching men, and the foremost among celestial maidens. They were perfumed with famous incense and adorned with fine necklaces: the first was named Rañjanī (Staining Desire);
the second was named Manoharā (Captivating the Mind).
The three daughters were lovely and delightful;
they all stepped forward together and said to their father,
"We do not know for what reason you are now so sorrowful."
The father immediately wrote down his thoughts and said to his daughters:

"In this world there is now a śramaṇa Gautama, who has donned the armor of the Dharma, grasped the bow of mastery, and fixed the arrow of wisdom; he seeks to subdue sentient beings and destroy my realm."
"If I am not superior, the sentient beings will believe in him and all will take refuge in him; my land would then become empty, and for this reason I am grieved.
Furthermore, before he has attained the Way, I wish to go and crush him, destroying his bridge."
Thereupon, the Māra King took up a powerful bow and held five arrows;
together with his retinue of sons and daughters, they all went at once to the foot of that Pippala tree.
He beheld the Muni, serene and unmoving, desiring to cross the ocean of the three realms of existence and birth-and-death.
At that time, the King of Māras took up his bow with his left hand and adjusted an arrow with his right, saying to the Bodhisattva:
"You of the Kṣatriya caste, death is truly terrifying; why do you not rise quickly?"

"You ought to cultivate the karma of a Wheel-Turning King; you should abandon the way of renunciation and instead practice the giving of alms-offerings to attain the bliss of rebirth in heaven—this path is the foremost, most excellent, and previously practiced.
You belong to the Kṣatriya lineage of Wheel-Turning Kings, yet you have become a mendicant; this is not what is appropriate for you."
"If you do not rise now, simply remain seated comfortably and do not abandon your original vow.

I shall test you by discharging a single sharp arrow; when ascetic seers hear the sound of my arrow, there is none who is not struck with terror and loses their senses—how much less could you, Gautama, endure such a poison?"
"If you rise quickly, you may attain safety.
When Māra spoke these words to terrify the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva remained serene, neither startled nor shaken;
the Demon King immediately drew his bow and loosed an arrow, while simultaneously advancing with the celestial maidens.
At that time, the Bodhisattva did not look at the arrow; it remained suspended in mid-air with its point facing downward, transforming into a lotus flower.
Then the three celestial maidens addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Benevolent One of supreme virtue, revered by devas and humans, you ought to have attendants to serve you."
"We are currently in the prime of our youth; among the celestial maidens, none is more beautiful than we.
Since the Lord has now sent us to provide for you, we pray to serve at your side through morning and evening, and while you sleep."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"You have planted small roots of merit and attained this celestial body, yet you do not contemplate impermanence and instead practice seductive charms. Though your physical form is beautiful, your mind is not upright; your lustful delusions are unwholesome, and upon death you will surely fall into the three evil realms to receive the bodies of birds and beasts, from which it is extremely difficult to escape.
You now wish to disturb my settled mind with an impure heart; you may leave at once, for I have no need of you."

At that time, the three celestial maidens transformed themselves into old crones with white hair and wrinkled faces; their teeth had fallen out and they drooled, their flesh wasted away until they stood as mere skeletons, their bellies as large as drums, walking feebly with staffs, unable to support themselves.
When the Māra King beheld such steadfastness, he thought to himself:
"In the past, while I was in the Snowy Mountains, I shot at this Maheśvara, who immediately became terrified and withdrew his virtuous resolve;
yet now he cannot be moved by Gautama. Since neither this arrow nor my three daughters can cause him to waver or give rise to desire or hatred," [he concluded].
"I must employ yet another expedient.
He then addressed the Bodhisattva with gentle words, saying:
"If you do not delight in receiving human pleasures, you may now ascend to the celestial palaces."
"I relinquish my celestial rank and all the five sensory pleasures; I give them all to you.
The Bodhisattva replied, "In a previous life, you cultivated the cause of a small gift, and for that reason, you have now become the sovereign King of Devas."
"This merit has its limit; one must eventually return to be born below, sinking into the three miserable realms, from which it is extremely difficult to escape and be rescued.
This is a cause for transgression, not something I require.
Thus the Māra spoke to the Bodhisattva.
"The karmic retribution of myself is what you know;
but as for the karmic retribution of yourself, who else could possibly know it?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Only this earth knows of my karmic retribution.
As soon as he had spoken these words, the great earth shook in six ways.
Thereupon, an earth goddess emerged from the ground holding a vase made of the seven precious gems, filled with lotus flowers, and addressed Māra, saying:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva gave his head, eyes, marrow, and brain to others; the blood he shed drenched the great earth.
He bestowed kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, and precious jewels in incalculable amounts.
For the sake of seeking the unsurpassed, truly correct path, for this reason, you should not now disturb or harass the Bodhisattva."
Upon hearing this, Māra was struck with fear and his hair stood on end;
at that moment, the earth goddess prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet, made offerings of flowers, and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Māra King thought to himself:

"I have used my powerful bow and sharp arrows, as well as my three daughters, and even employed skillful means and conciliatory speech to entice him, yet I have been unable to corrupt or disturb the mind of this Gautama."
"Now I shall employ various skillful means to assemble a vast multitude of troops and compel him by force.

While he was thinking this, a great host of soldiers suddenly arrived, filling the void of space; their appearances were diverse: some held halberds and wielded swords, some had great trees upon their heads, and some grasped golden pestles; they were fully equipped with all manner of weapons of war.
Others had the heads of pigs, fish, donkeys, horses, lions, dragons, bears, brown bears, tigers, rhinoceroses, and various other beasts.
Some have many heads on a single body;
some have a single eye in each face;
others have many eyes.
Some have large bellies and long bodies;
some are emaciated and without bellies;
some have long legs and large knees.
Some have large feet and thick calves;
some have long claws and sharp fangs;
some have their heads positioned upon their chests.
Some have two feet and many bodies;
some have large faces or faces on their sides;
some are the color of ash or dust.
Some emit smoke and flames from their bodies;
some carry mountains on their elephant-like forms;
others have disheveled hair and go naked.
Or again, their facial complexion may be half red and half white;
or their lips may hang down to the ground;
or they may be drawn upward to cover [the face].
Their faces or bodies were covered in tiger skins;
or lion or snake skins;
or their bodies were entirely entwined by snakes.
Some had flames burning upon their heads;
some glared with eyes wide and arms tensed;
some moved sideways or leaped and hurled themselves about.
Some whirled in the air;
some ran about, roaring and threatening.
There were such various forms of evil beings, beyond counting, who surrounded the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, some wished to tear apart the Bodhisattva’s body;

smoke arose from the four directions, its flames surging toward heaven; wild sounds erupted, shaking the mountains and valleys; wind, fire, smoke, and dust darkened everything until nothing could be seen;
and the waters of the four great oceans surged and boiled all at once.
"The devas who protect the Dharma, along with the nāgas, ghosts, and others, all grew indignant toward the hosts of Māra; their wrath intensified until blood flowed from the pores of their skin.
The assembly of Śuddhāvāsa devas, seeing this evil Māra harassing and disturbing the Bodhisattva, felt compassion and took pity upon him."
Thereupon they descended, filling the void of space.
Seeing the hosts of Māra, immeasurable and boundless, surrounding the Bodhisattva and raising a great, evil clamor that shook heaven and earth, the Bodhisattva remained steadfast in mind,
his countenance showing no sign of change, like a lion dwelling amidst a herd of deer.
They all exclaimed in praise: "Aha! How marvelous!
This has never occurred before; the Bodhisattva shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment."
These hosts of Māras urged one another on, each exerting their full power to crush the Bodhisattva;
some glared with bared teeth,
while others flew about wildly, hurling things in disorder.
The Bodhisattva regarded them as the play of children;
Māra, becoming increasingly sorrowful, resentful, and enraged, further increased his military forces.
By the power of his compassion, the Bodhisattva caused those who were carrying stones to be unable to lift them.
As for those who excel in martial prowess, they cannot strike downward;
flying blades and brandished swords are suspended in mid-air;
lightning, thunder, rain, and fire become five-colored flowers.
The evil dragons spat forth poison, which was transformed into fragrant breezes;
various malevolent forms sought to destroy the Bodhisattva, yet were unable to move him.
Māra had two sisters, one named Meghā and the other named Kālī; each held a skull-bowl in her hand and stood before the Bodhisattva, assuming various strange postures to disturb and vex him.
These hosts of Māras, with their various hideous forms, sought to terrify the Bodhisattva, yet in the end they could not move even a single hair on his body;
the Māras became even more sorrowful. A deity named Bhūta, who was in the air, remained invisible and spoke:
"I have now seen the Honored Muni; his mind is serene and free from thoughts of resentment."
These hosts of Māras give rise to poisonous minds, recklessly generating anger toward those who harbor no enmity.
These deluded and evil Māras merely exhaust themselves in vain, gaining nothing at all.
Today you ought to abandon thoughts of malice and harm; for you might as well be able to blow away Mount Sumeru until it collapses,
or make fire cold, or make water hot.
The nature of earth, though firm and solid, can be made supple;

yet you cannot destroy the four merits cultivated by the Bodhisattva over kalpas—namely, the fruits of wholesome deeds, right contemplation and concentration, diligent skillful means, and the pure light of wisdom—which no one is able to sever or obstruct.
You may create hindrances, but you shall not prevent his attainment of perfect enlightenment, for just as the light of a thousand suns must necessarily dispel the darkness.
By drilling wood one obtains fire; by digging the earth one finds water. Through diligent application of skillful means, there is nothing that cannot be attained.

Sentient beings in the world are submerged in the three poisons, and none have a savior; out of compassion, the Bodhisattva seeks the medicine of wisdom to eliminate their afflictions for the sake of the world.
Why do you now trouble and disturb him?
The sentient beings of the world are deluded, ignorant, and entirely attached to false views;
he now establishes the eye of Dharma and cultivates the right path, desiring to guide all beings.
How can you now trouble and disturb the Guide?
This is utterly impossible.
It would be like attempting to deceive the merchant leader while he is in the midst of a vast wilderness.
Sentient beings have fallen into the midst of great darkness, bewildered and ignorant of where they abide; the Bodhisattva has lit for them the lamp of great wisdom.
How can you now wish to blow it out?
Sentient beings are now submerged in the ocean of birth and death; the Bodhisattva has constructed a precious ship of wisdom for their sake.
Why do you now wish to cause them to drown?
With patience as its sprouts and firmness as its roots, the unsurpassed Great Dharma constitutes its great fruit.
Why do you now wish to wage war?
The fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion bind all sentient beings; through his ascetic practices, the Bodhisattva seeks to liberate them.
Today, he will certainly sit here beneath this tree in the full lotus posture and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
This ground is the adamantine seat of all past Buddhas;
while other directions may turn, this place remains unmoving. It is capable of sustaining sublime meditative concentration and cannot be destroyed by you.
"You should now give rise to a heart of joy and celebration, set aside your prideful thoughts, cultivate the perception of him as a spiritual friend, and serve him.

At that time, the Māra King heard the voice from the sky and, seeing that the Bodhisattva remained serene and unchanged, felt shame and remorse in his heart; he abandoned his arrogance and immediately retraced his path, returning to his celestial palace.

The hosts of māras were filled with grief and anxiety; they all dispersed and fled, their spirits crushed and their martial prowess vanished, leaving their various weapons of war strewn haphazardly across the forests and wilds.
When the evil Māras had retreated and dispersed, the Bodhisattva’s mind was pure, serene, and unmoving.
The heavens were free of smoke and mist; the wind did not sway the branches;
and as the setting sun paused its light, it shone with even greater brilliance.
The clear moon shone with penetrating brilliance, and the myriad stars gleamed radiantly;
even the most secluded and dark recesses were no longer obscured by shadows.
The devas in the void rained down exquisite flowers and perfumes, performing various musical arts as an offering to the Bodhisattva.
"At that time, by the power of his compassion, the Bodhisattva, having subdued Māra on the night of the seventh day of the second month, emitted a great radiance;
he then entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to contemplate the ultimate truths. Within all phenomena, he attained mastery in dhyāna.

He fully knew the good and evil deeds performed in the past, as well as the transitions from this life to the next, the parents and kinsmen, wealth and poverty, nobility and lowliness, longevity and brevity of life, and even names and surnames—all of which he understood with perfect clarity. Thereupon, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings."
And he thought to himself:
"All sentient beings have no one to rescue them; they transmigrate through the five realms of existence, not knowing the ford for escape. All things are entirely false and devoid of reality;
yet within them, suffering and pleasure arise pointlessly."
Reflecting thus, he reached the end of the first watch of the night.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva reached the middle watch, he immediately attained the divine eye;
he observed the world and saw through it all clearly, as if beholding the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror.
He saw that sentient beings are of immeasurable kinds, dying here and being born there, receiving retributions of suffering or joy according to their good or evil deeds.
He saw sentient beings being tortured and punished in the hells: some had molten copper poured into their mouths;
others were forced to embrace red-hot copper pillars.
Some lie upon iron beds;
some are boiled in iron cauldrons;
and some are roasted on spits over fires.
Some are devoured by tigers, wolves, hawks, or dogs;
others, seeking refuge from fire beneath trees, find their bodies sliced and mangled as the falling leaves turn into swords and blades;
some have their limbs hacked and dismembered with axes and saws.
Some are cast into rivers of boiling ashes;
others are thrown into pits of excrement.
They undergo all such various sufferings, yet due to the retribution of their karma, they do not die at the end of their lives.
Having witnessed such matters, the Bodhisattva reflected in his mind:
"These sentient beings originally committed evil deeds for the sake of worldly pleasure, yet now they have obtained a fruit that is nothing but great suffering;
if anyone were to see such an evil retribution, they should never again entertain thoughts of unwholesome action."
"At that time, the Bodhisattva further observed the animals, who, according to their various karmic actions, undergo diverse and loathsome forms;
some are killed for the sake of their bones, flesh, sinews, horns, hides, tusks, or feathers;
others are made to carry heavy burdens for humans, suffering from extreme hunger and thirst, yet no one takes note of them."
Some have their noses pierced;
some have their heads hooked;
they constantly offer their own flesh to others, and in turn, they devour one another among their own kind.
Experiencing such various sufferings as these, the Bodhisattva, having seen them, gave rise to great compassion and reflected:

"These sentient beings constantly provide for others with their physical labor, yet they are further subjected to the sufferings of flogging, hunger, and thirst; all of this is the karmic retribution for the evil deeds they have previously cultivated."
"At that time, the Bodhisattva next observed the hungry ghosts;
he saw that they dwell perpetually in darkness, never having even momentarily beheld the light of the sun or moon;
even those of their own kind do not see one another."
Having received this physical form, they grow large with bellies like Mount Tai, yet their throats are like needles; within their mouths, a great fire constantly blazes.
They are perpetually tormented by hunger and thirst for billions of years, never hearing the sound of food;
even if they encounter rain falling upon them, it turns into fiery pearls.
At times, when they approach rivers, seas, ponds, or streams, the water immediately transforms into molten copper and glowing coals;
the sound of their bodies moving and taking a step is like that of a person pulling five hundred wagons, and every joint and limb of their bodies is completely ablaze with fire.
Having seen them undergoing such various sufferings as these, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and reflects to himself:
"All of these beings now undergo this retribution for their sins because they originally practiced stinginess and greed, amassing wealth without practicing giving."
If one sees another undergoing such suffering, one ought to practice generosity without giving rise to stinginess;
even if one possesses no wealth, one should cut off one's own flesh to use for the sake of giving.

“At that time, the Bodhisattva next observed human beings; he saw them beginning to enter the womb from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), when their parents unite and, through perverted perceptions, give rise to thoughts of love.
They then take what is impure as their own body.
Once situated within the womb, between the receptacle for undigested food and the receptacle for digested food, their bodies are scorched and steamed, suffering like those in hell.”
Only after ten months have been fulfilled is one finally born;
at the moment of birth, one is held and grasped by outsiders, experiencing coarse and painful sensations as if being struck by swords and blades.
Not long after this, one returns once more to old age and death, becoming an infant again and revolving through the five realms of existence, unable to awaken on one's own.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and reflects to himself:

"All sentient beings suffer from such afflictions as these; why is it that amidst them, they remain addicted to the five desires, recklessly imagining them to be pleasure, and are unable to sever the root of their delusions?"

"At that time, the Bodhisattva next observed the various devas. He saw those sons of gods whose bodies were pure and free from dust and grime, like genuine lapis lazuli, possessing great radiance and blinking neither eye;
some dwelt upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, while others resided at the four corners of Mount Sumeru."
Or again, they may dwell within the midst of empty space;
their minds are always joyful, with nothing that causes them displeasure, as they entertain themselves with the sublime music of the heavens, unaware of day or night;
throughout the four directions and all realms of existence, there is nothing that is not exquisitely wondrous.
Gazing toward the east with such attachment that he forgot to turn for years;
looking toward the west with such immersion that he did not return for years;
and so it was likewise for the south and north.
Food, drink, and clothing arrive as soon as they are thought of.
Although such things provide him with satisfaction, he is still tormented by the fire of desire. Furthermore, when his heavenly merit is exhausted, the five signs of death appear:
first, the flowers upon his head wither.
Second, the eyes blink;
third, the light on the body fades away;
fourth, sweat breaks out from under the armpits.
Fifth, he spontaneously leaves his original seat.
When his retinue sees the five signs of death appearing upon the body of the devaputra, they feel deep affection and longing;
the devaputra likewise sees for himself that his own body bears these five signs of death.
Furthermore, seeing his retinue full of longing and attachment toward him, he experiences great anguish at that moment.
When the Bodhisattva sees those devas in such a state, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion and reflects to himself:
"These devas, having originally cultivated but little merit, have obtained celestial pleasures; yet as their karmic retribution is about to end, they give rise to great anguish."
Once their lives have ended and they have cast off that celestial body, some may fall into the three evil realms;
though they originally performed virtuous deeds in pursuit of pleasant retribution,
what they now obtain is little joy and much suffering, like a hungry person eating food mixed with poison— it may seem delicious at first, but in the end it becomes a great calamity.
How could a wise person take pleasure in this?
The devas of the form and formless realms, seeing that their lifespans are long, claim it is eternal bliss;
yet when they witness its decay and destruction, they give rise to great suffering and affliction, immediately conceiving false views and slandering the existence of cause and effect.
"Because of these matters, one wanders through the three miserable realms, undergoing all manner of sufferings.
With the power of his divine eye, the Bodhisattva observed the five destinies and gave rise to a heart of great compassion, reflecting to himself:
"Within the triple world, there is not a single joy."

Reflecting in this manner until the end of the middle watch of the night, the Bodhisattva then, during the third watch, contemplated the nature of sentient beings: "By what causes and conditions do old age and death come to be?"
One then knows that old age and death have birth as their root; if one is separated from birth, then there is no old age and death.
Furthermore, this birth does not arise from heaven, nor does it arise of itself;
it is not born without a condition, but arises from causes and conditions.
The existence of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) arises from karma.
Furthermore, when one contemplates from what these karmas of the three realms arise,
one knows that the karmas of the three realms arise from the four types of grasping (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, he contemplates from what the four types of clinging arise;
he immediately knows that the four types of clinging arise from craving.
He then further contemplates from what craving arises.
Even though he knows that craving arises from feeling,
he further contemplates from what feeling arises;
he then knows that feeling arises from contact.
Furthermore, he contemplates from what contact arises;
he immediately knows that contact arises from the six sense bases.
He then contemplates from what the six sense bases arise.
He then knows that the six sense bases arise from name-and-form.
Furthermore, he contemplates from what name-and-form arises;
he then knows that name-and-form arises from consciousness.
Furthermore, he contemplates from what consciousness arises;
he then knows that consciousness arises from formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, he contemplates from what formations arise.
Even though one knows that volitional formations arise from ignorance,
if ignorance is extinguished, then volitional formations are extinguished; if volitional formations are extinguished, then consciousness is extinguished.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of grasping, existence ceases;
with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
Thus, by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both direct and reverse order, he shattered ignorance during the third watch of the night;
as the light of dawn appeared, he attained the radiance of wisdom, severed the obstacles of habitual tendencies, and perfected all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself:
'The Eightfold Noble Path is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have practiced; it is the road leading to parinirvāṇa.
I have now trodden it; my wisdom has reached full penetration, and I am free from all obstructions.'"

At that time, the great earth shook in eighteen ways; drifting mists and flying dust were all completely cleared and purified. Celestial drums spontaneously produced wondrous sounds, and a fragrant breeze rose gently, soft and cool. Auspicious clouds of various colors descended as rain of nectar, and the flowers and fruits of the groves flourished beyond the need for their proper seasons.
Furthermore, there rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, golden flowers, silver flowers, and flowers of lapis lazuli;
as well as lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems, which surrounded the Bodhi tree, filling an area of thirty-six *yojanas*.

At that time, the various devas performed celestial music, scattered flowers, and burned incense; they sang hymns of praise, held celestial jeweled canopies, banners, and streamers, filling the void of space as they made offerings to the Tathāgata.
The offerings presented by the eight classes of dragon deities were likewise so.
At that time, all sentient beings were filled with loving-kindness and compassion, free from any thought of anger or malice.

They were filled with joy and exultation, as if beholding the traces of a sage; free from fear, their minds became gentle and pliant, and they were rid of arrogance, as well as any thoughts of stinginess, envy, flattery, or deception.
The gods of the five Pure Abodes, though already free from the faculty of joy and pleasure, were likewise filled with such rapture that they could not contain themselves;
even those in the hells found temporary relief from their agonies and gave rise to great joy.
All animals that prey upon one another no longer harbor malicious intent.
The hungry ghosts are fully satiated, free from any thought of hunger or thirst.
Within the world, even those dark and gloomy places that the majestic radiance of the sun and moon cannot illuminate, all become brilliantly bright.
The sentient beings therein were all able to see one another, each exclaiming:
"How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here?

Because the Great Sage, the Dharma King, has arisen in the world and, by means of the light of the Great Dharma, shattered the darkness of non-Dharma, he has caused everything to become perfectly clear and bright.
The former kings of the Ikṣvāku lineage abandoned their kingdoms to study the Way and became seers possessing the five supernatural powers;

furthermore, those who practiced the ten wholesome actions and were reborn in the heavens all traveled by means of their spiritual powers to the Bodhi tree. Remaining in mid-air, they joined their palms in joy and praised him, saying:
"Within our Ikṣvāku clan, you have been able to sever all outflows and achieve all-knowledge, becoming the Eye of the World—this is truly most extraordinary."
Everyone was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, except for the Māra King, whose heart alone was filled with sorrow.
At that time, the Tathāgata, for seven days, contemplated with single-minded focus upon the King of Trees, thinking to himself:
"In this place, I have exhausted all outflows; what was to be done is finished, and my original vow is fulfilled."
The Dharma I have attained is extremely profound and difficult to understand; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it.
All sentient beings in this world of five turbidities are shrouded and obstructed by greed, hatred, delusion, false views, arrogance, and deceit;
being of meager merit and dull faculties, they lack wisdom—how then could they understand the Dharma I have attained?

If I were now to turn the wheel of Dharma, they would surely be bewildered, unable to believe or accept it; instead, they would give rise to slander, fall into the evil realms, and undergo all manner of suffering.
"I would rather remain silent and enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke in verse:
"The Noble Path is exceedingly difficult to ascend; The fruit of wisdom is difficult to attain."
Within these challenges, I have already accomplished them all.
The wisdom I have attained is subtle, profound, and supreme;
yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull, and they are blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance.
"Flowing along with the current of birth and death, they are unable to turn back to its source;

how can such as these be delivered? At that time, after the Tathāgata had formed this thought, Great Brahmā King, seeing that the Tathāgata’s noble fruition was already accomplished yet remained silent and did not turn the wheel of Dharma, felt sorrow and distress in his heart and thought to himself:

“World-Honored One, in the past, for the sake of sentient beings, you remained long within birth and death for immeasurable billions of kalpas; you abandoned your kingdom, cities, wife, and children, as well as your head, eyes, marrow, and brain, undergoing all manner of sufferings. Only now has your original vow been fulfilled, and you have attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
"Why do you remain silent and not preach the Dharma?
For a long night, sentient beings have been submerged in birth and death; I shall now go to request that you turn the wheel of the Dharma.

Having formed this thought, he immediately departed from his celestial palace. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and then withdrew to stand to one side. Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, for the sake of sentient beings, the World-Honored One dwelt long in the cycle of birth and death;
he sacrificed his body, head, eyes, and marrow as offerings, underwent all manner of sufferings, and extensively cultivated the roots of virtue."
Having begun now to accomplish the unsurpassed path, why do you remain silent and not preach the Dharma?
Sentient beings have for a long night been submerged and drowned in birth and death, fallen into the darkness of ignorance, and it is extremely difficult for them to emerge.
However, there are sentient beings who, in past lives, drew near to virtuous friends, planted the roots of all virtues, were capable of hearing the Dharma, and received the Noble Path.
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, for the sake of these beings, will turn the sublime wheel of Dharma through the power of great compassion.

Śakra-devānām-indra, and likewise all the way up to the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, also made this request to the Tathāgata, entreating him to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the others, saying:

“I also wish to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; however, the Dharma I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep, difficult to understand and difficult to know.”
Sentient beings are unable to believe and accept this; they give rise to a mind of slander and fall into hell.
It is for their sake that I remain silent now.
At that time, the Brahma Kings and others made their request up to three times;
then the Tathāgata, having reached the completion of seven days, accepted it in silence.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted their invitation, the Brahma Kings and others prostrated themselves at his feet and each returned to their respective abodes.

"At that time, having accepted the invitation of the Brahma King and others, the World-Honored One further spent seven days observing all sentient beings with his Buddha-eye, examining their superior, middling, and inferior faculties, as well as their afflictions—whether inferior, middling, or superior. Thus, two full weeks passed."
At that time, the World-Honored One again reflected:
"I shall now open the Dharma-gate of the Deathless; who should be the first to hear it?"
"The seer Ārāḍa is wise and quick to understand; moreover, he previously made a vow that once he had attained the Way, he would deliver me.
While he was thinking this, a voice spoke from the air:
"The seer Ārāḍa passed away last night."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the voice from mid-air, saying:
"I also know that he passed away last night.
He then reflected further:
"The seer Kālaṇḍa was of sharp faculties and possessed clear understanding; he too should have heard it first.
Again, a voice spoke from the air:
"The seer Kālaṇḍa passed away last night."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied again, saying:
"I also know that he passed away last night.
Then, the World-Honored One further reflected to himself:

"Those five men, Kauṇḍinya and the others, who were sent by the king’s preceptor and great ministers to attend upon me, are all wise; furthermore, in a past life, they made a vow that they should be the first to hear the Dharma from me.
It is now fitting that I should open the gateway of the Dharma for these five men first."
He further reflected to himself:
"In the past, all Buddhas who turned the Wheel of Dharma did so at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park of Vārāṇasī; furthermore, the place where these five men reside is also there.
I should now go to that dwelling and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma."
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat and proceeded toward the country of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants traveling through a wilderness, with two men as their leaders: one named Bhadrasena and the other named Bhadraruci.
At that time, a deva spoke to him, saying:
"There is one who is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who has appeared in the world;
he is the supreme field of merit, and you should now be the very first to present offerings to him."
Then that merchant, having heard the words of the deity, replied to him, saying:
"Excellent! It shall be as you have told me."
He asked the deva again,
"Where is the World-Honored One now? The deva replied:
"The World-Honored One will arrive here before long.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, preceded and followed by immeasurable devas, arrived at the village of Dvāravatī.
At that time, the merchant, having beheld the Tathāgata’s majestic appearance and adornments, and seeing him surrounded before and behind by the devas, felt redoubled joy;
he then immediately offered honey-gruel to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The Buddhas of the past used the *pātra* (alms bowl) to receive their food.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing the Buddha's thoughts, each brought a bowl and came to where the Buddha was, offering them to him.
Thereupon the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If I now accept the bowl of only one king, the other kings will surely give rise to feelings of resentment.
He then accepted the bowls of all four kings, stacking them upon his palm, pressing them together so they became one, while causing the four rims to remain visible.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately offered this prayer of blessing:
"May those who now receive this gift have their physical strength replenished;
may those who give it obtain a healthy complexion, physical vigor, courage, and joy."
May you be peaceful, well, and free from illness, preserving your life-span until its end;
may all benevolent spirits and deities constantly follow and protect you;
through the giving of food, may you sever the roots of the three poisons and shall, in the future, obtain the retribution of the three steadfast dharmas.
Possessing intelligence and wisdom, they will have profound faith in the Buddha-dharma;
in every place where they are born, their right view shall never be obscured.
In this present life, their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen shall all flourish and prosper, free from all calamities, portents, and inauspicious events.

If, among my family and clan, there should be those whose lives have ended and who have fallen into the evil realms, may they, by virtue of the merit of these current offerings, be reborn among humans or devas; may they not give rise to false views, but instead increase their merit;
may they always be able to attend upon and draw near to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
may they hear the wondrous teachings, realize the Truth, attain realization, and have all their aspirations fulfilled.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his incantation and blessing, immediately accepted the food.
When the meal was concluded, he rinsed his mouth and washed his bowl, and then bestowed the Three Refuges upon the merchants:
first, taking refuge in the Buddha;
Second, he took refuge in the Dharma;
third, he took refuge in the Sangha of the future.
Having completed the three refuges, he parted from him and proceeded forward, his deportment composed and dignified, his gait like that of a king of geese.

On the road he encountered an outsider named Upaka; seeing that the Tathāgata was adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and that his faculties were tranquil and composed, he marveled at this wonder and spoke these verses:
"All sentient beings in the world Are bound by the three poisons;
Their faculties are light and fickle, Racing and wandering among external objects."
Now that I behold you, O virtuous one, your faculties are utterly tranquil;
you have surely reached the stage of liberation, of this there is no doubt.
As for the teacher from whom you have studied, what are his name and clan?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"I have now transcended The realm of all sentient beings;
The subtle, wondrous, and profound Dharma— I have now fully realized it."
The realms of the three poisons and five desires, he has forever severed without remainder;
like a lotus in the water, he is unstained by the muddy silt.
Having personally realized the Eightfold Noble Path, he is without teacher and without equal.
With pure wisdom, he has subdued the powerful Māra;
now having attained perfect enlightenment, he is worthy to be the Teacher of gods and humans.
Since his body, speech, and mind are perfected, he is thus called the Muni.
"I wish to proceed to Vārāṇasī to turn the wheel of the Deathless Dharma—
a wheel that neither gods, humans, Māras, nor Brahmās can ever turn.
When Upaga heard these verses, his heart was filled with joy, and he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
With palms joined in reverence, they circumambulated him and departed; looking back repeatedly, they stopped only when he was no longer in sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded further and arrived at the banks of the Ajapāla River; as evening fell, he stayed there for the night and entered meditative concentration.
At that time, there was wind and rain for seven days.
Within those waters, there was a great dragon king named Mucilinda; seeing the Buddha enter meditative concentration, he immediately encircled him with his body seven times.
When the seven days had passed, that dragon king transformed himself into human form, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, during these seven days here, did you not suffer greatly from the wind and rain?"
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“The joy of the five desires enjoyed by the various devas and the people of the world,
compared to the bliss of my meditative concentration, cannot serve as a metaphor.”
At that time, having heard these verses from the Buddha, the Dragon King was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his own abode.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded further on, traveling toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, until he reached the dwelling place of Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāma, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, and Vāṣpa.
At that time, those five men saw the Buddha approaching from afar and said to one another:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned his ascetic practices and returned to enjoy the pleasures of eating and drinking; he no longer possesses the mind for the Way."
Now that he has come here, we need not rise to welcome him; nor should we pay him homage, inquire after his needs, or prepare a seat for him. If he wishes to sit, let him do as he pleases.
Having spoken these words, they each remained silent.
At that time, when the World-Honored One arrived, the five men unconsciously rose from their seats, prostrating themselves to welcome him;
they took turns attending to his needs, with some even assisting him by carrying his robe and bowl.
Some took water for rinsing and cleansing; others washed their feet.
Each acted contrary to their original vows, yet they still addressed the Buddha as Gautama.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kauṇḍinya:
"You all made an agreement not to rise upon seeing me; for what reason now have you violated your prior vow and immediately risen in alarm to attend to my needs?"
At that time, those five men, hearing these words from the Buddha, felt deep shame and remorse, and immediately stepped forward and said:
"Gautama, in practicing the Way, have you not grown weary?"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the five men:
"How is it that you, toward one who is most honored and supreme, address him by his clan name with such haughty demeanor?"
My mind is like space; regarding all praise and blame, I make no distinctions.
It is only because of your arrogance that you invite this evil retribution.
For example, even in worldly etiquette, it is improper for a son to call his parents by name; how much more so am I now the parent of all beings?
At that time, those five men, hearing these words again, felt redoubled shame and remorse, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We were ignorant and lacked wisdom; we did not know that you had already attained perfect enlightenment."
Why is this? Previously, I saw the Tathāgata practicing austerities for six years, subsisting on a daily diet of hemp and rice; yet now he has returned to enjoying food and drink.
For this reason, I believe that he has not attained the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kauṇḍinya:
"Do not, by means of your limited wisdom, lightly measure whether my realization of the Way has been achieved or not. Why is this?"
When the form suffers, the mind becomes distressed and disordered;
when the body enjoys pleasure, the emotions become attached to it.
Therefore, both suffering and pleasure are not causes for the Way.
For example, if one pours water upon the fire produced by drilling for sparks, there will certainly be no light capable of dispelling darkness.
It is the same when drilling the fire of wisdom:
if there is the water of suffering and pleasure, the light of wisdom will not arise; because it does not arise, it cannot extinguish the dark obstruction of birth and death.

If one can now relinquish both suffering and pleasure and practice the Middle Way, the mind will become tranquil and concentrated, capable of cultivating that Noble Eightfold Path and departing from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"I have followed the practice of the Middle Way and attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

When those five men heard these words from the Tathāgata, their hearts were filled with great joy; they leaped for joy beyond measure, gazing up at his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the faculties of the five men were capable of receiving the Way, spoke to them, saying: "Kauṇḍinya!

You should know that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of losing prosperity and joy."
Kauṇḍinya! Whether possessing form or being formless, footless, one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—among all sentient beings, there are none who do not possess such suffering.
It is like covering fire with ashes; if it encounters dry grass, it will once again burst into flames.
All such sufferings have the self as their root;
if any sentient being gives rise to even a subtle notion of "I," they will once again undergo such suffering.
Greed, hatred, and delusion all arise, taking the self as their fundamental condition.
Furthermore, these three poisons are the causes of all suffering;
just as seeds can produce sprouts, sentient beings cycle through the three realms of existence because of them.
If one extinguishes the notion of self along with greed, hatred, and delusion, all sufferings will likewise be severed from their source.
There is nothing that does not proceed from those Eightfold Noble Paths, just as one might extinguish a raging fire by pouring water upon it.
All sentient beings who do not know the root of all suffering will continue to transmigrate within the cycle of birth and death.
Kauṇḍinya! Suffering should be known; its origin should be abandoned; its cessation should be realized; and the path should be cultivated. Kauṇḍinya!
Because I have known suffering, abandoned its origin, realized its cessation, and cultivated the path, I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, you now should likewise know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.
If a person does not know the Four Noble Truths, it should be known that this person will not attain liberation.
These Four Noble Truths are true and real:
suffering is truly suffering, its origin is truly its origin, its cessation is truly its cessation, and the path is truly the path.
"Kauṇḍinya! Do you understand? Kauṇḍinya replied:
"Understood, World-Honored One! Known, World-Honored One!
Because he had attained understanding and knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths, he was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

"When the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths in its twelve aspects for the third time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, regarding all dharmas, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye."
At that time, eighty thousand nayutas of devas in the void sky also became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
