Then, the Earth Deity, seeing the Tathāgata within her domain turning the wheel of the Dharma, was filled with great joy in her heart.
He cried out in a loud voice:
"The Tathāgata is here, turning the sublime Wheel of Dharma!

Upon hearing these words, the devas of the void were filled with exultation and passed the cry on from one to another until it reached the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Having heard it, all the devas rejoiced immeasurably and cried out in a loud voice:
"Today, the Tathāgata, in the land of Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages, has turned the Great Wheel of Dharma—
a wheel that none in all the world, whether devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, can turn."
At that time, the great earth shook in eighteen ways;
the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, performed various musical performances in the void, while celestial drums resounded spontaneously.
They burned various famous incenses, scattered myriad exquisite flowers, and offered praise through song and hymn, with precious banners, streamers, and canopies.
Within the world, there was spontaneous great illumination.
Among his disciples, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the foremost disciple because he was the first to attain awakening.
At that time, when those four, including Mahānāma, heard that the Buddha had turned the wheel of Dharma, Ājñātakauṇḍinya alone realized the path; he thought to himself:
"If the World-Honored One were to preach the Dharma for us once more, we too would surely realize the path."
Having formed this thought, he gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never for a moment turning away.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the four men, immediately expounded the Four Noble Truths for them once again in detail.
At that time, those four persons also became free from the dust and defilements regarding all phenomena and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
When those five persons had seen the path, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

We five have already seen the path and have already realized the path. We now wish to leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma; we only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant us permission."
Then the World-Honored One called out to those five men:
"Welcome, bhikṣus! Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robes were donned upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked those five men:
"O bhikṣus, do you know whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent or impermanent?"
Is this suffering or is it not suffering?
Is this empty or is it not empty? Does a self exist or does a self not exist?

When the five bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s teaching on these five aggregates, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated; they attained the fruit of arhatship and immediately replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are in truth impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Thereupon, for the first time in the world, there were six arhats; the Buddha as an arhat is the Jewel of the Buddha, and the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths is the Jewel of the Dharma.
The five types of Arhats constitute the Sangha Jewel;
thus, when these Three Jewels of the world are complete, they serve as the foremost field of merit for all devas and humans.

*The Sutra on Cause and Effect of Past and Present*, Scroll Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty:
"At that time, there was the son of an elder named Yaśas, who was intelligent, of keen faculties, and exceedingly great..."
He was immensely wealthy, the foremost in all of Jambudvīpa.
Adorned with celestial crowns and necklaces, and wearing priceless jeweled sandals, he amused himself in the middle of the night with various courtesans before they each returned to their rest.
Suddenly awakening from sleep, he saw the various courtesans; some were lying prostrate, while others slept on their backs;
their hair was disheveled and tangled, and saliva flowed from their mouths.
Musical instruments, garments, and playthings were strewn about in utter disorder;
having seen this, he conceived a mind of weary detachment and thought to himself:
"I am now within these calamities and monstrosities; amidst such impurity, I have falsely conceived the notion of purity."
While he was thinking this, by the power of the devas, a radiance appeared in the sky and the gate opened spontaneously; following the light, he departed for the Deer Park.
Passing by the Ganges River, he cried out in a loud voice:
"Alas! How strange!"
The Buddha said, "Yaśas!
You may come here; I now possess the Dharma for the cessation of suffering."
Having heard this, Yaśas immediately removed his precious sandals, which were worth as much as all of Jambudvīpa, and crossed the Ganges River to go to where the Buddha was.

Beholding the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his countenance preeminent and his majestic virtue complete, his heart was filled with great joy and he leaped for immeasurable delight. Prostrating himself on the ground with his five limbs, he bowed at the Buddha’s feet and said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will rescue and deliver me."
The Buddha said, "Excellent! Good son!"
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
The Tathāgata then taught the Dharma in accordance with his faculties, saying: "Yaśas!..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; do you understand this?
At that moment, upon hearing these words, Yaśas attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata again preached the Four Noble Truths; his outflows were exhausted, his mind was liberated, he attained mastery over his thoughts, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
He then replied to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are truly impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
At that time, the Tathāgata still saw Yaśas adorned with ornaments for the body, and he immediately spoke this verse:
"Though you dwell in a household, Wearing precious ornaments upon your body;..."
Well-restraining all the sense faculties, And feeling weary detachment toward the five desires;
One who can act in this way Is truly one who has gone forth.
Though the body may dwell in the wilderness And subsist on coarse and bitter food;
If the mind still craves the five desires, this is not true renunciation.
All that is created, whether good or evil, arises from the thoughts of the mind;
therefore, true renunciation takes the mind as its foundation.
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Tathāgata, Yaśas thought to himself:
"The reason the World-Honored One has spoken these verses is precisely because I am still wearing the seven-jeweled ornaments; I should now remove such garments."
He then prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! At these words, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, Yaśas’s father, when daybreak arrived, sought for Yaśas; not knowing where he was, his heart was filled with great anguish.
Wailing piteously and weeping with tears, he searched along the road until he reached the banks of the Ganges, where he saw his son’s sandals. He thought to himself:
"My son must have gone by this very path."
He immediately followed the tracks until he reached the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that [the father] had come here for the sake of his son, realized that if the man were to see Yaśas immediately, he would surely experience great suffering or perhaps die; thereupon, by means of his supernormal power, he concealed Yaśas’s body.
His father immediately went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, according to his faculties, preached the Dharma for him, saying: "Good son!..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; do you understand this?
When Yaśas’s father heard these words, he immediately became free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena and attained the pure Dharma-eye. He then replied to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are in truth impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
At that time, the Tathāgata, having already recognized that his views were directed toward the path of the stream-enterer and that his attachment was gradually diminishing, asked him:
"For what cause and condition have you come here?"
He immediately replied:

"I have a son named Yaśas, who suddenly disappeared during the night. This morning, while searching for him, I found his jeweled sandals by the side of the Ganges; following his footprints, I have come here."
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, whereupon the father was able to see Yaśas; his heart was filled with great joy, and he said to Yaśas: "Excellent!"
Excellent! That you have undertaken this matter is truly a source of joy; for you are able to deliver yourself and also deliver others.
Because you are here now, it has enabled me to come and perceive the tracks of the Path.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he received the three refuges.
Thus, within Jambudvīpa, this elder alone became the very first upāsaka to obtain the opportunity to make offerings to the Triple Gem.

At that time, there were fifty sons of elders who were companions of Yaśas. Hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world and further hearing that Yaśas had left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, they each thought to themselves:

"In this world there is now a Supreme Honored One. The elder’s son Yaśas was wise, eloquent, and possessed talents surpassing others; yet he was able to abandon his noble lineage and renounce the pleasures of the five desires, altering his appearance and maintaining his resolve to become a śramaṇa."
"What more do we have to look back upon or cling to that we would not go forth into homelessness?
Having had this thought, they went together to where the Buddha was.

Before they had arrived, they saw the Tathāgata from afar, his marks and signs exceptionally sublime and his radiance brilliantly blazing; their hearts were filled with great joy, their entire bodies felt refreshed and cool, and their feelings of reverence grew ever deeper.
They immediately went before the Buddha, joined their palms and circumambulated him, and prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.

These sons of elders, having planted roots of virtue in past lives, were intelligent and quick to understand; the Tathāgata then preached the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate for each:
"Sons of good family!..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; do you understand this?

When he had spoken these words, the sons of the elders, regarding all phenomena, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. They then replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are truly impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, “Welcome,
bhikṣu! His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One again preached the Four Noble Truths in detail for them.
Then fifty bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and minds liberated, attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that moment, there were fifty-six arhats in all.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus:

"You have accomplished what was to be done and are worthy to serve as the supreme field of merit for the world. You should each travel through various regions to teach and transform others, delivering all sentient beings with a heart of compassion;
I, too, shall now go alone to the kingdom of Magadha, to the city of Rājagṛha, to deliver the people there."
The bhikṣus said: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
At that time, the bhikṣus prostrated themselves at his feet, each taking up their robes and bowl, bidding him farewell and departing.
Then the World-Honored One reflected:
"Which sentient beings should I now deliver so that I may bring vast benefit to all humans and devas?"
There are only the three brothers, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his companions, who dwell in the kingdom of Magadha practicing the way of the rishis;
the king, ministers, and citizens all place their faith in them, and they are moreover intelligent, of sharp faculties, and quick to awaken.
Yet their pride is difficult to subdue; I shall now go there to deliver and liberate them.
Having reflected thus, he immediately set out from Vārāṇasī for the kingdom of Magadha; as the sun was about to set, he went to the dwelling place of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa.
At that time, Kāśyapa suddenly beheld the Tathāgata, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; his heart was filled with great joy, and he spoke these words:
"Young śramaṇa, from where have you come?"
The Buddha then replied:
"I am traveling from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to the kingdom of Magadha; as it is already late evening, I wish to stay the night here."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"As for providing lodging, there is no great objection; however, all the other rooms are occupied by my disciples.
There is only this stone chamber, which is extremely clean, though my implements for tending the sacrificial fire are all within it."
"This place of tranquility can accommodate you.
However, there is a malevolent dragon dwelling within it; I fear he might harm you!
The Buddha replied again:
"Although there is a wicked dragon, I shall lend it to you.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Its nature is fierce and violent; it will surely harm you. It is not that I am being stingy."
The Buddha replied again, "I shall simply lend it to you; there will certainly be no humiliation.
Kāśyapa spoke once more:
"If you are able to remain here, you may stay as you please.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
That very evening, he entered the stone chamber, sat down cross-legged, and entered samādhi.
At that time, the evil dragon’s poisonous heart grew even more intense, and smoke issued from its entire body.

The World-Honored One immediately entered the Fire-Light Samādhi. Upon seeing this, the dragon’s flames surged toward heaven, burning the stone cave. Kāśyapa’s disciples, having first seen this fire, returned and informed their master:
"That young śramaṇa, who was so intelligent and dignified, is now being consumed and harmed by the dragon's fire."
Kāśyapa rose in alarm and, seeing the dragon’s fire, was filled with grief;
he immediately commanded his disciples to douse it with water, but the water could not extinguish it—the fire grew even more fierce until the stone chamber was completely melted away.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained unmoving in body and mind, his countenance serene; he subdued that evil dragon, causing it to lose its venom, conferred upon it the Three Refuges, and placed it within his almsbowl.
When dawn had broken, Kāśyapa and his disciples went together to where the Buddha was and asked, "The young śramaṇa, the dragon’s fire was so fierce; could it not have been harmed by this?"
"The reason I did not lend my dwelling to the śramaṇa yesterday was precisely for this reason.
The Buddha said, "My inner nature is pure; I am ultimately not harmed by external calamities. That venomous dragon is now inside my bowl."
He then lifted up his alms-bowl to show it to Kāśyapa.

When Kāśyapa and his disciples saw that the śramaṇa remained unburned while in the midst of the fire, had subdued the evil dragon, and placed it within his bowl, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He said to his disciples,
"Though this young śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, he is nonetheless not equal to the true path of mine.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to Kāśyapa, saying:
"I now intend to remain here. Kāśyapa replied, "Excellent!"
"As you wish.
At that time, during the second night, the Tathāgata sat beneath a tree.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings came to the Buddha’s dwelling at night to listen to the Dharma together.
Each emitted a radiance that outshone both the sun and the moon.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and, seeing from afar a celestial light beside the Tathāgata, said to his disciples:
"This young śramaṇa also worships fire."
When dawn arrived the following day, he went to where the Buddha was and asked,
"Śramaṇa, do you tend the sacrificial fire?
The Buddha said:
"No, there are the Four Heavenly Kings who have come at night to listen to the Dharma;
it is their radiance. Thereupon, Kāśyapa said to his disciples:
"The young śramaṇa possesses great spiritual power, yet he still cannot match the truth of my Way.
On the third night, Śakra Devānām Indra descended to listen to the Dharma, emitting a great radiance like the rising sun.
A disciple of Kāśyapa, seeing from afar the celestial light beside the Tathāgata, addressed his teacher, saying:
"This young śramaṇa must surely be one who serves the fire."
When morning came, he went to where the Buddha was and asked the śramaṇa,
"Are you certain that you serve fire?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. Śakra Devānām Indra has descended to listen to the Dharma; this is merely his radiance.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke to his disciples, saying:
"The young śramaṇa’s spiritual virtue is indeed magnificent, yet it still does not equal the true reality of my Way.
On the fourth night, the Great Brahmā King descended to listen to the Dharma;
he emitted a great radiance like that of the sun at its zenith.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw a radiance beside the Tathāgata, thinking, "This śramaṇa must certainly be attending to the sacred fire.
The next day, he asked the Buddha,
"You surely attend to the fire?"
The Buddha said, "No.
It is the radiance of Mahābrahmā, who came last night to listen to the Dharma."
Thereupon, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although this young śramaṇa possesses such spiritual wonders, he is nevertheless not equal to the truth of my own Way."
At that time, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples, each of whom tended three fires, all wished to kindle them at dawn; however, the fires refused to ignite.
They all went to Kāśyapa and reported this matter in detail.
Having heard this, Kāśyapa thought to himself,
"This must surely be the work of the śramaṇa.
He then went with his disciples to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"My disciples each serve three fires; this morning they wished to kindle them, but the fires would not ignite.
The Buddha immediately replied, "You may return; the fires shall ignite spontaneously."
Kāśyapa then returned and saw that the fire was already ablaze;
he thought to himself, "Although this young śramaṇa possesses such spiritual wonders, he still does not equal the truth of my own Way."
When the assembly of disciples had finished making offerings to the fire and wished to extinguish it, they were unable to do so;
they immediately went to Kāśyapa and recounted this matter in detail.
Having heard this, Kāśyapa thought to himself,
"This too must be the work of the śramaṇa.
He then went with his disciples to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"My disciples wished to extinguish the fire this morning, yet the fire would not go out.
The Buddha replied, "You may return; the fire shall extinguish itself."
Kāśyapa then returned and saw that the fire had already been extinguished;
he thought to himself, "Although this young śramaṇa possesses such spiritual wonders, he still does not equal the truth of my own Way."

Śakra Devānām Indra, immediately understanding the Buddha’s intention, descended from the heavens in the time it takes a mighty man to bend and extend his arm. Arriving before the Buddha, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet;
he then pointed to the ground with his finger, creating a pool whose water was pure and possessed the eight meritorious qualities, which the Tathāgata then took and used.
Having finished washing and rinsing his mouth, he preached various dharmas for Śakra Devānām Indra.
Once Śakra Devānām Indra had heard the Dharma, he leaped for joy;
suddenly vanishing from sight, he returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, after the midday meal, Kāśyapa was walking in meditation among the trees.
He thought to himself:
"The young śramaṇa has finished his meal today and returned to the foot of the tree; I shall go there to see him."

Astonished, he asked the Buddha, "How is it that this pond has suddenly appeared here?"

having finished my meal, I require water for rinsing and washing my bowl."
“Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing my intention, came from the heavens and pointed to the ground with his finger, thereby forming this pond.

"At that time, on another day, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation among the trees when he saw some worn-out rags amidst the filth. He immediately picked them up, intending to wash them;

"Now I must have water.

Marvelling at this, he asked the Buddha, “For what reason do the branches of this tree bend down to provide shade?”

Thereupon, Kāśyapa, seeing the tree with its branches bent and hearing the Buddha’s words, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and thought to himself:

Excellent! How delightful!

Recently, you thought in your heart that you did not wish to see me; for this reason, I went to the northern continent of Uttarakuru merely to avoid you.

The Buddha then replied:

At that time, having heard these words from his disciples, Kāśyapa immediately went together with them to the place where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:

The Buddha said, “Welcome,

Upon hearing this teaching, Kāśyapa was freed from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye, and gradually progressed until he became an Arhat.

At that time, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples, having seen that their teacher had already become a śramaṇa, felt a heart of aspiration and joy, desiring likewise to leave the household life. They immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:

we too wish to follow our teacher's example in study. We only pray that the Great Sage will grant us permission to leave the household life."
The Buddha said, "Welcome,
Bhikṣu. His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One turned for them the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, five hundred disciples were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye and realizing the fruit of Srotāpanna;
through gradual cultivation, they eventually attained the fruit of Arhatship as well.
At that time, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples took all their various implements for fire-worship and cast them entirely into the Nairañjanā River;
then master and disciples together followed the Buddha and departed.

"At that time, Kāśyapa had two younger brothers: the first was named Nadī-Kāśyapa and the second was named Gayā-Kāśyapa. Each had two hundred and fifty disciples, and they resided on the banks of the Nairañjanā River downstream from their elder brother."
Suddenly he saw his elder brother along with his disciples and all the implements for worshipping fire being carried down by the current.
Greatly startled, he thought to himself:
"What ill omen has befallen my brother now that these fire-worship implements are following the flow of the water? Could it be that he has been harmed by some evil person?"
At that time, the two younger brothers rushed toward one another and consulted together, saying:
"If our elder brother has not been harmed by evil men this time, for what reason have these various objects come up from the water?"
Alas! How strange! We should quickly go together to our elder brother's place.
They then proceeded together upstream until they reached their elder brother’s dwelling, which was empty and silent, with no one there.
Their hearts were filled with overwhelming grief; they did not know where their brother and his disciples had gone.
Searching in all four directions, he encountered an old acquaintance and asked him, saying:
"I do not know the whereabouts of my venerable brother, the seer-sage, nor his disciples."
"Did you see them? The elder replied, "Your venerable brother,
the sage, together with his disciples, has abandoned his fire-offering implements and gone entirely to the place of Gautama to leave the household life and study the Way."
At that time, having heard these words, the two younger brothers were deeply distressed and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
They further thought to themselves:
"How can he abandon the path of Arhatship and seek yet another, different dharma?"
He immediately galloped to where his elder brother was.
Upon arrival, he saw that his brother and his attendants had shaved their hair and beards and were clad in *kāṣāya* robes; he then knelt and prostrated himself, asking his brother:

"Brother, you were originally a great *arhat*, possessed of such brilliant wisdom that none could equal you, and your fame resounded throughout the ten directions, such that all revered and looked up to you."
"Why have you now abandoned this path yourself and returned to learn from others?
This is no small matter.
At that time, Kāśyapa replied to his younger brother:
"I have observed that the World-Honored One has accomplished great kindness and great compassion, possessing three extraordinary qualities:
first, his supernormal powers and transformations;
second, his wisdom-mind, which is pure and transparent, having definitively accomplished all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
Third, he well understands the faculties of others and accordingly guides and receives them.
For this reason, he has left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.

Although I am now a king whose views are honored by ministers and subjects, and whose worldly eloquence and skillful debate cannot be refuted by anyone, this is not the Dharma that eternally cuts off birth and death.
Only that which the Tathāgata has expounded can bring an end to birth and death.
To encounter such a Great Sage and yet fail to exert oneself, failing to take him as one's supreme teacher, is to be without mind and without eyes.
The two younger brothers said, "If it is as our elder brother says, then this will certainly result in the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Everything we have known and attained is due to our brother's power; since you have now gone forth from home under the Buddha, we also wish to follow and train according to your example."
They then each said to their respective disciples:
"We now wish to follow our elder brother and leave the household life to study the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
What do you think?"
At that time, the disciples replied to their teacher, saying:
"The reason we have attained knowledge and vision is entirely due to the grace of our great teacher.
If you, Great Teacher, wish to go forth from home within the Buddha-dharma, we also pray to follow you."
Thereupon, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, each accompanied by two hundred and fifty disciples, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, we pray only that you will compassionately pity us and deliver us.”
The Buddha said, "Welcome,
bhikṣu. His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Then Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Our disciples now all wish to leave the household life and go forth in the Buddha’s Dharma; we only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and grant them permission."
The Buddha then replied: "Excellent! Excellent!"
At that time, the World-Honored One called out,
"Welcome, bhikṣu! His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robe appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested great supernatural transformations for Nadi-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and their disciples;
furthermore, in accordance with their minds, he preached the Dharma to them, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."
You should know that the world is all scorched and roasted by the fierce fires of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Since you have already been able to sever and abandon these three fires in the past, you must now eliminate these external afflictions as well.
"Now the fires of the three poisons still remain within your bodies; you ought to extinguish them quickly.
When the bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they became free from dust and defilement regarding all dharmas and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The World-Honored One further expounded the Four Noble Truths in detail for them, and they all attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"In the past, King Bimbisāra made a solemn vow before me: [If I attain enlightenment, you shall be my foremost lay disciple]."
"If the Way is realized, I pray that you will be the first to cross over.
"Now the time has come; it is fitting that I go there to fulfill his original vow.
Having formed this thought, he immediately set out for Rājagṛha with the Kāśyapa brothers and a retinue of a thousand bhikṣus, surrounding him, and approached King Bimbisāra.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, who had formerly granted a village to Uruvilvākāśyapa,
upon seeing that Kāśyapa and all his disciples had become śramaṇas, immediately returned to inform the king, recounting these events.
When the king and his ministers heard these words, their hearts were greatly struck with wonder and astonishment; they remained silent and speechless.
At that time, the people outside also heard these words.
They said to one another:
"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching; there is no one equal to him.
He is also advanced in years and has already attained arhatship. How is it that he has instead become a disciple of Gautama?"
"Ultimately, such a principle does not exist; one may only say that the śramaṇa Gautama is merely a disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually approached Rājagṛha and stayed at the Śāla Grove.
Then Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa immediately dispatched his usual messenger to say to King Bimbisāra:
"I have now gone forth within the Buddha’s Dharma to practice the Path."
"Now, having followed the Buddha, we have arrived at Śāṇa-vaṇa.
Great King, you should first pay him homage and make offerings.

Upon hearing these words from the messenger, the king definitively realized that Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa had become a disciple of the Buddha; he immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and, accompanied by his ministers, Brahmins, and the multitude of commoners, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the Śāla Grove, the king descended from his carriage, removed his royal regalia, and proceeded on foot to the presence of the Buddha.
At that time, a deva in the sky addressed the king, saying:
"The Tathāgata is now within this grove; he is the supreme field of merit for all devas and humans. Your Majesty should pay him respectful homage and make offerings."
"Furthermore, you should proclaim this to the people of the kingdom, ensuring that they all make offerings to the Tathāgata.
When the king had heard these words from the deva, his heart was filled with great joy, and he leaped for joy all the more.
He then proceeded into the forest and saw from afar the Tathāgata, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
he also saw Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his two brothers, together with their disciples, surrounding him before and behind.

Like the full moon amidst the host of stars, he leaped with joy at every step, unable to contain his exuberance. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated himself, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, do you know me? I am King Bimbisāra of Magadha, of the Lunar Lineage.”
The Buddha replied, "Excellent,
Great King! Thereupon, King Bimbisāra withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the brahmins, the great ministers, and the multitude of people all took their seats.
When the World-Honored One saw that the assembled crowd was comfortably seated,
he addressed King Bimbisāra with a Brahma-voice, saying:
"Great King! Are the four great elements ever peaceful and secure?
In governing the affairs of the people, are you not perhaps overburdened with toil?"
The King immediately replied, "By the grace of the World-Honored One, I have fortunately attained peace and security.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, along with other great learned brahmins, householders, lay devotees, ministers, and the common people, having seen that Kāśyapa had become a disciple of the Buddha, said to one another:
"Alas! The Tathāgata possesses great supernormal power and profound wisdom that is inconceivable; he is thus able to subdue such a person as this and take him as a disciple."
At that time, there were yet other people who thought to themselves:
"Uruvilvā Kāśyapa possesses great wisdom and is universally revered and trusted by the people of the world; how could he become a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama?"
His mind was filled with doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, spoke to Kāśyapa:
"You should now manifest various supernatural transformations."
At that time, Kāśyapa ascended into the air; from his upper body he emitted water and from his lower body he emitted fire;
from his upper body he emitted fire and from his lower body he emitted water;
or he manifested a massive body that filled the entirety of space.
Or again, they manifest as small;
or they divide a single body into immeasurable bodies;
or they manifest entering the earth and then leaping back out.
In the midst of the void, he walked, stood, sat, and lay down.
When the entire assembly saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and all exclaimed:
"The Great Supreme Rishi!"

At that time, after Kāśyapa had manifested this transformation, he descended from the air and arrived before the Buddha. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are truly the Teacher of gods and humans; I am now truly your disciple.”
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha then replied: "So it is, so it is!"
“Kāśyapa! What benefit do you see in my Dharma that you have abandoned your fire implements and gone forth?
Thereupon Kāśyapa replied in verse:
"By the merit of serving the sacrificial fire in days of yore,
I was born among gods and humans, and experienced the pleasures of the five senses."
Thus one revolves perpetually, drowning in the ocean of birth and death;
seeing these faults and calamities, I have therefore abandoned it.
Furthermore, through the merit of serving fire, one may be reborn among gods and humans.
It increases greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, I have abandoned it.
Furthermore, the merit of serving fire is for the sake of seeking future birth;
since there is already birth, there will inevitably be old age, sickness, and death.
Having seen these matters as they truly are, I have therefore abandoned the practice of fire-worship.
Though the merit of performing sacrificial assemblies and practicing austerities, as well as serving the sacrificial fire,
may lead to rebirth in the Brahma Heaven, this is not the ultimate state.
For these reasons, I have abandoned the practice of fire-worship.
Having seen the Dharma of the Tathāgata— the state that transcends birth, old age, sickness, and death,
the ultimate place of liberation— I have therefore gone forth into homelessness.
The Tathāgata’s true liberation makes him the teacher of gods and humans;
for this reason, I take refuge in the Great Holy Honored One.
The Tathāgata, with great compassion, manifests various skillful means.
"And by means of your various supernormal powers, you have guided me;
how could I possibly continue to serve the rites of fire?

At that time, King Bimbisāra and the great assembly, having heard these verses spoken by Uruvilvākāśyapa, were filled with great joy. They conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Tathāgata, becoming certain that the Tathāgata would surely attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and they clearly recognized that Kāśyapa was indeed a disciple of the Buddha.
At that time, the various devas in the void rained down a multitude of celestial flowers and performed exquisite music, singing with one voice in unison: "Excellent!"
"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa has spoken this verse most excellently.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the minds of the great assembly were resolved and free from further doubt, and observing that their faculties were all fully matured, immediately preached the Dharma for them:
"Great King, you should know!"
This body of the five aggregates has consciousness as its basis.
Because of consciousness, the faculty of mind arises;
because of the faculty of mind, form arises.
Moreover, this material form arises and perishes without ceasing.
Great King!
If one can contemplate in this way, then one will be well able to know impermanence regarding the body.
Contemplating the body in this manner, one does not grasp at the characteristics of the body; thus, one can become detached from the self and what belongs to the self.
If one can contemplate form and become detached from the self and what belongs to the self, one will know that the arising of form is itself the arising of suffering.
If one knows that the cessation of form is itself the cessation of suffering,
and if a person can cultivate such an observation, this is called liberation.
If a person cannot cultivate this observation, this is called bondage.
The Dharma is fundamentally without self or what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
Due to inverted perceptions, one falsely conceives of a self and what belongs to a self; yet no such real phenomena exist.
If one can sever these inverted delusions and perceptions, that is liberation.
At that time, King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
"If one says of sentient beings that there is a self, it is called bondage."
"All sentient beings are entirely without self.
Since there is no self, who is it that receives the retribution of karmic results?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying:
"Regarding all sentient beings, the good and evil they perform, as well as the karmic retributions they receive, none are created by me, nor are they received by me.
Yet, there currently exist those who perform good and evil and receive their retributions. Great King, listen attentively; I shall explain this for you."
"Great King!
It is simply because the mind, the sense objects, and consciousness conjoin that defilement arises toward objects, and accumulated thoughts proliferate.
For this reason, one wanders through birth and death, fully experiencing the retribution of suffering."
If one is unstained by objects and brings to rest the thoughts of affliction, then one attains liberation.

Through the causal conditions of the three factors—sentiment, sense-objects, and consciousness—one collectively gives rise to good and evil and undergoes their retributive fruits; there is no separate self apart from these.
It is like drilling for fire: by means of the hand turning the fire-drill, fire is produced.
Yet the nature of that fire does not arise from the hand nor emerge from the drill, and yet it is not separate from the hand and the drilling of the drill.
“Those sense objects, faculties, and consciousnesses are likewise. Then King Bimbisāra further reflected:

“If it is because of the conjunction of the sense objects, faculties, and consciousness that there is the experience of the retribution of good and evil, then they would be eternally conjoined and should not be separated.”
"If they were not constantly joined, this would constitute annihilation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the king's thoughts, replied:
"These mental objects, sense faculties, and consciousnesses are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation."
Why is this? Because through conjunction there is no annihilation, and through separation there is no permanence.
It is like depending upon earth and water, and with that seed as a cause, sprouts and leaves arise.
Since the seed has already perished, it cannot be called permanent;
since it produces sprouts and leaves, it cannot be called annihilated.
Because it is free from both annihilation and permanence, it is called the Middle Way.
"The causal conditions for these three matters are likewise thus.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard this Dharma, his mind opened and his understanding was clarified;
regarding all phenomena, he became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Eighty thousand nayutas of brahmins, ministers, and commoners also attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement.
Furthermore, nine million six hundred thousand nayutas of devas also attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement.
At that time, King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“How wonderful!
World-Honored One!”
He was able to renounce the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, leave the household life to study the Way, and attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

In the past, I was foolish and wished to detain the World-Honored One to govern a small kingdom; now that I behold his compassionate countenance and have heard the True Dharma, I am filled with shame and remorse for my past transgressions.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, will accept my repentance.
In the past, I said to the World-Honored One:
"When you attain the Way, I pray that you will deliver me first."
"Today, at last, my long-cherished vow has been fulfilled.
Grateful for the World-Honored One’s grace, I have attained the fruits of the Path.
From this day forward, I shall provide offerings to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, ensuring that the four requisites never lack for them."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain at the Bamboo Grove, so that the kingdom of Magadha may enjoy peace for a long night.
The Buddha then replied, “Excellent!”
"Great King!
You are indeed able to renounce these three non-solid things and seek the three solid rewards;
thus, may the King's wishes be fulfilled."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation to stay at the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
Once the king had returned to the city, he immediately commanded his ministers to construct various halls and dwellings within the Bamboo Grove.

Having adorned it in various ways to make it exceedingly magnificent, and having hung silk banners and canopies, scattered flowers, and burned incense—all these preparations being complete—he then prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The repairs to the Veṇuvana Monastery are now finished."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will go and reside there together with the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the bhikṣus and immeasurable devas in front and behind, entered the city of Rājagṛha.
When the Tathāgata stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the musical instruments within the city sounded of their own accord without being struck;
the narrow gates became wider and the gateways became higher;
all mounds and ruins were entirely leveled and made smooth.
Foul odors and impurities naturally become fragrant and pure;
the deaf regain their hearing, the mute are able to speak,
the blind regain their sight, and the insane regain their sanity.
All ailments and chronic diseases were universally healed;
withered trees burst into bloom, and decaying grass flourished and grew lush;
parched ponds surged with waves, and fragrant breezes blew gently and purely.

Phoenixes, sparrows, peacocks, and emeralds; wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks—birds of diverse species gathered in profusion, fluttering and assembling while emitting harmonious and elegant sounds;
such were the various auspicious omens.
Having entered the city, he went together with King Bimbisāra to the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the devas filled the void of space;
then the king immediately took a precious vessel in his hand, filled it with scented water, and before the Tathāgata spoke these words:
"I now offer this Bamboo Grove to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus; I only pray that you will compassionately accept it for my sake.
Having spoken these words, he immediately released the water.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted [the offering] in silence and spoke these verses as a prayer of blessing:
“If a person can practice giving, they will sever stinginess and greed;
If a person can practice patience, they will forever leave behind anger and hatred.”
If a person can perform wholesome deeds, they will remain far removed from folly;
by being able to fulfill these three practices, one will swiftly reach parinirvāṇa.
If there is a poor person who has no wealth to give as an offering;
"When seeing others practicing generosity, one should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
the karmic reward of such sympathetic joy is equal to that of the act of giving itself.
At that time, the brahmin minister and the other people, seeing the king offer a monastery to the Tathāgata, all leaped for joy and gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having offered the monastery to the Saṃgha, was filled with great joy; he prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet and withdrew to his residence.
Among all the kings in Jambudvīpa who have seen the Buddha, King Bimbisāra is the foremost.
Among all the monasteries, the Bamboo Grove Monastery was the very first.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling with the bhikṣus at the Bamboo Grove Monastery;
meanwhile, in the city of Rājagṛha, there were two brahmins who were clever, of sharp faculties, and possessed great wisdom.
He was thoroughly proficient in all scriptures and treatises; in debate and discussion, none could defeat him.
He belonged to the Kauṣṭhila clan and was named Upatiṣya; because his mother’s name was Śārī, the whole world called him Śāriputra.
The two sages were Maudgalyāyana and Maṅkhaliputra;
each had one hundred disciples who were universally revered by the people of the land.
The two men were mutual friends, holding one another in the highest esteem, and they both made a solemn vow together:
"If you have previously heard any of the sublime Dharmas, you must certainly enlighten one another; do not be stingy or withholding.
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. He had well-restrained his sense faculties, and his deportment was dignified and orderly;
all who saw him on the road gave rise to reverence.
At that time, Śāriputra suddenly encountered Aśvajit by the wayside; the latter had his sense faculties well-restrained and his deportment was dignified and orderly.

As Śāriputra’s roots of goodness were already mature, upon seeing Aśvajit, his heart was filled with great joy; his entire body leaped with exultation, and he stood still gazing at him, unable to look away for even a moment.
Even if one were to ask:
"In my view, you appear to have newly gone forth from home, yet you are able to thus restrain all the sensory faculties.
I wish to ask something; I only pray that you will grant me an answer."
"What is the name of your Great Teacher now?
What instructions does he give, and what Dharma does he proclaim?
At that time, Aśvajit replied to him calmly and composedly:
"My Great Teacher has attained all-knowledge; he is of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the teacher of gods and humans, whose marks and signs, wisdom, and supernormal powers are peerless."
"I am still young and have but recently begun my study of the Way; how could I possibly proclaim the wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata?
Nevertheless, according to what I do know, I shall speak for you.
He then spoke these verses:
“The root of all phenomena arises through causes and conditions and has no master;
if one can understand this, one will attain the true path.”
When Śāriputra had heard these verses spoken by Aśvajit, he immediately became free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the path of the Dharma, his heart leaped with great joy; all his sensory faculties were filled with delight, and he thought to himself:
"All sentient beings are attached to a self, and it is because of this that they wander in saṃsāra within birth and death."
If one eliminates the notion of a self, one will likewise become free from all that belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
Just as sunlight can dispel darkness, so too the notion of non-self can completely destroy the obscuration of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
"Whatever I have practiced and studied from the past has all been based on false views;
only that which I have now attained is the true and correct path.
Having formed this thought, he prostrated at the feet of Aśvajit and returned to his dwelling.
At that time, Aśvajit went before [the Buddha] to beg for alms, and having finished, returned to the Bamboo Grove.
Meanwhile, Śāriputra returned to his own dwelling.

Then, Maudgalyāyana, whose roots of goodness were already mature, saw that Śāriputra’s faculties were tranquil and settled, his deportment was dignified and orderly, and his countenance was serene and joyful, unlike on any other day.
Even if one were to ask:
"I observe you now; your faculties and countenance differ from what they usually are; you must have already attained the wondrous Dharma of the Deathless."
"In the past, we made a solemn vow together that if either of us heard the wondrous Dharma, we would certainly inform and awaken the other.
Since you have attained something, I pray that you will speak of it for my sake.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately replied:
"I have now truly attained the Dharma of the Deathless.
Having heard this, Maudgalyāyana was filled with immeasurable joy and exclaimed, "Excellent!"
"Please explain this to me at that time.

Śāriputra said, "Just now, as I was going out, I encountered a bhikṣu carrying his robes and bowl, entering a village to beg for food; his faculties were tranquil and his deportment was dignified and composed."
Having seen him, I conceived deep reverence; approaching his presence, I asked him:
"In my observation, you appear to have newly left the household life, yet you are able to restrain your sensory faculties in such a manner."
I wish to ask something; I pray that you will grant me an answer.
What is the name of your current teacher?
What instructions do you provide, and what Dharma do you expound?
Then Aśvajit, remaining composed and calm, replied:
"My Great Teacher has attained all-knowledge; he is of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the teacher of gods and humans."
"In his physical marks and signs, wisdom, and supernormal powers, there is no one equal to him.
Since I am young and have but recently begun my study of the Way, how could I possibly proclaim the Tathāgata’s sublime Dharma?"
"Nevertheless, based on what I know, I shall explain it for you.
He then spoke in verse:
"The root of all phenomena Arises from causes and conditions; there is no master."
"If one can understand this, one shall immediately attain the true path.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana became free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having each attained the nectar of the Buddha-dharma, said to one another:
"We have both obtained benefit within the Buddha-dharma; it is now fitting that we go together to the Buddha's presence to seek ordination."
Having spoken these words, they each summoned their disciples and said to them:
"We have now, within the Buddha-dharma, attained the flavor of the Deathless; this alone is the path that transcends the world."
"I now wish to go seek the Buddha and leave the household life.
What do you think? His disciples replied to their teacher:
"What we now know and perceive is entirely due to the power of our Great Master.
If the Master renounces the world, we shall all follow him.
Thereupon, the two men, leading their two hundred disciples, went to the Bamboo Grove.

Having entered the gate, he saw from afar the Tathāgata, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of bhikṣus; his heart was filled with great joy, and his entire body leaped for gladness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had arrived together with their disciples, addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that these two men, leading their disciples, have come to my presence desiring to leave the household life."
One is named Śāriputra, and the other is named Maudgalyāyana;
they shall be the foremost disciples within my Dharma.
Of these, Śāriputra shall be the most preeminent in wisdom.
"Maudgalyāyana is, among those with supernormal powers, unsurpassed.
Having arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Within the Buddha’s Dharma, I have already attained the fruit of the path; I desire to leave the household life and pray that you will grant me permission at this time."
At that time, the World-Honored One called out to him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu.
His hair and beard fell away naturally, the kāṣāya robe appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, when those two hundred disciples saw that their teacher had become a śramaṇa, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We also wish to follow our teacher and leave the household life; we only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and grant us permission."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One called out to him again,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the kāṣāya robe was donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths for Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; the two men immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Furthermore, for those two hundred disciples, he extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths; immediately regarding all phenomena, they became free from dust and defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and even achieved the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus—all of whom were great arhats—was extensively benefiting sentient beings in the kingdom of Magadha.
Among the bhikṣus, there were many whose names were Maudgalyāyana; therefore, the World-Honored One designated this Maudgalyāyana as Mahāmaudgalyāyana (the Great Maudgalyāyana).

“At that time, in the kingdom of Thūlakoṭṭhaka, there was a brahmin named Kāśyapa who possessed the thirty-two marks. He was intelligent and wise, having recited the four Vedas; he was thoroughly proficient in all books and treatises, extremely wealthy, and skilled in the practice of giving.”
His wife was so exceptionally beautiful that she was peerless throughout the entire kingdom.
Yet, the two of them naturally lacked any desire for sensual pleasure; they did not even share a single room for sleeping.
Because they had planted roots of goodness long ago in the past, they took no delight in living as householders or experiencing the pleasures of the five senses.
Day and night he contemplated with weariness and detachment toward the world, diligently seeking the way of renunciation.
Having searched in this manner without success, he abandoned his household affairs and entered the mountain forests, thinking in his heart and speaking with his mouth:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, left the home life to cultivate the Way; I too shall now follow the Buddhas and leave the home life."
He immediately cast off his precious robe woven with golden threads, worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold, and donned a dyed, coarse hempen garment, then shaved his own beard and hair.
At that time, the devas, having seen Kāśyapa leave the household life for the religious path from within the midst of the void,
spoke to him, saying:
"O son of good family!

Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the son of King Śuddhodana named Sarvārthasiddha left the household life to study the Way, attained all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā), and is universally known as Śākyamuni Buddha.
"I am now with twelve hundred and fifty arhats, dwelling in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha.
When Kāśyapa heard these words from the deva, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his hair stood on end, and he immediately set out for the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that [the Buddha-to-be] was coming, reflected to himself:
"Observing his roots of goodness, it is fitting that I go to deliver him.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went out to meet him at Upatishya and encountered Kāśyapa.
At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One’s physical marks, excellence, and deportment were exceptionally venerable, Kāśyapa immediately joined his palms and spoke these words:
“The World-Honored One is truly the One Possessing All-Knowledge; he is truly compassionate, the savior of sentient beings; he is truly the refuge for all.”
He then prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are now my Great Teacher;
I am your disciple.”
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha then replied:
"It is so, Kāśyapa; I am your teacher."
"You are my disciple.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that if anyone who is not truly possessed of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) were to wish to accept you as his disciple, his head would split into seven pieces."
Again he addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Kāśyapa! How wonderful, Kāśyapa!"
"You should know that this body of the five aggregates of clinging is a great mass of suffering.
At that time, having heard these words, Kāśyapa immediately attained the vision of the truths and eventually realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned with Kāśyapa to the Bamboo Grove.
Because this Kāśyapa possessed great majestic virtue, wisdom, and intelligence, he was therefore named Mahākāśyapa (Great Kāśyapa).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When the Tathāgata Samantaraśmi appeared in the world, was the seer Suprajñā anyone else? [It was none other than me.]”
I am that very person.

As for the five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners whom I encountered on the road with whom I debated, and those who rejoiced in it, they are now the brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his kin, these one thousand bhikṣus in this assembly.
The flower-seller at that time was none other than the present Yaśodharā.

When the Seer Supuṣpacandra spread his hair upon the ground, there were two men nearby sweeping the ground before the Buddha, as well as two hundred people who followed with sympathetic joy; these are now Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and their two hundred disciples among the monks in this assembly.

The devas of the void, seeing the seer Suprabuddha spread his hair upon the ground, all rejoiced and offered praise; these were the eighty thousand devaputras, King Bimbisāra and his retinue of eighty thousand nayutas of people, and nine million six hundred thousand nayutas of devas, who, when I first attained the Way in the Deer Park and began to turn the Wheel of Dharma, likewise rejoiced and praised me.
"You should know that the causes sown in the past do not perish, even after the passage of immeasurable kalpas.
Because I, in former times, diligently cultivated all wholesome deeds and made great vows with a mind that never regressed, I have now attained the realization of all-knowledge."
"You all should diligently cultivate the path of practice; do not be indolent.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received it with joy and reverence, prostrated themselves, and withdrew.
The Sutra on the Causes and Effects of Past and Present, Scroll Four.
